The rectangles marched across the continent for the next century, ignoring rivers, hills, and everyone already living there. From an airplane over the Midwest today, the 1785 grid is still the visible shape of the country.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Clearing unleashed" -->
Independence voided the King's tree reservations, and clearing accelerated as settlement crossed the Appalachians into the new survey squares. The settlers' journeys belong to `migration`; the axe-work belongs here.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ebenezer-mudgett" name="Ebenezer Mudgett" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Ebenezer Mudgett
> **Who:** a sawmill owner in Weare, New Hampshire, fined for cutting the King's white pines. · **When and where:** the Pine Tree Riot, Weare, April 14, 1772.
Sheriff Benjamin Whiting rode into South Weare on April 13 with a warrant; Mudgett promised to pay in the morning. At dawn he came back with 20 to 30 men, faces blackened with soot, who beat the sheriff and his deputy with rods and drove them out of town. The rioters got off with small fines, the mast law went unenforced afterward, and some historians credit the riot as a forerunner of the Boston Tea Party a year and a half later — an ordinary mill owner, a tree law, and one of the first open fights over who owns American trees.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ebenezer-mudgett" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="land-environment" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Rivers and forests were put to work at industrial scale — and the first American voices said out loud that something was being lost. Both things are true of this era at once: the East hit its barest, and the argument for keeping some land wild was born.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dams stop the fish" -->
Mill and factory dams walled off the rivers. The first dam across the Connecticut (Turners Falls, 1798) cut salmon off from their spawning water — by the War of 1812 no salmon entered the river. The Great Stone Dam at Lawrence (1847–48) blocked the Merrimack 30 miles from the sea. Atlantic salmon were gone from southern New England rivers by 1865, and the shad runs that had fed towns every spring collapsed with them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The bare East" -->
By 1850 an estimated 60 to 80 percent of New England was cleared (estimates vary — some put the remaining forest as low as a quarter); one driver with a number was sheep — about 4 million in New England by 1840 eating pastures that had been woods. Eastern forest cover bottomed out around 1872 at roughly half its 1620 extent. Wood was still fuel, fencing, and building material; the forest was being spent like money.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="First voices" -->
The painter George Catlin, watching the bison and the Plains nations from the upper Missouri in 1832, proposed "a nation's park" to keep both — forty years before anyone built one. Audubon painted the birds while they were still uncountable; Thoreau moved to a pond to see what was left of the wild close to home.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-james-audubon" name="John James Audubon" movie="John James Audubon: Drawn from Nature (2007)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John James Audubon
> **Who:** painter and naturalist; *The Birds of America* — 435 life-size bird portraits, published 1827–1838, about 18 years of work. · **When and where:** the American frontier and Atlantic cities, 1785–1851. · **Movie:** *John James Audubon: Drawn from Nature* (PBS American Masters, 2007).
In 1813, riding toward Louisville, he passed under a single passenger-pigeon flock that darkened the sky for three days; his own arithmetic made it more than a billion birds. He painted species that readers of his book would outlive — his pigeon plate is one of the few windows on a bird no one alive has seen.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-james-audubon" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="henry-david-thoreau" name="Henry David Thoreau" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Henry David Thoreau
> **Who:** writer, and a working land surveyor — the man who argued for wild land measured woodlots for a living. · **When and where:** Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts, July 4, 1845 to September 6, 1847 — two years, two months, two days in a cabin he built himself.
*Walden* (published 1854) made the case that a life could be measured by something other than what it cleared, built, and earned — and that the wild remnants close to town were worth keeping. Later conservationists from Muir onward read him first.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="henry-david-thoreau" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="land-environment" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The half-century of the biggest taking — the bison brought from tens of millions to hundreds, the passenger pigeon from billions toward zero — and, in the same decades, the invention of protection as public policy: the first national park, the first forest reserves, the first conservation club with lawyers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The bison slaughter" -->
Roughly 30 million bison in the early 1800s; fewer than 1,000 by 1900 — one 1884 count found 325. The transcontinental railroad (1869) carried hide hunters out and hides back; a good team killed dozens a day for dollar-or-two hides; the Army encouraged it because the herds fed the Plains nations' independence. What the collapse did to those nations is `native-nations`' telling; ours is the animal and the grassland — an ecosystem's keystone shot out from under it in one generation.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The pigeon collapse" -->
Peak population an estimated 3 to 5 billion — possibly four of every ten North American birds. The 1871 Wisconsin nesting held an estimated 136 million breeding birds across 850 square miles. At Petoskey, Michigan in 1878, professional netters worked one of the last great nestings at a reported 50,000 birds a day for months, shipping barrels to city markets by rail while the telegraph told hunters where every new nesting was. By the mid-1890s the wild flocks were effectively gone. The finish arrives in the next era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Protection invented" -->
- Yosemite Grant, June 30, 1864: Lincoln signed the first federal set-aside of land for preservation and public use (given to California to manage; national park 1890).
- Yellowstone, March 1, 1872: Grant signed the act making it the first national park — kept by the federal government "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people."
- George Perkins Marsh's *Man and Nature* (1864) argued civilizations fall when they destroy their forests and soils; it helped produce the Forest Reserve Act of 1891, the start of the national forests.
- The Sierra Club, founded May 28, 1892, John Muir its first president — citizens organized to defend land in courts and Congress.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-muir" name="John Muir" movie="John Muir in the New World (2011)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Muir
> **Who:** Scotland-born wanderer, writer, and campaigner; the loudest American voice for keeping wild land wild. · **When and where:** California's Sierra Nevada from 1868; Sierra Club president 1892–1914. · **Movie:** *John Muir in the New World* (PBS American Masters, 2011).
His magazine pieces turned Yosemite's valleys and sequoias into a national cause and helped make Yosemite a national park (1890). He believed wild places had worth beyond board-feet and acre-prices — the position that would lose its biggest fight, at Hetch Hetchy, in the next era.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-muir" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frank-mayer" name="Frank Mayer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Frank Mayer
> **Who:** a buffalo runner — one of the professional hide hunters — from 1872 to 1878. · **When and where:** the southern Plains; died Fairplay, Colorado, 1954, at a reported 104.
His memoir *The Buffalo Harvest* (told at about age 100, published 1958) lays out the trade's arithmetic — rifle, wagons, hired skinners, hides at a dollar or two — and ends in plain regret at what the runners did. Caveats told with the story: a memoir set down in extreme old age, the numbers his own. The other side of the slaughter, in the voice of a man who did it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frank-mayer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="land-environment" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Conservation became federal work — a president who used it as presidential power, new agencies, a corps of young men planting trees — and the era also delivered two lessons in what failure costs: a bird extinct in a zoo cage, and the southern Plains blowing to the Atlantic.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The conservation presidency" -->
Theodore Roosevelt, 1901–1909: about 230 million acres put under federal protection — 150 national forests, 5 national parks, the first 18 national monuments, 51 federal bird reservations, 4 game preserves (counts vary slightly by source). Pelican Island, Florida (March 14, 1903), the first federal bird refuge. The U.S. Forest Service created in 1905 with Gifford Pinchot as first chief; the Antiquities Act (June 8, 1906) let presidents protect land by proclamation — Devils Tower first, that September.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="theodore-roosevelt-land-environment" name="Theodore Roosevelt" movie="The Roosevelts: An Intimate History (2014)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Theodore Roosevelt
> **Who:** the president who made protecting land a central use of presidential power. · **When and where:** the White House, 1901–1909; Yosemite, May 1903. · **Movie:** *The Roosevelts: An Intimate History* (PBS, Ken Burns, 2014) — a documentary about the family.
In May 1903 he slipped his handlers for three nights of camping with John Muir — under the Grizzly Giant sequoia, in a snowstorm near Sentinel Dome, in a meadow by Bridalveil Fall. A hunter who watched species vanishing, he treated the land as a national inheritance to be defended by law — and used every legal tool he had, sometimes ahead of Congress's wishes.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="theodore-roosevelt-land-environment" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hetch Hetchy — use it or keep it wild" -->
Conservation split into its two lasting camps over one valley. San Francisco, rebuilding after the 1906 earthquake and fire, wanted Hetch Hetchy Valley — inside Yosemite National Park — for a reservoir. Pinchot's camp said conservation means careful use for the greatest good; Muir's said a national park must mean never. Congress sided with the city (Raker Act, signed December 19, 1913); Muir died the next year; the O'Shaughnessy Dam finished in 1923, and the valley is under water today. The National Park Service (Organic Act, August 25, 1916) was created partly in reaction — a bureau whose whole job is the parks.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gifford-pinchot" name="Gifford Pinchot" movie="Seeking the Greatest Good (2013)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Gifford Pinchot
> **Who:** America's first professionally trained forester; first chief of the Forest Service (1905–1910); later twice governor of Pennsylvania. · **When and where:** Washington and the national forests, 1898–1910. · **Movie:** *Seeking the Greatest Good* (WVIA/PBS, 2013).
His rule for the public lands: "the greatest good to the greatest number for the longest time" — cut, graze, and dam, but carefully, forever. He and Muir were friends until Hetch Hetchy made their two conservations enemies; American land policy has argued their argument ever since.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gifford-pinchot" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Extinction, witnessed" -->
The passenger pigeon's end had names and dates: the last confirmed wild bird shot in Ohio in 1900, the last of the species dead at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914 — the first time Americans watched a species they had numbered in billions go to zero on a known day. Topic documentary: *From Billions to None* (2014).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="press-clay-southworth" name="Press Clay Southworth" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Press Clay Southworth
> **Who:** the 14-year-old Ohio farm boy who shot the last confirmed wild passenger pigeon — and the person through whom the bird's whole ending can be told. · **When and where:** Pike County, Ohio, March 24, 1900; the Cincinnati Zoo to September 1, 1914.
He saw a strange bird eating corn, asked his mother's permission, and used the family 12-gauge; nobody in the family recognized it until a neighbor did. Mounted with button eyes, "Buttons" is held by the Ohio History Connection; Southworth told the story himself decades later. Fourteen years after his shot, Martha — the species' last bird — died in her Cincinnati Zoo cage, about age 29; keeper Sol Stephan had saved her molted feathers in a cigar box (his accounts of where she hatched never stayed consistent — said plainly). Her body went to the Smithsonian frozen in a 300-pound block of ice. A boy with a shotgun, a zookeeper with a cigar box, and the space between them is the extinction.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="press-clay-southworth" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Dust Bowl — the soil itself" -->
War wheat prices and tractors had plowed up tens of millions of acres of native shortgrass; drought came in 1931, and the sod that held the southern Plains was gone. By December 1934 about 35 million acres of farmland were essentially destroyed for crops and 100 million more had lost most of their topsoil; in 1935 alone an estimated 850 million tons blew away. Black Sunday, April 14, 1935: a black wall of soil moving 60 miles an hour. That spring, as soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett testified in Washington, Plains dust darkened the sky outside the hearing room — "This, gentlemen, is what I've been talking about" (accounts differ on the exact day). Congress declared soil erosion "a national menace"; the Soil Conservation Service began April 27, 1935 — contour plowing, shelterbelts, grass put back. The exodus west is `migration`'s story; the storms as calamity are `disasters`'; the plowing and the soil are ours. Topic documentary: *The Dust Bowl* (Ken Burns, 2012).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="caroline-henderson" name="Caroline Henderson" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Caroline Henderson
> **Who:** a Mount Holyoke graduate who homesteaded the Oklahoma Panhandle in 1907, farmed it through the dust years — and stayed. · **When and where:** near Eva, Oklahoma; her letters ran 1908–1966.
Her "Letters from the Dust Bowl" in the *Atlantic Monthly* (May 1936 the best known) told the country what the dust actually did — fields drifted like snow, wheat dead, neighbors leaving one by one — from a kitchen table inside the storm. The Secretary of Agriculture wrote to thank her. Where `migration` follows the families who left, she is the documented voice of the ones who stayed with the soil.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="caroline-henderson" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The tree army and the fire rule" -->
- The Civilian Conservation Corps (1933–1942) put about 3 million young men to work; they planted between 2 and 3.5 billion trees (estimates vary; "about 3 billion" is the common figure), fought fires, terraced eroding farmland, and built the parks' trails and shelters.
- After the 1910 "Big Burn" (3 million acres, 78+ dead), the Forest Service set out to kill every fire; the 1935 "10 a.m. policy" ordered each one controlled by the morning after it was spotted, and CCC manpower made that real. Smokey Bear arrived in 1944 ("Only YOU can prevent forest fires," 1947; the living cub rescued from a New Mexico fire, 1950). The policy stood until 1978 — and a century of unburned fuel is part of era 10's megafires.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="aldo-leopold" name="Aldo Leopold" movie="Green Fire: Aldo Leopold and a Land Ethic for Our Time (2011)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Aldo Leopold
> **Who:** Forest Service forester turned professor who gave American conservation its ethics. · **When and where:** the Southwest, then a worn-out Wisconsin sand-county farm; 1887–1948. · **Movie:** *Green Fire: Aldo Leopold and a Land Ethic for Our Time* (2011).
He pushed through the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico (1924) — the world's first designated wilderness area — then bought a spent farm and spent weekends planting it back to life. He wrote about watching the "green fire" die in a wolf's eyes and changing his mind about predators. He died of a heart attack fighting a neighbor's grass fire in April 1948; *A Sand County Almanac* (1949) appeared after his death: people as plain members of the land community, not its conquerors.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aldo-leopold" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="land-environment" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Pollution became visible — in eagle nests, on a burning river, in a schoolyard over a chemical dump — and then became law. In one decade the country built nearly its whole environmental legal system, and ordinary people, more than experts, forced the building.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The quiet poison" -->
DDT, sprayed everywhere from the mid-1940s, moved up food chains and thinned raptor eggshells until eggs broke under the parents. Bald eagles — the national symbol — were down to 417 nesting pairs in the lower 48 by 1963.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rachel-carson" name="Rachel Carson" movie="Rachel Carson (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Rachel Carson
> **Who:** marine biologist and writer, formerly of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; author of *Silent Spring*. · **When and where:** Silver Spring, Maryland; the book September 1962; died April 14, 1964. · **Movie:** *Rachel Carson* (PBS American Experience, 2017).
*Silent Spring* laid out, with citations, what persistent pesticides were doing to birds, soil, water, and people, and asked whether a spring without birdsong was the price of convenience. The chemical industry attacked her as hysterical; she answered on national television (CBS Reports, April 3, 1963) already sick with the cancer that killed her seventeen months later. The DDT ban (1972) and much of the coming decade's law trace to her book.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rachel-carson" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The river that burned" -->
On June 22, 1969, an oil slick on the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland caught fire — about twenty minutes, quickly controlled, and at least the thirteenth fire on that river since 1868 (the 1952 fire did $1.3 million in damage; the 1912 fire killed five men). What changed was the audience: *Time* magazine showed the burning river to the country, and Mayor Carl Stokes — the first Black mayor of a major U.S. city — stood at the riverbank the next day demanding action. The same year, a well blowout blackened Santa Barbara's beaches.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The environmental decade" -->
- Earth Day, April 22, 1970 — an estimated 20 million Americans, one in ten, turned out.
- The laws, in five years: NEPA (Jan 1, 1970) · the EPA opens (Dec 2, 1970) · Clean Air Act (1970) · DDT banned and the Clean Water Act (1972) · Endangered Species Act (Dec 28, 1973).
- The proof came with feathers: bald eagles climbed from 417 pairs (1963) to about 10,000 by 2007, when the bird left the endangered list.
- Wolves came back on purpose: gray wolves from Canada released in Yellowstone starting January 1995 — the first deliberate return of a top predator to reshape land the government had once paid to clear of them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Love Canal and the buried waste" -->
Hooker Chemical buried about 21,000 tons of chemical waste in an abandoned canal in Niagara Falls, New York (1942–1953), then sold the covered site to the school board for one dollar. A school and hundreds of homes went up. By the 1970s chemicals were rising into yards and basements, and the neighborhood counted miscarriages, birth defects, and sick children. State and federal emergencies (1978, 1980) moved about 900 families out; Congress answered with Superfund (December 1980) — polluters pay for toxic cleanups.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lois-gibbs" name="Lois Gibbs" movie="Lois Gibbs and the Love Canal (1982)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Lois Gibbs
> **Who:** a 27-year-old housewife with no political experience whose son attended the school built on the dump. · **When and where:** Love Canal, Niagara Falls, New York, 1978–1980. · **Movie:** *Lois Gibbs and the Love Canal* (CBS television film, 1982).
Told there was no problem, she went door to door with a health survey, founded the Love Canal Homeowners Association (August 1978), and out-organized the state of New York and the federal government until her neighbors were moved to safety. She then spent the rest of her life teaching other neighborhoods to do the same (Center for Health, Environment & Justice; Goldman Prize, 1990). The era's proof that the person who forces the law can be anyone.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lois-gibbs" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Who lives next to the dump" -->
Warren County, North Carolina, September 1982: the state trucked PCB-laced soil to a landfill in Afton, in a mostly Black rural county; residents and civil-rights leaders lay down in front of the trucks; about 500 were arrested. The landfill was built anyway — and the fight named a pattern and a movement: environmental justice, the question of whose neighborhood gets the waste. It returns, with a victory, in the last era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="land-environment" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A warming climate reached into everything this chapter has covered — fire, water, soil, coasts, wildlife. 2024 was the warmest year ever measured, both globally and in the United States (NOAA and NASA agree; the U.S. ran 3.5°F above its 20th-century average). The era's fights are over how the land copes — and its clearest hope is that management has started coming full circle to the continent's first managers. Current through August 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fire comes back bigger" -->
A century of put-out-every-fire left the woods loaded with fuel; heat and drought dried it. The Camp Fire (November 8, 2018) killed 85 people and burned the town of Paradise, California — about 19,000 buildings. The 2020 California season burned about 4.2 million acres, four percent of the state; the August Complex alone passed one million acres — the first "gigafire" of modern record. The reversal followed: agencies that once banned all burning now plan and set fires on purpose.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="margo-robbins" name="Margo Robbins" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Margo Robbins
> **Who:** Yurok tribal member who co-founded the Cultural Fire Management Council to bring traditional burning back to Yurok land. · **When and where:** the Klamath River country, northern California; first community burn 2012, council formed 2013.
She wanted hazel shoots that grow straight after a burn — for weaving the baskets that carry Yurok babies, starting with her own grandchildren. The council's burns brought back hazel and the deer, and its training exchanges now teach cultural burning to government fire crews — the practice this chapter opened with, outlawed and suppressed for a century, taught back to the people who banned it. Native continuity past 1900, on the ground.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="margo-robbins" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The shrinking river" -->
Tree rings say 2000–2021 was the driest 22-year stretch in the Southwest in at least 1,200 years, and a study in *Nature Climate Change* (2022) attributes about 42 percent of its severity to human-caused warming. Lake Mead and Lake Powell — the Colorado River's two great reservoirs, water for some 40 million people — hit record lows in 2021–22, Mead down to about a quarter full. In May 2023 Arizona, California, and Nevada agreed to cut about a tenth of the lower basin's use through 2026. The deals run out as this book is written; the river is not refilling.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Poison, plastic, and justice" -->
- Environmental justice moved from protest to some victories: see Margie Richard, below.
- Plastic is now weather: a *Science* study (2020) measured more than 1,000 tons of microplastic — mostly clothing fibers — falling with rain and dust on western parks and wilderness every year.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="margie-richard" name="Margie Richard" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Margie Richard
> **Who:** a schoolteacher from the Old Diamond neighborhood of Norco, Louisiana — four generations of her family 25 feet from a Shell Chemical fence line. · **When and where:** Louisiana's petrochemical corridor; campaign to 2002; Goldman Environmental Prize, April 2004.
Her neighborhood, wedged between a chemical plant and a refinery, counted cancers, birth defects, and neighbors killed in plant accidents. She led a roughly 13-year campaign — bucket air samples, shareholder meetings, a trip to Shell's headquarters in the Netherlands — until Shell agreed in 2002 to fund the relocation of any Old Diamond family that wanted out, cut emissions 30 percent, and pay $5 million toward community development. First African American winner of the Goldman Prize. The Warren County question — who lives next to the plant — answered once, by one neighborhood that refused to stay put quietly.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="margie-richard" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Comebacks" -->
The recoveries are real and countable: bald eagles at roughly 71,400 nesting pairs; bison at about 420,000 in commercial herds and 20,500 in conservation herds — and the National Bison Range itself returned to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (2020–2022); wolves at about 500 in the Yellowstone region and 1,600-plus in the northern Rockies, their legal status still fought over. None of it is the old abundance — 30 million bison are not coming back — but extinction stopped being the automatic ending.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Whose land — Bears Ears" -->
Bears Ears, Utah — a monument proposed by five tribes (Hopi, Navajo, Ute Mountain Ute, Ute Indian Tribe, Zuni) — has become the live test of whether protection lasts: proclaimed at 1.35 million acres (December 28, 2016), cut about 85 percent (2017), restored (October 8, 2021), co-managed with the five tribes under a first-of-its-kind 2022 agreement — then cut again to about 121,000 acres, nine percent of its restored size, with the tribal commission terminated (July 13, 2026; the proclamation cites minerals; tribes and conservation groups have vowed suit — live news as this book is written, labeled as such). Protection, this era shows, is a decision each government can remake.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<!-- hb-note -->
# Part 2 — Coming, Moving, Settling
<!-- /hb-note -->


<a id="chapter-04-immigration"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="04" slug="immigration" title="Immigration to America" part="2" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 04: Immigration to America

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-07
**Angle:** Arrival from other lands to stay — who came, when, from where, why, and how they were received.
**Keep out:** the Middle Passage and forced arrival (`slavery-freedom`); movement once here (`migration`); city growth (`city-building`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/immigration.md` · **Research bank:** `research/research-immigration.md` (verified, all ten eras) · **Reference prose:** `_reference/manuscript-v1/ch02-immigration/` and `_reference/manuscript-v1/ch02-migration-MERGED-draft/`
**Scope (ruling 1):** `slavery-freedom` owns the Middle Passage, forced arrival, Kossola and the *Clotilda*. This chapter notes forced arrival in one or two plain sentences and does not retell it.
**Placement notes (ruling 3, boundary rule):** Carl Schurz (immigrated 1852) and Annie Moore (January 1, 1892) sit in 1850–1900, not where the older draft had them; the writer may note the 1848 hinge for Schurz. Emma Lazarus (US-born, not an arrival) is folded into the 1850–1900 span, not a person box.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="immigration" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
No overseas immigration yet. Immigration here means newcomers arriving into an inhabited continent, not an empty one — hundreds of Native nations and hundreds of languages already here. Population north of Mexico in 1492 is genuinely debated: about 3.8 million is a common scholarly figure, with estimates running from about 1 million to as high as 18 million (Denevan; Fixico — no settled number).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The land bridge and the Norse" -->
The first people to reach this land came on foot across the ice-age land bridge — the original arrival, told in full in `exploration`. The only crossing from overseas before 1500, the Norse about 1000 at L'Anse aux Meadows, lasted about ten years and did not stay.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="immigration" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Europeans arrive but almost none stay: soldiers, explorers, sailors, and missionaries — conquest, not settlement. The land stays overwhelmingly Native all century.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="St. Augustine, and the failures" -->
St. Augustine, Florida, founded September 8, 1565 by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés with about 600 soldiers and settlers — the first enduring European town, small and often in danger (NPS). The failures show how hard staying was: the French Fort Caroline (1564) destroyed by Menéndez in 1565; the English Roanoke colony (1587) found abandoned in 1590, its people's fate unknown (NPS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="immigration" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first people who came to stay. Reasons split between religious freedom and the chance to get land or a living, and a large share of English arrivals came bound to years of unpaid labor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Jamestown, Plymouth, and indentured servitude" -->
Jamestown 1607 (the Virginia Company, then tobacco). Plymouth 1620 (about 102 aboard the *Mayflower*). Massachusetts Bay 1630 (the Winthrop Fleet, 11 ships, about 700 people) and the Puritan migration of the 1630s — roughly 20,000 to New England, out of about 80,000 who left England that decade (New England Historical Society). Dutch New Amsterdam on Manhattan, taken and renamed New York in 1664. New Sweden on the Delaware, 1638–1655. Indentured servitude: about 80–90 percent of European immigrants to the Chesapeake in the 1600s arrived under indenture; across all the colonies over the whole colonial era, roughly half to two-thirds (Smithsonian; EH.net — the two figures measure different areas). The first enslaved Africans landed in Virginia in late August 1619 — arrival that was not chosen; the telling belongs to `slavery-freedom`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="anne-hutchinson-immigration" name="Anne Hutchinson" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Anne Hutchinson
Born 1591 in Alford, England. In the fall of 1634 she crossed on the *Griffin* with her husband William and their children, among about 200 passengers, following their minister John Cotton to Boston to worship as they believed. The colony she joined for religious freedom put her on trial in 1637 for her religious meetings and banished her; she moved to Rhode Island in 1638, then to Dutch territory, where she and several of her children were killed in a Siwanoy attack in 1643. Arrival angle only — the trial and her ideas are told in `religion` and `rights-movements`. (Sources: Mass Moments; National Women's History Museum.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="anne-hutchinson-immigration" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="richard-frethorne-immigration" name="Richard Frethorne" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Richard Frethorne
An indentured English boy who arrived in Virginia in December 1622 on the *Abigail*, bound to Martin's Hundred plantation. His surviving letters of March–April 1623 beg his parents to buy out his indenture or send food — "I never ate anything but peas and loblollie." He was recorded among the dead at Martin's Hundred by February 1624. One of the very few ordinary colonial arrivals whose own words survive. The daily-labor angle is `work-workers`; ours is the crossing and what the promise of America actually bought him. (Sources: Virtual Jamestown transcription; Encyclopedia Virginia.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="richard-frethorne-immigration" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jewish-refugees-1654" name="The first Jewish refugees (1654)" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### The first Jewish refugees (1654)
23 refugees from Recife, Brazil, aboard the *Ste. Catherine*, plus Jacob Barsimson who came earlier that year; Governor Peter Stuyvesant tried to expel them and the Dutch West India Company overruled him. (Sources: Jewish Women's Archive; Gilder Lehrman.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jewish-refugees-1654" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="immigration" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The colonial population diversifies beyond the English, and much of the arriving labor is unfree or bound.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Germans, Scots-Irish, and convict transport" -->
Germans from the Rhineland (the Pennsylvania "Dutch," from *Deutsch*): about 2,100 Palatines reached New York in 1709–1710, and roughly 12,000 German speakers had come to Pennsylvania by 1749. Scots-Irish from Ulster: about 200,000 between 1710 and 1775, most through Pennsylvania and then down the Appalachian backcountry. French Huguenots after 1685; small Sephardic Jewish communities at Newport, New York, Charleston, and Savannah (42 Jews landed at Savannah July 11, 1733). Britain shipped about 50,000 convicts (some counts up to 60,000) to the colonies as bound labor after the Transportation Act of 1718, until 1775 — roughly a quarter of British emigrants that century (Encyclopedia Virginia). Indentured servitude continued alongside.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-peter-zenger-immigration" name="John Peter Zenger" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Peter Zenger
Born 1697 in Rumbach, in the German Palatinate. His family joined the mass Palatine migration in late 1709; they sailed for New York in April 1710, and his father died on the voyage. Thirteen-year-old John Peter arrived in June 1710 with his widowed mother and two siblings, and in 1711 was apprenticed to the printer William Bradford. The poor refugee boy became the printer whose 1735 acquittal began press freedom in America — that trial is told in `government-politics` and `news-communication`; ours is the arrival. Died 1746. (Sources: Immigrant Entrepreneurship (German Historical Institute); Encyclopedia.com.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-peter-zenger-immigration" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="immigration" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The Revolution slows arrivals, and the new country writes down for the first time who is allowed to become an American.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Naturalization Act of 1790, and refugees from Saint-Domingue" -->
War interrupted the flow: convict transport ended in 1775, and tens of thousands of Loyalists left during and after the war — an outflow, not an arrival. The Naturalization Act of 1790 limited naturalization to a "free white person" of good character with two years' residence — the first federal word on belonging, a racial limit not fully removed until 1952 (Library of Congress). Refugees from the Haitian Revolution (begun 1791) reached U.S. cities: more than 3,000 in Philadelphia by 1794, nearly 20,000 across the 1790s and 1800s (Smithsonian; 64 Parishes).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alexander-hamilton-immigration" name="Alexander Hamilton" movie="Hamilton (2020)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Alexander Hamilton
> **Movie:** *Hamilton* (2020) — the filmed Broadway musical; a dramatization, not a documentary.

Born on the Caribbean island of Nevis on January 11, 1755 or 1757 (sources genuinely disagree on the year); orphaned young; a teenage trading-house clerk on St. Croix. After a hurricane wrecked the island on August 31, 1772, his published letter describing the storm (dated September 6, 1772) so impressed local men that they raised money to send him to school in North America. He sailed in late 1772 or early 1773 (accounts differ), entered King's College in New York, and stayed — the immigrant who became the first Secretary of the Treasury. His money-and-government work is told in `economy`, `money`, and `government-politics`; ours is the arrival. (Sources: National Constitution Center; Library of Congress; Gilder Lehrman.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alexander-hamilton-immigration" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="pierre-toussaint" name="Pierre Toussaint" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Pierre Toussaint
Born about 1766 in Saint-Domingue (Haiti), enslaved. In 1787 the Bérard family brought him to New York as they fled the colony's unrest — an arrival that was not his choice, part of the refugee stream from Saint-Domingue. Apprenticed to a hairdresser, he became one of New York's most sought-after hairdressers and quietly supported the widowed Madame Bérard for years while still enslaved. Freed July 2, 1807, he took the surname Toussaint, and spent his earnings on orphans, plague victims, and the city's first Catholic charities. Died June 30, 1853; declared Venerable by the Catholic Church in 1996; buried in the crypt of St. Patrick's Cathedral. The slavery system itself is `slavery-freedom`'s telling. (Sources: New York Public Library Toussaint papers; New York Almanack.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="pierre-toussaint" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="immigration" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first great voluntary wave — and the first organized movement against immigrants.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Irish and German waves begin" -->
Legal arrival from Africa ended January 1, 1808 under the Act signed March 2, 1807 (the earliest date the Constitution allowed); smuggling continued — that story is `slavery-freedom`'s. Irish arrivals surged with the Great Famine (1845–1852): about a million died in Ireland, nearly two million left in that decade, and more than 1.5 million Irish arrived at U.S. ports between 1845 and 1855, most settling poor in northeastern cities. Germans became the largest immigrant group from about 1840 — roughly six million came between 1820 and World War I, pushed by crop failures and, for a few thousand ("Forty-Eighters"), the failed democratic revolutions of 1848. Ports: New York chiefly, also Boston and New Orleans. Anti-Irish and anti-Catholic feeling grew through the 1840s; the organized Know-Nothing movement peaked in the next era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="patrick-kennedy-bridget-murphy" name="Patrick Kennedy and Bridget Murphy" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Patrick Kennedy and Bridget Murphy
Patrick Kennedy, born 1823 on a farm at Dunganstown, County Wexford, left famine Ireland in 1848 or 1849 (accounts differ). He worked as a cooper — a barrel maker — in East Boston, and in September 1849 married Bridget Murphy, who had made the same crossing from Wexford. They had five children. Patrick died of cholera on November 22, 1858, at 35, leaving Bridget a widow with four young children. Their youngest son's grandson, John F. Kennedy, became president in 1961 — a famine immigrant's great-grandson. (Sources: JFK Library; NPS.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="patrick-kennedy-bridget-murphy" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jette-bruns" name="Jette Bruns" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Jette Bruns
Henriette "Jette" Geisberg Bruns, born 1813 in Oelde, Westphalia (Germany). In 1836 she arrived at the Westphalia Settlement in central Missouri with her husband Bernhard, a doctor sold on the promise of cheap land, plus their baby son, her two brothers, and a maid. For more than fifty years she wrote letters home to her brother Heinrich — published as *Hold Dear, As Always* (University of Missouri Press, 1988) — recording frontier sickness, grief, work, and the long strangeness of a new country. Widowed and left nearly penniless during the Civil War, she ran a boardinghouse across from the Missouri state capitol. Died 1899 in Jefferson City. (Sources: State Historical Society of Missouri; Univ. of Missouri Press.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jette-bruns" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="immigration" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The largest wave yet, and the first door closed by law against a named nationality.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Castle Garden, Ellis Island, and the Chinese Exclusion Act" -->
Castle Garden at Battery Park was the immigrant depot from August 1855 to April 1890, processing about 8 million of roughly 11 million arrivals through New York; Ellis Island opened January 1, 1892 as the federal station. German arrivals peaked — over 950,000 in the 1850s, about 220,000 in 1854 alone — and the nativist Know-Nothing (American) Party swept Massachusetts in 1854, then split over slavery. Chinese immigration began with the Gold Rush — about 325 in 1849, some 20,000 in 1852, about 105,465 Chinese in the country by 1880, most from Guangdong. The Page Act of 1875 was the first restrictive federal immigration law; the Chinese Exclusion Act, signed May 6, 1882, was the first U.S. law to bar a group by nationality — renewed and widened, repealed only in 1943. New sources: Italians, Poles, Hungarians, Greeks, and more than two million Jews from the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1914, fleeing pogroms after 1881. The Statue of Liberty was dedicated October 28, 1886; Emma Lazarus (New York-born, 1849–1887) wrote "The New Colossus" in 1883, and the plaque mounted inside the pedestal in 1903 is how the statue became a symbol of welcome. In 1860 the schooner *Clotilda* landed captives illegally at Mobile — the last known slave ship; that telling belongs to `slavery-freedom`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="carl-schurz" name="Carl Schurz" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Carl Schurz
Born 1829 near Cologne; joined the failed German revolution of 1848–49 and fled when Prussia crushed it; immigrated in 1852 and settled in Watertown, Wisconsin. Union general, first German-born U.S. senator (Missouri, 1869–1875), Secretary of the Interior (1877–1881); died 1906. Sits here by arrival date (1852); the writer may note the 1848 hinge with the era before. (Sources: Britannica; Senate Bioguide.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="carl-schurz" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="annie-moore" name="Annie Moore" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Annie Moore
First immigrant processed at Ellis Island, January 1, 1892 — age 17, from County Cork aboard the *Nevada*, with her two younger brothers; presented a $10 gold piece. For a century the celebrated "Annie Moore who went west" was the wrong woman; genealogist Megan Smolenyak's 2006 search found the real Annie, who never left New York's Lower East Side, married a fish-market clerk, and died in 1924 at 50. Statues stand at Ellis Island and Cobh, Ireland. (Sources: NPR 2006; Smolenyak.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="annie-moore" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="wong-kim-ark" name="Wong Kim Ark" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Wong Kim Ark
Born in San Francisco in 1873 to Chinese immigrant parents; worked as a cook. Returning from a visit to China in August 1895 on the steamship *Coptic*, he was refused permission to land in his own birthplace — the exclusion laws applied to him, said the government, because his parents were Chinese. Held aboard ship while his lawyers filed suit, he took the fight to the Supreme Court and won: on March 28, 1898, the Court ruled 6–2 that anyone born in the United States is a citizen. The door-closing angle is ours; the case as law is `government-politics`, the fight against discrimination `rights-movements`. (Sources: National Archives; Supreme Court Historical Society.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="wong-kim-ark" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="irving-berlin" name="Irving Berlin" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Irving Berlin
Born Israel Beilin in 1888 in the Russian Empire (accounts differ on the place; the family gave May 11 as his birthday). His only memory of Russia was watching their house burn during anti-Jewish violence. The family of a poor cantor arrived at Ellis Island on September 14, 1893, when he was five. From singing for pennies on the Lower East Side he became the country's most successful songwriter — "White Christmas," "Easter Parade," and "God Bless America," the unofficial anthem written by an immigrant. Died 1989, aged 101. (Sources: Library of Congress; JewishGen; Wikipedia cross-checked.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="irving-berlin" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="immigration" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The wave peaks, then the gates shut — and stay shut through the years people most needed to get out.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ellis Island's peak, Angel Island, and the 1924 quotas" -->
Ellis Island's busiest year was 1907: 1,004,756 admitted, 11,747 on the single busiest day (April 17); about 12 million passed through from 1892 to 1954. The phrase "melting pot" spread from Israel Zangwill's play of that name, which opened in Washington October 5, 1908. Angel Island opened in 1910 in San Francisco Bay to enforce the exclusion laws — detentions from days to as long as two years, about 175,000 Chinese processed 1910–1940, poems carved into the barrack walls and saved after a ranger found them in 1970. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924 tied quotas to old censuses — Italy's yearly allotment fell from over 42,000 to fewer than 6,000, nearly all Asian immigration was barred, the total cap sat near 165,000, and the great wave ended. The MS *St. Louis*, May 1939: 937 passengers, almost all Jewish refugees, refused by Cuba, the United States, and Canada; 254 were later killed in the Holocaust. The Displaced Persons Act of 1948 was the first U.S. refugee law. Mexican arrivals grew with the Revolution (about 350,000 in the 1910s), reversed in the Mexican Repatriation of 1929–1936 (roughly 500,000 pressured or forced out, many U.S. citizens), then the Bracero Program brought contract farmworkers from August 1942.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frank-capra" name="Frank Capra" movie="Frank Capra's American Dream (1997)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frank Capra
> **Movie:** *Frank Capra's American Dream* (1997) — a documentary about him, hosted by Ron Howard.

Born Francesco Capra in 1897 in Bisacquino, Sicily. In 1903, when he was six, the family crossed in the cheapest steerage berths of the steamship *Germania*, passed through Ellis Island, and rode a train across the country to Los Angeles. He became one of Hollywood's most honored directors — three Academy Awards for directing in the 1930s, then *It's a Wonderful Life* (1946). (Sources: Britannica; TCM.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frank-capra" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="doukenie-bacos" name="Doukenie Bacos" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Doukenie Bacos
Doukenie Babayanie Bacos, born 1904 to a Greek family in Thrace. A teenager determined to leave, she sailed from Piraeus on the *King Alexander* and reached Ellis Island on January 5, 1921, at sixteen (parts of her record also give 1919 — the dates in the file disagree). Traveling underage, she heard older girls whisper she might be sent back, and later said she thought of jumping into the water rather than return. She was admitted, and told her whole story to the Ellis Island Oral History Project in 1991 — one of nearly 2,000 recorded immigrant voices. (Sources: Ellis Island Oral History Project interview EI-049; Statue of Liberty–Ellis Island Foundation.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="doukenie-bacos" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lee-puey-you" name="Lee Puey You" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Lee Puey You
Arrived 1939 as a "paper daughter," faced an interrogation of about 170 questions, was detained on Angel Island roughly 20 months — among the longest known — and was deported in November 1940 ("cried a bowlful of tears"). She returned in 1947, after the exclusion law's repeal, and settled in San Francisco. (Source: Judy Yung, "A Bowlful of Tears Revisited.")
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lee-puey-you" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="immigration" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The doors reopen and the map of where immigrants come from is redrawn.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hart-Celler, refugee waves, and IRCA" -->
The Bracero Program ran to 1964 — about 4.5 million short-term contracts for Mexican farmworkers, labor invited in but not asked to stay. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Hart-Celler) ended the national-origins quotas and rebuilt the system on family ties and skills; over the following decades the main sources of immigration shifted to Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Caribbean. Cuban waves followed Castro's 1959 revolution, including the Mariel boatlift of April–October 1980 (~125,000). Southeast Asian refugees came after 1975 — Vietnamese, Hmong, Cambodian, Laotian; nearly 281,000 Vietnamese resettled 1981–1990 alone. The Refugee Act of 1980 built the permanent refugee system. IRCA, signed November 6, 1986, legalized about 2.7 million long-term unauthorized residents and set the first employer penalties.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="antonio-garcia-bracero" name="Antonio García" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Antonio García
Born June 13, 1937 in Tepehuanes, Durango, Mexico; left school after fourth grade to work. At seventeen he had his military ID card altered to say eighteen so he could join the bracero program; his first contract sent him to the cotton fields of Texas, where he fell seriously ill within a week. He worked under contracts on and off into the early 1960s in California, Colorado, New Mexico, and Texas, passing through the crowded contracting centers at Chihuahua and Empalme. His oral history was recorded in Chicago in 2003 for the Bracero History Archive — one of more than 700 such interviews; whether he settled permanently in the United States the record does not say. (Source: Bracero History Archive / UTEP Institute of Oral History, interview March 12, 2003.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="antonio-garcia-bracero" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="tung-trinh" name="Tung Trinh" movie="Bolinao 52 (2008)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Tung Trinh
> **Movie:** *Bolinao 52* (2008)

1988: 110 people aboard a boat out of Vietnam whose engine failed, 37 days adrift, more than 20 ships passing without helping, 52 survivors landed at Bolinao in the Philippines; Tung Trinh resettled in Orange County, California. (The bank flags cannibalism during the drift — kept out of the prose; tell it as danger, survival, and rescue.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="tung-trinh" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="reinaldo-arenas" name="Reinaldo Arenas" movie="Before Night Falls (2000)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Reinaldo Arenas
> **Movie:** *Before Night Falls* (2000) — a drama based on his autobiography, with Javier Bardem as Arenas.

Born 1943 near Holguín, Cuba; a writer whose books were banned at home and who was imprisoned by the Castro government for his writing and for being gay. In May 1980 he got out through the port of Mariel, one of about 125,000 Cubans in the boatlift. He kept writing in New York, finishing his life story, *Before Night Falls*, while sick with AIDS; he ended his life in December 1990, at 47. Hard parts told plainly: persecution, exile, illness. (Sources: Britannica; Duke University Press; EBSCO.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="reinaldo-arenas" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sergey-brin" name="Sergey Brin" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sergey Brin
Born 1973 in Moscow. His Jewish family faced blocked careers and discrimination in the Soviet Union; they got exit permission in 1979 — the peak year of Soviet Jewish emigration, about 51,000 people — and arrived in the United States on October 25, 1979, when Sergey was six. His father taught mathematics at the University of Maryland; his mother became a NASA researcher. In 1998 Sergey Brin and Larry Page founded Google. (Sources: EBSCO; Immigrant Learning Center; Wikipedia cross-checked.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sergey-brin" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="immigration" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The foreign-born share climbs back toward its early-1900s peak, and the argument over immigration becomes one of the country's loudest. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A near-record foreign-born share" -->
About 47.8 million foreign-born people, 14.3 percent of the population, in the 2023 American Community Survey — the highest share since 1910 (14.7 percent), near the all-time high of 14.8 percent in 1890, against a low of 4.7 percent in 1970. Largest origins in 2023: Mexico about 11 million, India 3.2 million, China 3 million, the Philippines 2.1 million, Cuba 1.7 million (Pew). The unauthorized population estimated near 11–12 million, with real uncertainty. DHS created after 9/11 (Act of 2002; operating 2003). DACA from June 15, 2012. Voluntary African and Caribbean immigration grew fast — the sub-Saharan African immigrant population roughly tripled from 2000 to about 2.5 million by 2024 (Migration Policy Institute).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="giannis-antetokounmpo" name="Giannis Antetokounmpo" movie="Rise (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Giannis Antetokounmpo
> **Movie:** *Rise* (2022) — a Disney film about the Antetokounmpo family's journey; a dramatization made with the family.

Born 1994 in Athens to Charles and Veronica Antetokounmpo, Nigerian immigrants without legal status in Greece. Because Greece grants no citizenship by birth, Giannis grew up stateless, selling sunglasses and watches on the street with his brothers. Greece granted him citizenship in 2013, weeks before the Milwaukee Bucks drafted him at 18 — his arrival in America. He became a two-time NBA Most Valuable Player and led Milwaukee to the 2021 championship, and his parents and brothers joined him in the United States. (Journalism-sourced: Britannica; EBSCO; NBC.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="giannis-antetokounmpo" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lost-boys-of-sudan" name="Peter Dut and Santino Chuor, Lost Boys of Sudan" movie="Lost Boys of Sudan (2003)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Peter Dut and Santino Chuor, Lost Boys of Sudan
> **Movie:** *Lost Boys of Sudan* (2003) — an Emmy-nominated documentary that follows these two young men themselves.

Peter Nyarol Dut and Santino Majok Chuor, Dinka teenagers orphaned by Sudan's civil war, survived a walk of hundreds of miles and years in Kenya's Kakuma refugee camp. In 2001 they were among roughly 4,000 "Lost Boys" resettled in the United States. The documentary follows their first year: jobs, night classes, loneliness, and small footholds — Santino in Houston, Peter leaving for Kansas to chase a high-school diploma. (Sources: the film; PBS POV.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lost-boys-of-sudan" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<a id="chapter-05-migration"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="05" slug="migration" title="Migration Across America" part="2" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 05: Migration Across America

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-07 (restructure pass; seed replaced).
**Angle:** People moving and being moved across the land once here — Native movements and the horse, colonial internal migrations, the trails, forced removals, the Great Migration, the Dust Bowl, the Sun Belt.
**Keep out:** who found the routes (`exploration`); arrival from abroad (`immigration`); city growth (`city-building`); the vehicles and roads as machines (`transportation`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/migration.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-migration.md` (verified, all ten eras; "Restructure additions 2026-08-07" holds the new material) · **Reference:** `_reference/manuscript-v1/ch03-migration-west/` and `_reference/manuscript-v1/ch02-migration-MERGED-draft/` (finished v1 prose to mine).
**Rulings applied:** ruling 2 — the domestic slave trade is told in BOTH chapters; this chapter LEADS on the forced journey (routes, coffles, ships, numbers), `slavery-freedom` leads on the system and the families. Ruling 3 — Amelia Stewart Knight (1853) sits in 1850–1900. Placement fix: the Acadian expulsion (1755) sits in 1750–1800, not 1700–1750 where the seed had it.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="migration" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The land was already crossed by Native movement for thousands of years. Migration here does not begin with wagons. People moved to build, moved when places were left, followed the seasons, and traded along paths that laced the whole continent.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cahokia, Chaco, and the Athabascan migration" -->
Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, the largest town north of Mexico, peaked about 1100 at roughly 10,000–20,000 people, dispersed by about 1350, and was empty by the 1400s (causes debated — drought, floods, strain on wood and food; no settled answer). Chaco Canyon broke up after droughts around 1140 and was left by about 1200, its people regathering into the Pueblo communities. The long Athabascan (Dené) migration south — ancestors of the Navajo and Apache moving from western Canada and Alaska toward the Southwest; the arrival date is unsettled (about the 1200s to about 1525 — state the disagreement). Seasonal rounds, and long trade routes carrying turquoise, shells, copper, and obsidian hundreds of miles. No documented named individual survives from these journeys; zoom 3 stays empty on purpose.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="migration" label="The 1500s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Still Native land coast to coast, with no mass settler movement across the interior. Two changes mark the century's edges: the horse comes back, and in 1598 the first wagon-borne settler colony rolls north into New Mexico.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The horse returns" -->
The Spanish bring the horse back (Columbus 1493; onto the mainland with Coronado 1540–42). Horses had died out here after the ice age. The transformation of Plains life comes later.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Oñate up the Camino Real, 1598" -->
Juan de Oñate leaves Santa Bárbara in northern New Spain in January 1598 with about 400 men — about 130 of them with families — plus 83 wagons and carts and more than 7,000 head of livestock: soldiers, friars, farmers, servants, and enslaved people, moving to stay. The column cuts across the Chihuahuan Desert, crosses the Rio Grande at El Paso del Norte in late April, claims New Mexico for Spain on April 30, 1598 (La Toma), and in July sets its headquarters at San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh) — extending the road by more than 600 miles. The route becomes El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road of the interior. The land they moved into was Pueblo homeland; in 1599 Oñate's soldiers attacked Acoma Pueblo — that story belongs to `native-nations`. Shared with: `transportation` (the Camino Real as a road) · `native-nations` (the Pueblo world and Acoma).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="juan-de-onate" name="Juan de Oñate" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Juan de Oñate
Led the 1598 colony column up the Camino Real — about 400 men, 83 wagons and carts, 7,000 head of livestock, from Santa Bárbara to Ohkay Owingeh. The first documented settler-colony migration inside the future United States. His soldiers' 1599 attack on Acoma Pueblo goes with the nations' story (`native-nations`); this chapter says it plainly in one sentence and hands off.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="juan-de-onate" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="migration" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Newcomers cling to the Atlantic coast; the Appalachians and powerful Native nations hold them near the ocean. The century's movement stories are the horse spreading among Native nations, and colonists' first short moves inland.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The horse spreads" -->
Traditional account: the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 frees perhaps more than 1,500 Spanish horses, which move north and east by trade to the Ute, Apache, Comanche, Lakota, and others. Newer account: a 2023 *Science* study (Taylor and Lakota, Comanche, Pawnee, and other partners) finds horses kept and cared for among Plains and Rockies nations by the early 1600s, matching Native oral histories. State both; the timing is unsettled. Effect: mounted nations could follow the buffalo and travel farther and faster.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="First colonial moves inland" -->
Hooker's congregation walks to Hartford in 1636 (story below); Roger Williams leaves Massachusetts for Providence the same year (his banishment and ideas → `religion`); settlement crawls up the Chesapeake rivers. These are moves of miles, not continents — the interior stays Native land.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-hooker" name="Thomas Hooker" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Thomas Hooker
Pastor at Newtown (now Cambridge), Massachusetts. In May–June 1636 he led about 100 members of his congregation on a roughly two-week walk along Native trails to the Connecticut River, driving 160 cattle and living partly on the cows' milk — Winthrop's journal (May 31, 1636) records the departure, Hooker's wife carried on a horse litter. They settled Hartford; the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut followed in 1639 (the document → `government-politics`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-hooker" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="migration" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Coastal land fills and prices rise, so settler families push inland into the backcountry — while whole Native nations are also on the move, north and onto the Plains. Everything beyond the mountains is still Native land.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Great Wagon Road and the backcountry" -->
The Great Wagon Road: about 730 miles from Philadelphia through the Shenandoah Valley to Augusta, Georgia, heavily used from the 1720s and busier after the 1744 Treaty of Lancaster opened the valley. Who moved: German and Scots-Irish families finding Pennsylvania land too costly (their arrival from Europe → `immigration`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Nations on the move" -->
The Tuscarora migration north, 1713–1722: after the Tuscarora War in North Carolina, about 1,500 survivors move roughly 500 miles in stages toward Pennsylvania and New York and, sponsored by the Oneida, become the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in 1722 — a nation moving whole. Shared with: `native-nations` (the confederacy politics; the journey is ours). The Comanche move onto the southern Plains by the early 1700s (their power and economy → `native-nations`). No documented named traveler survives from this era's journeys; zoom 3 stays empty rather than invented.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="migration" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first big crowds cross the Appalachians, Congress lays a grid over land it has not yet settled — and a whole deported people finds its way to Louisiana.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Wilderness Road and the land ordinances" -->
Cumberland Gap and the Wilderness Road — Boone cut it in 1775 (`exploration`); as many as 300,000 settlers went through into Kentucky and beyond between 1775 and about 1810; Kentucky became a state in 1792. After the Revolution settlers pour into the Ohio Valley and Northwest Territory. The Land Ordinance of 1785 (townships six miles square, 36 sections of 640 acres, one reserved for schools) and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (path to statehood; slavery barred north of the Ohio).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Acadian expulsion and the road to Louisiana" -->
Between 1755 and 1764 British forces deport about 11,500 Acadians — French-speaking Catholic farm families — from Nova Scotia and nearby areas, out of a population of about 14,000–18,000, scattering them to the thirteen colonies, England, and France. Death counts are disputed: one accounting says close to 5,000 died of disease, shipwreck, or violence; some sources say as many as half — state the range. Between 1764 and 1785 about 2,600–3,000 reach Louisiana; in 1785 seven Spanish-funded ships carry 1,596 Acadians from France, the first arriving at New Orleans on July 29, 1785. Their descendants become the Cajuns — the word comes from "Acadian." Shared with: `immigration` (the 1785 ships arrived from France — flag for the director) · `religion` (Catholic families in a new land).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-broussard" name="Joseph Broussard (Beausoleil)" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Joseph Broussard (Beausoleil)
Acadian resistance leader, about 1702–1765. Fought the deportation, was held at Halifax until the 1763 peace, chartered a ship with about 600 Acadians to Saint-Domingue in late 1764, then led about 193–200 on to Louisiana, arriving at New Orleans in February 1765. Named militia captain and commander of the "Acadians of the Attakapas" on April 8, 1765; died that October in an epidemic. One of the first Cajun founders.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-broussard" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="migration" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The country doubles in size and the trails fill. Most of this era's movement is toward the West — and some of it is at gunpoint: removal marches and a million people moved by the slave trade.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The trails" -->
Louisiana Purchase, 1803: about 827,000 square miles for $15 million. "Manifest Destiny" — a phrase coined by John O'Sullivan in 1845; an idea people held, not a force. The trails, most starting at Independence or St. Joseph, Missouri: the Santa Fe Trail (1821, William Becknell), mainly freight; the Oregon Trail, about 2,000–2,170 miles and four to six months, with the 1843 "Great Migration" of roughly 1,000 people and 120 wagons proving families could make it; the California Trail, which exploded after 1849; the Mormon Trail, whose 1847 vanguard company of about 148 people covered some 1,300 miles, with more than 70,000 following by 1869. Wagon-train life: the real killers were disease (cholera, typhoid), accidents, and river crossings, not attacks; roughly one in ten emigrants died.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Forced journeys: removal and the domestic slave trade" -->
The Indian Removal Act of 1830 and the Trail of Tears of 1838–39: more than 16,000 Cherokee driven from Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina; over 4,000 dead (the traditional estimate; some scholars argue higher); the overland walk about 800 miles. Shared with: `native-nations` (lead — the nations broken, the treaties ignored) · `rights-movements` (the campaign against removal). The domestic slave trade — this chapter leads the journey (ruling 2): more than 1 million enslaved people moved from the Upper South to the Deep South, about 1790–1860, roughly 200,000 a decade from 1820 — marched overland in chained coffles or shipped down the coast to New Orleans, the country's largest slave market. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (lead on the system — people as property, families broken by sale).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Gold Rush and the Mexican Cession" -->
Gold found at Sutter's Mill in 1848; about 80,000 forty-niners in 1849 and about 300,000 to California from 1848 to 1855, half by sea and half overland; California's non-Native population goes from about 14,000 to about 250,000. Shared with: `exploration` (the searching) · `economy` (the money) · `city-building` (San Francisco's leap). The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) opens the far West.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rebecca-neugin-migration" name="Rebecca Neugin" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Rebecca Neugin
Cherokee child on the Trail of Tears, about three years old in 1838; rode in a wagon while her mother, father, and older brother walked the whole way. Her memory was recorded in 1932, near the end of her life — one of the last firsthand survivor voices of the removal journey. (The nation's story → `native-nations`, which features her separately.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rebecca-neugin-migration" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="charles-ball-migration" name="Charles Ball" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Charles Ball
Enslaved man sold away from his wife and children in Maryland about 1805 and chained into a coffle of 52 people — iron collars padlocked to a hundred-foot chain — that walked more than a month to Columbia, South Carolina. He later escaped, walked back north by night, was seized again, escaped again, and dictated his story (published 1837). Dates approximate; the narrative passed through another man's pen — say so.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="charles-ball-migration" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="brigham-young" name="Brigham Young" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Brigham Young
Led the 1847 Mormon vanguard company — about 148 people, some 1,300 miles from Winter Quarters to the Salt Lake Valley, arriving July 1847.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="brigham-young" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="migration" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Railroads and free land pull settlers onto the Plains, handcart companies walk to Utah, Black Southerners try Kansas as an escape, Native nations are marched onto reservations — and the Census declares the frontier line gone.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homesteads, the railroad, and the cattle drives" -->
Homestead Act, 1862: up to 160 acres after five years' residence and farming; about 4 million claims and 270 million acres (roughly 10 percent of U.S. land) over its life. Transcontinental railroad completed May 10, 1869, cutting a coast-to-coast trip from about four months to about a week. Shared with: `transportation` (lead — the line) · `native-nations` · `immigration` · `work-workers`. Cattle drives north from Texas to Kansas railheads — more than 5 million head between 1866 and 1884, fading by the mid-1880s.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The handcart companies, 1856" -->
More than 1,000 Latter-day Saint emigrants in the late-starting Willie company (about 500 people, left Florence, Nebraska Territory, August 17, 1856) and Martin company (left August 27) pull two-wheeled handcarts toward Salt Lake City. An early blizzard strikes October 19 in present-day Wyoming, just after the Martin company wades the North Platte. More than 300 rescuers with wagons bring the survivors in. Death counts differ — state the range: about 67–77 in the Willie company, about 103–150 in the Martin company; older accounts say 200–250 across the stranded companies and their wagon trains.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Exodusters and the land rush" -->
Exodusters, about 1879: up to 40,000 Black Southerners toward Kansas and the Plains, some 6,000 in the spring of 1879 alone. Oklahoma Land Rush, April 22, 1889: about 1.9 million acres opened, some 50,000 racers, about 2 million acres claimed in a day; the early sneaks were the "Sooners." The land had been taken from Native nations — `native-nations` carries that loss.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Forced onto reservations, and the frontier line gone" -->
The Long Walk of the Navajo, 1863–64: about 8,500 people marched more than 300 miles to Bosque Redondo; about 200 died on the march, thousands more at the reservation before the 1868 return home. Shared with: `native-nations` (lead). The 1890 Census found no continuous frontier line; Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 essay named the change.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="amelia-stewart-knight" name="Amelia Stewart Knight" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Amelia Stewart Knight
Oregon Trail diarist, 1853 — Iowa to the Willamette Valley with her husband and seven children, pregnant the whole way; reached Oregon September 17 and gave birth the next day. Her diary records rain, dust, sick children, and river crossings. Placed here by director ruling 3 (1853 sits in 1850–1900).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="amelia-stewart-knight" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="levi-savage" name="Levi Savage" movie="17 Miracles (2011)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Levi Savage
> **Movie:** 17 Miracles (2011) — feature film about the Willie handcart company, built around Savage's journal.
Sub-captain of the Willie handcart company, age 36. At Florence on August 13, 1856, he urged the roughly 500 emigrants to wait until spring, warning of snow and death with over 1,000 miles to go; he was overruled and reprimanded — then stayed with the company and worked through the blizzards to keep people alive. His journal anchors most modern tellings.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="levi-savage" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-pap-singleton" name="Benjamin 'Pap' Singleton" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin "Pap" Singleton
Born enslaved near Nashville about 1809, escaped north and to Canada, returned about 1871, printed circulars and formed the Edgefield Real Estate and Homestead Association; testified that his work helped move more than 7,400 people and steered upward of 20,000 toward Kansas between 1877 and 1879 — the "Father of the Exodus."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-pap-singleton" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="laura-ingalls-wilder" name="Laura Ingalls Wilder" movie="Little House on the Prairie (NBC series, 1974-1983)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Laura Ingalls Wilder
> **Movie:** Little House on the Prairie (NBC series, 1974-1983) — nine seasons, 205 episodes, Michael Landon; loosely based on the books.
A real migrating family, documented move by move. Born February 7, 1867, near Pepin, Wisconsin; the family went to Kansas (1869–71) — the cabin stood on the Osage Diminished Reserve, land that still belonged to the Osage Nation — back to Pepin, then Walnut Grove, Minnesota (grasshopper plagues took the wheat, 1875–76), Burr Oak, Iowa, Walnut Grove again, and De Smet, Dakota Territory (1879, a railroad-camp job, then a homestead). In 1894 Laura, Almanzo, and Rose drove about 650 miles to Mansfield, Missouri; her trip diary was published as *On the Way Home* (1962). Tell honestly what the novels change: her Kansas age is raised, Burr Oak is left out, and the family was on Osage land it had no right to.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="laura-ingalls-wilder" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="migration" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The two largest internal movements of the century begin: Black Americans out of the South, and Plains farm families to California.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Great Migration" -->
About 6 million people, roughly 1910–1970; the first wave to 1940 heads to Northern and Midwestern cities, mostly by train. City Black populations 1910–20: Chicago up 148 percent, Detroit up 611 percent, Philadelphia up 500 percent, New York roughly doubled. The South held about 90 percent of Black Americans in 1900 and under 55 percent by 1970. Shared with: `city-building` (where they settled) · `rights-movements` (what drove them out and met them) · `work-workers` (the jobs).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Dust Bowl move" -->
Drought and windstorms strip the southern Plains in the 1930s; more than 250,000 people go to California about 1935–40 (Oklahoma's net out-migration about 440,000 — a different measure; state both), many on US Route 66.
