<a id="chapter-12-landmarks"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="12" slug="landmarks" title="Landmarks" part="3" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 12: Landmarks

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-08 — all ten eras verified against `research/research-landmarks.md`; every date, number, and name in this outline is sourced there.
**Angle:** Notable built structures and monuments — who built them, how, what it cost, and what has been argued about them.
**Keep out:** cities as wholes (`city-building`, incl. skyscrapers as urban form); houses as household life (`home-family`); engineering method (`technology`); the immigrant meaning of the Statue of Liberty (`immigration`); the battles at these places (`war`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/landmarks.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, cleared verify-queue, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-landmarks.md` (verified, all ten eras, inline sources).
**Date error fixed from v1:** Castillo de San Marcos (begun **1672**) sits in **the 1600s**; St. Augustine's founding (1565) stays in the 1500s.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="landmarks" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The oldest built landmarks in the country are Native, and some are enormous. Centuries before any European arrived, people here raised earthen mounds bigger at the base than Egypt's Great Pyramid, stone buildings of hundreds of rooms, and villages built into cliff walls. These are American landmarks — the first ones.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Monks Mound and the mound builders" -->
- Monks Mound at Cahokia (Illinois), built mostly c. 1050–1200: about 100 feet tall with a base of about 14 acres — a bigger footprint than the Great Pyramid of Giza (about 13 acres), though the pyramid is far taller. The largest earthen structure in the Americas. Shared with: `native-nations` (lead — the nation that built it) · `city-building` (Cahokia as a planned city).
- Poverty Point (Louisiana), c. 1700–1100 BC: five mounds and six concentric ridges built by hunter-fisher-gatherers; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.
- Serpent Mound (Ohio): a quarter-mile earthen snake. Builder dispute stated honestly — radiocarbon tests point to the Fort Ancient culture (c. 1070 AD) in one study and the Adena culture (c. 300 BC) in another; it may have been built and rebuilt in more than one period. Nobody resolves this by picking a side.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Stone buildings of the Southwest" -->
- Chaco Canyon great houses (New Mexico, c. 850–1150): Pueblo Bonito rose four stories and held some 600–650 rooms.
- Mesa Verde's Cliff Palace (Colorado, c. 1190–1280): about 150 rooms and 23 kivas built under a cliff overhang.
- No individual builder's name survives from any of these places; the book does not invent people.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="tribal-preservation-officer" name="(target) a tribal preservation officer at a mound or great-house site" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a tribal preservation officer
Research target — the honest Zoom 3 for this era is a documented modern descendant or tribal historic preservation officer who cares for one of these sites today (Native continuity to the present).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="tribal-preservation-officer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="landmarks" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Thin era, honestly: nothing the European newcomers built in this century still stands. Their forts were wood and earth, burned and rebuilt again and again — what survives of them is archaeology. The Native landmarks of the last era kept standing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="St. Augustine's founding site" -->
St. Augustine, Florida, founded September 1565 by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés — the oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the continental U.S. Francis Drake burned it in 1586. The era's landmark is the site itself; the stone fort comes in the next century. Shared with: `city-building` (lead — the town and the Laws of the Indies).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="landmarks" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The oldest European-built structures still standing in the country date from this century: a Spanish stone fort in Florida, an adobe chapel in Santa Fe, a wooden meetinghouse in Massachusetts.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The fort that swallowed cannonballs" -->
Castillo de San Marcos, St. Augustine — begun October 1672, finished 1695; the oldest masonry fort in the continental U.S. Built of coquina, a soft stone made of packed seashells. When English cannons fired on it — a two-month siege in 1702, a 27-day siege in 1740 — the balls did not shatter the walls; the shell stone crushed where they hit and the balls sank in or bounced off. Both sieges failed. In 1702 the town burned; the fort and the people sheltering inside it survived. Now a National Monument.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The oldest churches, told honestly" -->
- San Miguel Chapel, Santa Fe: adobe church built c. 1610–1626 by Tlaxcalan workers from Mexico; burned in the 1680 Pueblo Revolt; rebuilt 1710 on the old foundations. Often called the oldest church in the country — honest version: the site and foundations are that old, the standing walls are mostly the 1710 rebuild.
- Old Ship Meetinghouse, Hingham, Massachusetts, 1681: the only surviving 17th-century Puritan meetinghouse, and the oldest church building in continuous use in the U.S. Its timber roof frame looked to the congregation like a ship's hull turned upside down.
- The Palace of the Governors in Santa Fe (c. 1610) is `city-building`'s story.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="castillo-builder" name="(target) a laborer who built the Castillo" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a laborer who built the Castillo
Research target — Spanish records document the Castillo's 23-year workforce (Spanish, conscripted, and Native workers) collectively; a documented named individual has not yet been verified.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="castillo-builder" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="landmarks" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial towns start building public structures meant to last: churches with tall steeples, a lighthouse at a harbor mouth, a statehouse of brick with a bell tower.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Steeples and a statehouse" -->
- Old North Church, Boston, 1723 — the oldest church building standing in Boston; its steeple (finished 1740) was the tallest thing in town. Its fame came later: the two lanterns of April 18, 1775 (that night's events belong to `war`).
- Independence Hall, Philadelphia — built 1732–1753 as the Pennsylvania State House, designed by Andrew Hamilton with master carpenter Edmund Woolley; the bell inscribed "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land" hung in the new tower in 1753. What was signed inside is `government-politics`; the building is ours.
- The Alamo — Mission San Antonio de Valero, founded 1718 in San Antonio; stone church cornerstone laid May 8, 1744; that church collapsed in the 1750s, and the famous stone front begun in 1758 was never finished by the missionaries — no bell towers, no dome. The 1836 battle is `war`'s.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first lighthouse" -->
Boston Light, on Little Brewster Island — first lit September 16, 1716, the first lighthouse in the colonies. The British blew it up in 1776; the tower standing today is the 1783 rebuild. Say both dates plainly.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="george-worthylake" name="George Worthylake" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### George Worthylake
> **Who:** the first lighthouse keeper in America, at Boston Light from 1716. · **When and where:** Little Brewster Island, Boston Harbor, 1716–1718.
Keeping the light meant living on a bare island with his family. On November 3, 1718, returning from a sermon in town, Worthylake's canoe capsized within sight of the lighthouse; he drowned with his wife Ann, his daughter Ruth, and three others, including Shadwell, a man he enslaved. A 12-year-old Boston boy named Benjamin Franklin printed a street ballad about the drowning, "The Lighthouse Tragedy," and sold it in the streets — Franklin later called his own verses "wretched stuff," and no copy survives. Days later the replacement keeper drowned too. The light stayed lit anyway; someone always kept it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="george-worthylake" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="landmarks" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The new country starts building for itself — a president's house and a capitol modeled on ancient temples. Enslaved people did much of the building. That is a verified fact, and this chapter says it plainly.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Raising the capital's buildings" -->
- The President's House (the White House): cornerstone October 13, 1792; designed by Irish-born architect James Hoban. The U.S. Capitol: cornerstone September 18, 1793, laid by George Washington. Neither was finished by 1800 — John Adams moved into a house of wet plaster and bare stairs.
- Enslaved workers labored at every stage of both buildings: quarrying the sandstone, cutting timber, making bricks, sawing, carpentry. The government hired them from their owners, and the owners collected the pay. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the system itself) · `city-building` (L'Enfant's street plan, theirs).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="white-house-enslaved-carpenters" name="Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry, and Daniel" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry, and Daniel
> **Who:** five enslaved carpenters who helped build the White House, known by name from a surviving payroll. · **When and where:** the President's House construction site, Washington, May 1795.
The May 1795 carpenters' payroll lists them by first name only: Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry, Daniel. Four were held by the architect James Hoban himself, one by his assistant Pierce Purcell. That month Peter and Ben each worked 28 days, Daniel 25, Harry 9 — and Hoban signed for their wages, because the pay went to the owners, not the workers. The building they raised became the most famous house in the country. Their last names, their lives before and after — not recorded.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="white-house-enslaved-carpenters" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Landmark houses" -->
Mount Vernon and Monticello — the era's most visited houses today, both built and run by enslaved workers. Monticello: Jefferson began it in 1769, tore into it again from 1796, called it done about 1809. (The households inside are `home-family`'s subject; these appear here as built landmarks only.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-jefferson-landmarks" name="Thomas Jefferson" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Thomas Jefferson
> **Who:** author of the Declaration who was also the new country's most influential amateur architect. · **When and where:** Monticello, begun 1769, rebuilt 1796–1809; his temple-form Virginia Capitol design, 1785.
Jefferson designed Monticello himself and kept redesigning it for forty years — visitors found it half-built for most of his life. His Virginia State Capitol, modeled on a Roman temple, helped set the classical look that Washington's public buildings copied. The skilled hands executing his drawings were largely enslaved craftsmen; one of them, the joiner John Hemmings, carries the next era's story.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-jefferson-landmarks" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="landmarks" label="1800 to 1850" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Thinner era: the country begins putting up monuments to its own short history — and shows it cannot yet finish them. Both of the era's big obelisks stalled for lack of money.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Two obelisks, slowly" -->
- Bunker Hill Monument, Charlestown: cornerstone June 17, 1825, with Lafayette present; funds ran out repeatedly; a women's fair organized by Sarah Josepha Hale in 1840 raised $30,000 of the cost; the 221-foot granite obelisk was finished in 1842 and dedicated in 1843.
- The Washington Monument: cornerstone July 4, 1848, before a crowd of about 20,000. By 1854 the money was gone and work stopped at about 150 feet. That year members of the anti-Catholic Know-Nothing movement stole the marble block donated by Pope Pius IX — the "Pope stone" — and by the usual account threw it in the Potomac; it was never found. Know-Nothings then seized the monument society itself (1855–58). The stub stood for a generation. The finish belongs to the next era.
- The Smithsonian's red sandstone Castle went up 1847–1855 (architect James Renwick Jr.).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-hemmings-landmarks" name="John Hemmings" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### John Hemmings
> **Who:** enslaved master joiner whose hands made Monticello's finest woodwork. · **When and where:** Monticello and Poplar Forest, Virginia; his lead years c. 1800–1826.
Trained from age 17 under hired white joiners, Hemmings (1776–1833) made the decorative moldings, doors, and furniture of the rebuilt Monticello and led the woodwork at Jefferson's Poplar Forest retreat. Jefferson's will freed him in 1826 — one of only five people it freed — and gave him the tools of the joiner's shop he had worked in all his life. The house tourists admire is, room after room, his craftsmanship. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the Hemings family's larger story, theirs).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-hemmings-landmarks" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="landmarks" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Iron, steel, and stone make structures nobody could have built fifty years earlier: a bridge hung from steel cables, a copper woman taller than any building around her, a stone obelisk finished at last as the tallest structure on earth.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Finishing the Capitol dome" -->
The Capitol's new iron dome rose through the Civil War, topped December 2, 1863 by the bronze Statue of Freedom — cast with the skill of an enslaved craftsman who was a free man by the day it was raised.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="philip-reid-landmarks" name="Philip Reid" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Philip Reid
> **Who:** enslaved foundry craftsman who helped cast the Statue of Freedom for the Capitol dome. · **When and where:** Clark Mills' foundry outside Washington, 1860–1863.
When the Italian sculptor-foreman demanded extra pay to reveal how to take apart the statue's plaster model, Reid — born enslaved in Charleston about 1820 — worked out how to do it himself with a pulley and tackle. He was paid $1.25 a day, more than the laborers around him, but only Sunday's pay was his; his owner took the other six days. Congress freed the capital's enslaved people on April 16, 1862, so when Freedom was bolted onto the dome in December 1863, Philip Reid was a free man. He stayed in Washington and worked as a plasterer under the name he chose to sign: Philip Reed.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="philip-reid-landmarks" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Brooklyn Bridge" -->
Opened May 24, 1883 — the longest suspension bridge in the world then, hung from steel cables between two stone towers. It cost the family that built it: at least 20 workers died, and caisson disease — "the bends," from working in compressed air underwater — crippled many more. Shared with: `technology` (suspension-bridge engineering as method) · `work-workers` (the caisson crews).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="roeblings" name="John, Washington, and Emily Roebling" movie="Brooklyn Bridge (1981)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John, Washington, and Emily Roebling
> **Who:** the designer of the Brooklyn Bridge, the son who built it, and the wife who carried the work when the son could not. · **When and where:** New York, 1869–1883. · **Movie:** *Brooklyn Bridge* (1981) — Ken Burns' first documentary, about the bridge; Academy Award nominee.
John Roebling designed the bridge but never built it: in 1869 a ferry crushed his foot during surveying, he refused doctors' treatment, and died of tetanus within weeks. His son Washington took over — then wrecked his health in the compressed-air caissons and directed the rest of the work part-paralyzed from a Brooklyn room, watching through a telescope. His wife Emily Warren Roebling became the connection: for 11 years she studied cable construction and bridge mathematics so she could carry accurate instructions to the engineers, answer their questions, and face down trustees who tried to fire her husband. Honest version of a popular claim: Washington kept the title and made the engineering decisions; Emily held the whole enterprise together, and the engineers dealt with her daily. At the opening she crossed first by carriage, carrying a rooster for victory.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="roeblings" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Washington Monument, finished" -->
Congress took the stalled stub over in 1876; Army engineers restarted work in 1879 and set the capstone December 6, 1884 — with a 100-ounce aluminum tip, a metal then so rare it cost about a dollar an ounce, a day's wage. At 555 feet it was the tallest structure in the world until the Eiffel Tower (1889). About 150 feet up, the marble visibly changes shade — the restart used stone from different quarry beds. The 25-year stop is written on the monument itself.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Building the Statue of Liberty" -->
France gave the statue; America had to build the pedestal. Bartholdi's completed right arm and torch stood at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial fair, then in Madison Square Park for five years, to coax donations. Gustave Eiffel engineered the iron skeleton inside (from 1879) — a copper skin about as thick as two pennies put together, hung on an iron frame. Pedestal money stalled until publisher Joseph Pulitzer's New York World campaign of 1885: about 120,000 donors, most giving less than a dollar — schoolchildren's pennies among them — every name printed in the paper. Dedicated October 28, 1886. Emma Lazarus's poem went up on a plaque in 1903; what the statue came to mean to arriving immigrants is `immigration`'s story. Shared with: `immigration` (lead on its meaning) · `news-communication` (Pulitzer's newspaper as engine).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederic-auguste-bartholdi" name="Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi
> **Who:** French sculptor of the Statue of Liberty. · **When and where:** Paris workshops, 1870s–1884; New York Harbor, dedicated October 28, 1886.
Bartholdi spent over 15 years on one statue: sketching the harbor figure by 1870, scaling plaster models up stage by stage, shipping the finished statue to New York in 350 pieces packed in 214 crates. He toured America selling the idea, put the torch arm in a Philadelphia fairground and the head at a Paris fair, and lived to see the statue lit in the harbor.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederic-auguste-bartholdi" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What else the era built" -->
Biltmore House, Asheville (1889–1895): George W. Vanderbilt's 250-room house, about 179,000 square feet — still the largest privately owned house in the country. The first steel-frame tall office buildings rose in Chicago from 1885 — as a change in how cities grew, they are `city-building`'s story. Yellowstone became the first national park in 1872 — parks as land policy are `land-environment`'s.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="landmarks" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The most photographed American structures nearly all go up in one stretch between the wars: a marble memorial, four faces on a mountain, the tallest building on earth, the longest bridge span, the biggest dam. The stories underneath them are harder than the postcards.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Lincoln Memorial" -->
Dedicated May 30, 1922 — Henry Bacon's marble temple, Daniel Chester French's seated Lincoln. The dedication crowd was segregated, and the one Black speaker, Robert Russa Moton, had his speech text vetted first. Seventeen years later, on Easter Sunday 1939, after the Daughters of the American Revolution barred her from Constitution Hall, Marian Anderson sang from its steps to about 75,000 people. The concert is `rights-movements`' story; the memorial that became the country's stage for it is ours. Shared with: `rights-movements` (lead on the concert and the 1963 March).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mount Rushmore — both halves of the story" -->
Carved October 1927 to October 31, 1941 by about 400 workers — 90 percent of the shaping done with dynamite, no worker killed. Both halves told plainly: the mountain is Tunkasila Sakpe, the Six Grandfathers, in the Black Hills — land guaranteed to the Lakota by the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty and taken after gold was found in 1874. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the taking violated the treaty; the Lakota refused the payment — over a billion dollars with interest now — because the land was never for sale. Shared with: `native-nations` (lead — the Black Hills and the treaty) · `art` (mountain sculpture as art).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gutzon-borglum" name="Gutzon Borglum" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Gutzon Borglum
> **Who:** the sculptor of Mount Rushmore — told honestly, including where he worked before. · **When and where:** Stone Mountain, Georgia, 1915–1925; the Black Hills, 1927–1941.
Before Rushmore, Borglum carved the Confederate memorial at Stone Mountain, a project funded partly by the revived Ku Klux Klan; historians document that he attended Klan meetings and was deep in Klan politics, though no membership record survives. Fired from Stone Mountain after quarrels, he took the South Dakota job and drove it for 14 years — engineering the pointing machine that scaled his models up, directing the dynamite crews, fighting for funding through the Depression. He died in March 1941, months before the money ran out and the carving stopped for good. Both facts stand together: the four faces are his work, and so is the company he kept.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gutzon-borglum" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nick-clifford" name="Nick Clifford" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Nick Clifford
> **Who:** the youngest Mount Rushmore worker, hired at 17 — and the last one living. · **When and where:** Keystone, South Dakota, 1938–1940; died 2019 at 98.
Donald "Nick" Clifford got the job partly because the Borglums wanted a pitcher for the crew's baseball team. He earned 55 cents an hour running the winch that lowered drillers down the faces, and drilled dynamite holes himself. He outlived every other carver, spent his last decades answering visitors' questions at the memorial, and died in November 2019 — the last person alive who had hung off that mountain.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nick-clifford" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Empire State Building" -->
Opened May 1, 1931 — 102 stories, built in about 410 days, the steel frame rising four and a half floors a week with up to 3,400 workers a day. Five workers died — the official count; the "hundreds" of legend is false. Lewis Hine photographed the riveting gangs for *Men at Work*; among them were Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake, whose community had built high steel since the 1880s — Native builders on the tallest thing in the world. Shared with: `work-workers` (lead on Hine's photographs and the trade) · `city-building` (the skyscraper as urban form).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Golden Gate Bridge" -->
Opened May 1937 — 200,000 people walked it on opening day. Credit told honestly: chief engineer Joseph Strauss got the statue and the plaque, but structural engineer Charles Ellis did the detailed design and calculations in 1929–31, was fired by Strauss before construction, and was only given principal design credit by the bridge district in 2007. Eleven workers died — ten of them on one day, February 17, 1937, when a falling work platform tore through the safety net. Shared with: `disasters` (the February 1937 collapse) · `technology` (suspension engineering).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-strauss" name="Joseph Strauss" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Joseph Strauss
> **Who:** chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge, whose real innovation was safety. · **When and where:** San Francisco, 1933–1937.
Strauss spent about $130,000 of Depression money on something no big American bridge job had used: a giant rope net slung under the whole deck. It caught 19 falling men over four years — they formed the "Halfway to Hell Club." He also required hard hats. The honest ledger: he took more design credit than he had earned (Charles Ellis's numbers held the bridge up), and his safety net saved more lives than any calculation he made.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-strauss" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="al-zampa" name="Al Zampa" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Al Zampa
> **Who:** ironworker who fell off the Golden Gate Bridge and lived — a founding member of the Halfway to Hell Club. · **When and where:** the Marin tower side, October 19, 1936.
Alfred Zampa, from Crockett, California, slipped on wet steel and fell — but near the shore the net sagged onto the rocks, and he broke four bones in his back. Twelve weeks in the hospital, two years in a steel brace, then back onto high steel for the rest of his career. In 2003 California named the new Carquinez Strait bridge the Alfred Zampa Memorial Bridge — a major American bridge named for a working ironworker.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="al-zampa" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hoover Dam" -->
Dedicated September 30, 1935. The deaths, honestly: the official count is 96 industrial fatalities — and it leaves out the tunnel men whose deaths were recorded as "pneumonia," which many historians read as carbon-monoxide poisoning, so the true toll is higher and not exactly known. And the legend, debunked plainly: nobody is buried in the concrete. The dam was poured as many small blocks in shallow layers with crews working over every pour — a body could not have been left inside. Shared with: `work-workers` (conditions in the canyon) · `energy` (the power it made) · `land-environment` (what damming the river did).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="landmarks" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The era builds a steel arch taller than any monument before it and twin towers taller than any building — and then, at its end, a memorial that is not a statue or a temple at all, but a wall of names cut into the ground.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Gateway Arch" -->
Eero Saarinen won the St. Louis design competition in 1948; he died in 1961, before a single piece was set. Built February 1963 to October 28, 1965: 630 feet tall, 630 feet wide, stainless steel. Insurers predicted 13 deaths; no worker died. On July 14, 1964, activists Percy Green and Richard Daly climbed 125 feet up the unfinished north leg to protest that no Black workers were on the job — the landmark's own construction became a civil-rights stage. Shared with: `rights-movements` (lead on the campaign) · `migration` (the westward-expansion meaning it memorializes).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="harold-mccomber" name="Harold McComber" movie="High Steel (1965)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Harold McComber
> **Who:** Mohawk ironworker from Kahnawake, one of the high-steel men who built New York's skylines. · **When and where:** Manhattan skyscrapers and the Kahnawake community near Montreal, filmed 1965. · **Movie:** *High Steel* (1965) — National Film Board short documentary about McComber himself.
Kahnawake men had worked high steel since the 1880s, through the 1907 Quebec Bridge collapse that killed 33 of them (that calamity is the disasters chapter's), and on to the Empire State Building and the towers after it. The 1965 documentary follows McComber at work on the beams above Manhattan and home in Kahnawake — Native builders, generations deep, still raising the country's landmarks. Native continuity past 1900, on film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="harold-mccomber" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The World Trade Center" -->
Ribbon-cut April 4, 1973 — Minoru Yamasaki's twin 110-story towers; the North Tower's 1,368 feet briefly the world's tallest, passed within weeks by Chicago's Sears Tower. The Space Needle (1962, 605 feet, built in about 400 days for Seattle's World's Fair) marks the same years' confidence.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="philippe-petit" name="Philippe Petit" movie="Man on Wire (2008)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Philippe Petit
> **Who:** French high-wire walker who crossed between the Twin Towers on a cable. · **When and where:** New York, August 7, 1974. · **Movie:** *Man on Wire* (2008) — Academy Award winner, Best Documentary Feature; about the walk itself.
Petit and his friends spent months planning, smuggled their equipment to the top floors, and rigged a cable between the roofs overnight. At dawn he stepped out — about 1,350 feet up, no net — and crossed eight times in 45 minutes while police waited at both ends. Charges were dropped in exchange for a free children's show in Central Park. The stunt did what the buildings' owners had struggled to do: it made New Yorkers love the towers.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="philippe-petit" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Vietnam Veterans Memorial" -->
Dedicated November 13, 1982: two walls of polished black granite set into the Mall, carrying the names of the more than 58,000 dead in the order they fell. The design was attacked before it was built — one veteran called it "a black gash of shame" — and the compromise added Frederick Hart's Three Servicemen statue nearby in 1984. Then people came, touched the names, left letters and boots and photographs at its base, and it became the most visited memorial in Washington. Shared with: `war` (the war and its veterans, theirs).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="maya-lin" name="Maya Lin" movie="Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision (1994)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Maya Lin
> **Who:** the 21-year-old college student whose design won the Vietnam Veterans Memorial competition. · **When and where:** Yale and Washington, D.C., 1981–1982. · **Movie:** *Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision* (1994) — Academy Award winner, Best Documentary Feature; about Lin herself.
Lin drafted the design for a college class, entered the blind competition, and her entry number 1,026 beat 1,420 others — the judges did not know the winner was a Chinese American undergraduate. Through months of public attack on her design and on her, she defended the idea that a memorial could be a quiet cut in the earth that hands you the names and lets you grieve. Her name went unmentioned at the 1982 dedication ceremony. The wall vindicated her; she spent the rest of her career building memorials and art on her own terms.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="maya-lin" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Restoring the old landmarks" -->
The Statue of Liberty was stripped and restored for its centennial, its 1886 torch replaced with a gold-leafed replica, and rededicated July 4, 1986. Ellis Island — added to the Statue of Liberty National Monument in 1965 — had its ruined main building restored into the Immigration Museum by 1990. The arrival stories those buildings hold are `immigration`'s; their rescue as structures is ours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="landmarks" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Current through 2026. The country builds memorials to loss — the towers' footprints turned to pools, a museum sheathed in bronze lattice — while taking down hundreds of older monuments and arguing about which should stand.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ground Zero rebuilt" -->
The National September 11 Memorial opened September 11, 2011: two recessed pools in the Twin Towers' footprints, the victims' names in bronze around the rims — "Reflecting Absence," by architect Michael Arad with Peter Walker, chosen from 5,201 competition entries. The museum below opened May 21, 2014. One World Trade Center opened November 3, 2014 — 1,776 feet to the spire, the number chosen for the Declaration's year. The attacks are `america-world`'s and `disasters`' to tell; what was built afterward is ours. Shared with: `america-world` (the attacks, lead) · `disasters` (the response).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="michael-arad" name="Michael Arad" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Michael Arad
> **Who:** the architect of the 9/11 Memorial. · **When and where:** New York, competition won 2004, memorial opened 2011.
Arad, a 34-year-old architect then working for a New York City government agency, first imagined the memorial as two voids torn in the Hudson River — absence made visible. His competition entry beat 5,200 others, then survived seven years of redesigns, budget fights, and grieving families' demands about how the names should be arranged. He held to the core: the footprints stay open, the water falls, the names surround it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="michael-arad" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="New monuments on the Mall" -->
The Martin Luther King, Jr. Memorial was dedicated October 16, 2011 — the first memorial to an African American on the National Mall area. The National Museum of African American History and Culture opened September 24, 2016, its three-tiered bronze "corona" designed by architect David Adjaye, the lattice patterned on ironwork made by enslaved and free Black craftsmen in the South.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Monuments coming down — ongoing history" -->
After the Charleston church murders (2015), the deadly Charlottesville rally held around a Lee statue (2017), and the George Floyd protests (2020), hundreds of Confederate monuments were removed — the Southern Poverty Law Center (an advocacy group's count, labeled as such) tallied at least 168 Confederate symbols removed in 2020 alone; Richmond's giant Robert E. Lee statue came down September 8, 2021 (news accounts: Washington Post, AP). Hundreds still stand, and the argument continues — what monuments are for is the `how-we-know` afterword's question. Also in these years: the Gateway Arch grounds became Gateway Arch National Park (2018), and Angel Island's poem-carved barracks — National Historic Landmark since 1997 — finished restoration in 2009.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

<a id="chapter-13-elements"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="13" slug="elements" title="The Elements" part="3" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 13: The Elements

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-08 (enriched from the verified bank; research pass was done 2026-07-23)
**Angle:** Chemical elements as used, mined, named, and discovered in connection with the U.S. **No false firsts.**
**Keep out:** weapons use (`war`); the cyclotron as machine (`technology`); mining money (`economy`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/elements.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-elements.md` (Jon's master element table verified, 7 cells corrected; all ten eras sourced; corrections log at the end)
**Honesty rules:** helium, aluminum, and oxygen were discovered abroad — the American story is use, process, supply, or production. Priority disputes with Soviet labs are stated, not resolved. Superheavy elements are international collaborations: atoms made at Dubna, joint teams, IUPAC crediting the collaborations — "made together," never "discovered by the U.S."
**Film note:** *Radium Girls* (2018) rides with `work-workers`' Grace Fryer story (the court fight is their lead); this chapter's radium story carries no Movie line.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="elements" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
People here worked metals for thousands of years without any idea of an element — because nobody on Earth had that idea yet. The land was entirely Native land, and its metalworkers are known through their pits and tools, not their names.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="among the world's first coppersmiths" -->
- The Old Copper Complex of the Lake Superior country (present-day Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota): Native miners dug veins of pure "native" copper and hammered it into spearpoints, knives, awls, fishhooks, and ornaments. A 2021 re-dating (53 radiocarbon dates, Pompeani et al., *Radiocarbon*) puts the start **at least 9,500 years ago** — about 3,500 years earlier than once thought, peak about 7,000–5,000 years ago. Say "among the world's first coppersmiths," not "the first" — the oldest documented Middle East copper pendant is about 8,700 years old (*Science* news, Mar 2021; Archaeology Magazine).
- Lake Superior copper moved hundreds of miles on Native trade networks, the same routes that carried shells, turquoise, and obsidian. Shared with: `native-nations` (the nations and their trade).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="iron from the sky" -->
- Before smelting, the only workable iron metal on the continent fell from space. Twenty-two iron beads from Hopewell burial mounds near Havana, Illinois (excavated 1945), made about 2,000 years ago, came from the Anoka, Minnesota meteorite — metal carried or traded several hundred miles and worked with the same hammering skills used on copper (McCoy et al., *Journal of Archaeological Science* 2017; Smithsonian).
- Also in use: gold and silver ornaments in some regions, red and yellow ochre pigments (iron oxides), salt gathered and traded, flint and chert tools — materials skill without atomic theory. No named individuals are documented this far back; this era has no featured story on purpose.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="elements" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A thin era, said plainly: element science existed nowhere on Earth yet — Europe was still in the age of alchemy, and the metals in use here were the same copper, gold, and meteoritic iron as before.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="gold hunts that found nothing" -->
- Spaniards came hunting two elements. De Soto (1539–43) crossed the Southeast and Coronado (1540–42) the Southwest chasing stories of golden cities; neither found gold or silver in the future United States. The century's great silver strikes were in Mexico and South America. Shared with: `exploration` (the journeys themselves).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="elements" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first American industry that made a metal was iron, and it took two tries — one ended in an attack, one ran for about two decades.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Falling Creek and Saugus" -->
- Falling Creek, Virginia: the Virginia Company began building an ironworks in 1619 near present-day Richmond; on March 22, 1622, forces coordinated by the Powhatan leader Opechancanough destroyed the works and killed twenty-seven people there, part of the wide 1622 attacks. It was never successfully rebuilt (Encyclopedia Virginia; Virginia DHR). Shared with: `native-nations` (the 1622 war from the Powhatan side).
- Saugus, Massachusetts: the works called Hammersmith, begun 1646 under Richard Leader on the Saugus River — the first integrated ironworks in North America: blast furnace, forge, and a rolling and slitting mill on one site, powered by seven waterwheels, fed on bog iron scooped from swamps and ponds. It ran until about 1668–1670 and is now Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site (NPS; ASME).
- The iron story here is use and industry, not discovery — iron had been smelted in the Old World for thousands of years. Abroad, chemistry began separating from alchemy (Boyle's *Sceptical Chymist*, 1661); every element discovery of the century (phosphorus, Hamburg, 1669) happened in Europe.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="elements" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial iron grew from a few furnaces into a world-scale industry — everyday metals, no discoveries. Element science was still entirely European.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="iron third in the world, and the Iron Act" -->
- Ironworks spread through New England, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, and New Jersey; by mid-century the colonies exported raw iron to Britain. By the Revolution colonial iron was commonly ranked third in the world, ahead of England and Wales (Britannica; Penn Libraries).
- Parliament's Iron Act of 1750 welcomed colonial raw iron but banned new colonial mills for finished ironware. Colonists ignored it — more than sixty new works were built in defiance, about twenty in Pennsylvania (Britannica "Iron Act").
- Other elements in colonial life: lead for shot and pewter, copper and brass for kettles and buttons, silver and gold arriving as Spanish coin. Shared with: `money` (coin as a money system).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="elements" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In Europe, chemistry became a science and defined what an element is (Lavoisier, Scheele, and others). The American contribution was use, ore — and one immigrant who had already made his discovery before he arrived.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="three elements in every pocket" -->
- The Coinage Act of April 2, 1792 created the U.S. Mint and a coinage of gold (eagles), silver (dollars and smaller), and copper (cents) — element chemistry as daily money (U.S. Mint history). Shared with: `money` (lead — the money system).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-priestley" name="Joseph Priestley" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Joseph Priestley
> **Who:** the English chemist credited with discovering oxygen, who spent his last decade as an immigrant in Pennsylvania. · **When and where:** discovered oxygen August 1, 1774, in England; emigrated 1794; Northumberland, Pennsylvania, until his death February 6, 1804.
Heated mercuric oxide with a burning lens and isolated the gas later named oxygen — state the shared history honestly: Scheele in Sweden found it earlier but published later, and Lavoisier named it. Priestley also invented carbonated water (Leeds, 1767) and gave rubber its English name in 1770, for rubbing out pencil marks. A dissenting minister, he saw a mob burn his Birmingham home and laboratory in 1791 and left England in 1794. At Northumberland he built the best chemical laboratory in the young country (house finished 1798) and identified carbon monoxide there. American chemists met at his house in 1874, on the oxygen centennial — a gathering that led toward the American Chemical Society (1876); the house is a National Historic Landmark (ACS landmark; Science History Institute; Joseph Priestley House). **No false first: the discovery was English.** Shared with: `immigration` (the arrival).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-priestley" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="conrad-reed" name="Conrad Reed" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Conrad Reed
> **Who:** the 12-year-old farm boy who found the first authenticated gold in the United States. · **When and where:** Little Meadow Creek, Cabarrus County, North Carolina, 1799.
Pulled a heavy yellow rock — a 17-pound gold nugget — out of the creek on his father John Reed's farm. The family did not know what it was and used it as a doorstop for about three years, until a jeweler identified it in 1802 and bought it from John Reed for $3.50, roughly a week's wages, when it was worth about $3,600. The first authenticated U.S. gold discovery; the mining it set off unfolds in the next era (NCpedia; Reed Gold Mine state historic site). By the boundary rule he stays here in 1750–1800.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="conrad-reed" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="elements" label="1800 to 1850" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
America's first mineral rushes began — and the first big one was copper, not gold. Still no American element discovery: while Davy, Berzelius, and others isolated element after element in Europe, none was found here. An honest "not yet."
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="gold in the South, copper in the North" -->
- Mining grew at Reed's farm and neighboring North Carolina creeks from 1803; the Georgia gold rush followed in 1829. North Carolina led U.S. gold production until California (NCpedia). Shared with: `migration` (the 1849 crowds) · `economy` (the money).
- The nation's first mineral rush was Michigan copper. After state geologist Douglass Houghton reported on the Keweenaw Peninsula's pure native copper in the early 1840s, thousands of prospectors poured into the Upper Peninsula from 1843 — five years before California gold. By 1849 the district produced 96 percent of U.S. copper, dug from veins Native miners had worked for thousands of years (NPS Keweenaw NHP).
- Lead mining grew in the Galena district of Illinois and Wisconsin — the town of Galena is named for the lead ore — and in Missouri. Shared with: `economy` (mining as business).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Ontonagon Boulder" -->
- A 3,708-pound boulder of pure native copper from the Ontonagon River country, long known and held sacred by the Ojibwe, was hauled away in 1843 by Detroit merchant Julius Eldred, seized by the War Department, and placed in the Smithsonian in 1860. The Keweenaw Bay Indian Community formally asked for its return in 1991; the Smithsonian refused. State the taking and the still-open request plainly (Smithsonian records; The Mining Gazette 2025). Shared with: `native-nations` (lead — the taking and the refused repatriation).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="elements" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The periodic table was published abroad, and the first great American element story was not a discovery but a process — a woodshed experiment that cut aluminum's price roughly ninety percent within a decade.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="silver underfoot, and a table from Russia" -->
- The Comstock Lode, Virginia City, Nevada, 1859 — the richest silver deposit found in North America (Britannica). Shared with: `migration` (the rush) · `money` (the silver question).
- Dmitri Mendeleev published the periodic system in Russia in 1869 and used it to predict undiscovered elements. Context the chapter needs: the table every later American discovery slotted into was a Russian invention — a fact that pays off in 1955 when Berkeley names element 101 for him.
- Copper became the nerve metal of cities as electric light and the telephone spread; Michigan, then Butte, Montana, supplied the wire. Shared with: `technology` (the inventions) · `economy` (the copper business).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="aluminum: from Tiffany's showpiece to everyday metal" -->
- In 1884 the government capped the finished Washington Monument with a 100-ounce aluminum pyramid — aluminum then a semiprecious rarity at about $1 an ounce, the price of silver. Philadelphia foundryman William Frishmuth cast it for $225, the largest aluminum casting yet made; before installation it sat on the floor at Tiffany's in New York so visitors could step over the top of the Washington Monument. Set in place December 6, 1884 (NPS; TMS/JOM; National Archives *Prologue*). Shared with: `landmarks` (the monument itself).
- After Hall's 1886 process reached industry, aluminum fell from about $12 a pound in the early 1880s to about $2, then under $1 by the mid-1890s (about 78 cents by 1893). His backers' Pittsburgh Reduction Company (1888) became the Aluminum Company of America — Alcoa — in 1907. A metal displayed at Tiffany's became foil and pots-and-pans cheap (Science History Institute; ACS landmark). Shared with: `economy` (Alcoa as an industry).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="charles-martin-hall-julia-brainerd-hall" name="Charles Martin Hall and Julia Brainerd Hall" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Charles Martin Hall and Julia Brainerd Hall
> **Who:** the 22-year-old Ohio college graduate who invented the cheap way to make aluminum, and the chemist sister whose notes helped win the patent fight. · **When and where:** the family woodshed, Oberlin, Ohio, February 23, 1886.
Fresh out of Oberlin College, working with homemade batteries, Hall dissolved aluminum oxide in molten cryolite, ran electricity through it, and got beads of aluminum metal. His older sister Julia Brainerd Hall, an Oberlin chemistry graduate, assisted, witnessed, and documented the experiments — her notes later mattered in the patent fight. The Frenchman Paul Héroult hit the same process independently the same year (both men born 1863, both discovered it 1886, both died 1914), so it is fairly called the Hall–Héroult process — it still makes the world's aluminum (ACS National Historic Chemical Landmark, dedicated at Oberlin 1997; Science History Institute). **No false first on the element: aluminum was known abroad; the American story is the process.**
<!-- hb-story:end slug="charles-martin-hall-julia-brainerd-hall" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the helium near-miss" -->
- About 1890, USGS chemist William Hillebrand extracted an unreactive gas from uranium ore and recorded it as nitrogen. In 1895 William Ramsay in London, following up that paper, ran the gas through a spectroscope and saw the yellow line of helium — known in the sun since 1868, never before found on Earth. The element credit is British; the ore-gas trail ran through American rock, and the American helium story proper starts in the next era (Chemistry World; Ramsay biographies).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="elements" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In fifty years the United States went from no element discoveries to making elements that had never existed — and part of the era's element story was paid for in workers' bodies.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the well that would not burn" -->
- May 1903: a drilling company hit a roaring gas well on William Greenwell's farm near Dexter, Kansas. The town pushed a burning hay bale toward the gusher to light a celebration flame — and the gas put the fire out. Locals scoffed at the "wind gas"; geologist Erasmus Haworth carried samples to the University of Kansas, where Hamilton P. Cady and David F. McFarland showed on December 7, 1905 that it was 1.84 percent helium — an element thought vanishingly rare on Earth, sitting in quantity under the Great Plains (ACS landmark 2000; KU History).
- Helium went strategic: the Helium Act of 1925 created federal production and the Federal Helium Reserve, stored underground in the Bush Dome at the Cliffside field near Amarillo, Texas — for decades nearly all the world's helium. A 1927 law barred exports, which is why Germany's Hindenburg flew on flammable hydrogen and burned at Lakehurst on May 6, 1937. After the disaster FDR weighed selling helium to Germany; Interior Secretary Harold Ickes refused after Hitler annexed Austria in 1938 (Texas State Historical Association; State Dept. FRUS 1938). Shared with: `economy` (lead — the helium industry) · `war` (strategic supply) · `disasters` (the Hindenburg fire).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the radium craze" -->
- Radium — discovered by the Curies in France in 1898, no false first — was painted onto watch dials, sold in quack tonics, and marketed as health itself. This chapter's angle is the element: what radium is, why it glows, and how it settles in bone.
- Wealthy Pittsburgh industrialist Eben Byers drank about 1,400 bottles of Radithor, radium dissolved in water, from 1927–30; it destroyed his bones and killed him in 1932, and his death pushed the government to act against radioactive cures. (Writer's caution from the bank: the famous "jaw came off" headline is a 1990 retrospective, not from 1932.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="radium-girls-elements" name="The Radium Girls" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### The Radium Girls
> **Who:** young women — many teenagers — who painted glowing radium numbers on watch and instrument dials and were poisoned by the paint. · **When and where:** U.S. Radium Corporation, Orange, New Jersey, from 1917; Radium Dial, Ottawa, Illinois, into the 1930s.
Taught to point their brushes with their lips — "lip, dip, paint" — they went home glowing; some were called ghost girls. The radium settled in their bones like calcium; jaws crumbled ("radium jaw"), and women in their twenties began dying. Grace Fryer, painting from April 10, 1917, led four dying co-workers into court in 1927; the company settled in June 1928 — $10,000 each, a $600-a-year pension, and medical bills. In Illinois, Catherine Wolfe Donohue, so ill she collapsed testifying, won in 1938 and died within months (Library of Congress "Living Dead Women"; History.com). The court fight and what it changed for workers leads in `work-workers`, which carries the film *Radium Girls* (2018) with Fryer's story; the health science is `health`'s. This chapter leads on the element itself.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="radium-girls-elements" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a false first, and the machine that opened the door" -->
- 1931: physicist Fred Allison of Alabama Polytechnic (now Auburn) announced element 85 ("alabamine") and element 87 ("virginium"), found with his "magneto-optical" apparatus. No other lab could reproduce it; the method was an illusion of the equipment, and the claims died — a false American first the chapter states plainly. Element 85 was really made at Berkeley in 1940 (Encyclopedia of Alabama; *Time* 1932).
- Ernest Lawrence's first cyclotron (Berkeley, 1930–31) was glass, sealing wax, and bronze, small enough to hold in one hand; it whirled charged particles to high speed in a spiral. Bigger versions followed — the 60-inch of 1939 had a 220-ton magnet — and turned the Radiation Laboratory into an element factory. Nobel Prize in Physics, 1939 (LBL; APS News). Shared with: `technology` (lead — the machine itself) · `science` (the Rad Lab as institution).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ernest-lawrence-elements" name="Ernest Lawrence" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Ernest Lawrence
> **Who:** inventor of the cyclotron, the machine behind nearly every American element discovery. · **When and where:** Berkeley, California, 1930s–1950s; Nobel Prize 1939; died 1958.
This chapter keeps the element-factory framing: his machines made technetium's foil, astatine, and plutonium's ingredients, and element 103 — lawrencium — carries his name. The machine story itself belongs to `technology`. No film about him exists; he appears as a character in *Oppenheimer* (2023), which belongs to `war` — flagged, not adopted.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ernest-lawrence-elements" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="elements made by people" -->
- Technetium, 1937 — the first artificial element. Lawrence mailed a molybdenum deflector foil from the 37-inch cyclotron to Palermo, Sicily, where Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier dug a few billionths of a gram of element 43 out of it and named it "the artificial one." Honest split credit: Italian chemistry, American machine. (Technetium-99m later became a workhorse of hospital imaging — `health`'s slice.) (LANL; Guinness.)
- 1940: astatine — element 85, the one "alabamine" was supposed to be — made by bombarding bismuth in the 60-inch cyclotron (Corson, MacKenzie, Segrè); and neptunium, the first element past uranium (McMillan and Abelson), named for the next planet out (Nobel Foundation; OSTI).
- Plutonium: produced December 14, 1940 (Seaborg, McMillan, Kennedy, Wahl) and chemically proved the night of February 23–24, 1941, in Room 307 of Gilman Hall, now a National Historic Landmark. Seaborg picked the symbol Pu instead of "Pl" as a joke — "pee-yoo," like a smell — and the committee accepted it. Wartime secrecy fell over the work at once; the bomb is `war`'s story (Atomic Heritage; symmetry magazine). Shared with: `war` (lead — the Manhattan Project and the weapons).
- Curium (summer 1944) and americium (1944–45), made in the wartime Met Lab circle, were revealed when a boy on the radio show *Quiz Kids* asked Seaborg on November 11, 1945 whether any new elements had turned up during the war. He said yes — five days before his formal announcement (LANL; RSC podcast).
- Promethium, 1945: Marinsky, Glendenin, and Coryell fished the last missing rare earth out of uranium fission products at Oak Ridge; announced 1947. Grace Mary Coryell suggested naming it for Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods — a pointed name from inside the bomb project. Still the only element ever discovered in Tennessee (Britannica; ORNL).
- December 1949: berkelium — inside this era by two weeks (boundary rule).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="emilio-segre-elements" name="Emilio Segrè" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Emilio Segrè
> **Who:** the Italian physicist stranded by Mussolini's anti-Jewish laws who stayed in America and co-discovered two elements. · **When and where:** Palermo and Berkeley, 1937–1940s; stayed in the U.S. from 1938; died 1989.
Co-identified technetium in Palermo from Lawrence's mailed foil (1937). Visiting Berkeley in summer 1938, he learned Italy's new racial laws had stripped Jews like him of university posts; he stayed, became an American, helped find astatine (1940), and showed with Seaborg that plutonium-239 was fissile. Nobel Prize 1959, for the antiproton (Nobel Foundation; Britannica). Shared with: `immigration` (the immigrant-scientist thread) · `science` (features him separately).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="emilio-segre-elements" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="glenn-seaborg" name="Glenn Seaborg" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Glenn Seaborg
> **Who:** the chemist whose teams found plutonium and nine more elements — and the first living person to have an element named for him. · **When and where:** Berkeley and wartime Chicago, 1940–1974; died 1999.
Led plutonium's discovery (produced December 14, 1940; proved February 23–24, 1941, Gilman Hall 307) and in all co-discovered ten elements — with the honest footnote that one of the ten, nobelium, was later credited to Dubna. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1951, shared with McMillan. The named stories ride with him: the Pu symbol joke, the *Quiz Kids* reveal, mendelevium as Cold War diplomacy, and seaborgium in his lifetime (1997) — he could receive mail addressed entirely in elements: Seaborgium, Lawrencium, Berkelium, Californium, Americium (Nobel Foundation; Science History Institute). His seaborgium naming fight sits in the next era's span; he is placed once, here, at the plutonium anchor.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="glenn-seaborg" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="elements" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
For four decades American labs made new elements almost faster than anyone could name them — and fought Soviet labs for decades over who got there first. The disputes are stated, not resolved: some credits went to Berkeley, some to Dubna, some were split.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="elements from a hydrogen bomb" -->
- Californium: made at Berkeley in early 1950, announced March 17, 1950 — in this era by the boundary rule, named for the state and the university (Britannica).
- The Ivy Mike test (November 1, 1952, Enewetak Atoll) vaporized an island; drone planes flew through the mushroom cloud trailing filter papers, and tons of blasted coral were shipped to Berkeley. In the debris, Ghiorso and teams from Berkeley, Argonne, and Los Alamos found elements 99 and 100, where uranium had swallowed floods of neutrons. The discoveries were classified until August 1, 1955; the names — einsteinium and fermium — went public only after both namesakes had died (Fermi November 1954, Einstein April 1955), neither told an element would bear his name (Science History Institute "Element Hunting in a Nuclear Storm"; LANL). Shared with: `war` (the H-bomb test itself).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="one atom at a time" -->
- Mendelevium, 1955: the Berkeley team bombarded a target of about a billion einsteinium atoms — all that existed — and caught 17 atoms of element 101 with Ghiorso's new recoil method, the first element identified atom by atom. Ghiorso wired the detector to the building fire alarm as a celebration bell — and, left connected, it set off a late-night evacuation (anecdote-grade sourcing, flagged in the bank). Naming it for Mendeleev, a Russian, at the height of the Cold War took U.S. government approval (LANL; Britannica; Atomic Heritage).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Transfermium Wars" -->
- Nobelium, an honest American miss: a Stockholm claim (1957) was retracted, Berkeley's 1958 claims were judged insufficient, and the decisive 1966 work was Dubna's — the IUPAC/IUPAP Transfermium Working Group credited Dubna, and the Swedish name stuck anyway (TWG report, *Pure Appl. Chem.* 1993).
- Lawrencium (Berkeley 1961, Dubna 1965–67): credit ruled shared; the name honors Ernest Lawrence — the cyclotron man got element 103.
- Berkeley and Dubna both claimed elements 104 (1964/1969) and 105 (1968/1970); the naming fight ran for decades in dueling journals. The Working Group (1992–93) split the credit for both and credited Berkeley for 106 (1974). The final 1997 package: rutherfordium, dubnium — putting the Russian lab's town on the table — and seaborgium, the first element named for a living person, after IUPAC first tried to ban living namesakes in 1994. Seaborg kept a periodic table with Sg on it until his death in 1999 (IUPAC 1997; Science History Institute "The Transfermium Wars").
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="albert-ghiorso" name="Albert Ghiorso" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Albert Ghiorso
> **Who:** the instrument-builder who co-discovered more elements than anyone in history — without a doctorate. · **When and where:** Berkeley, 1944–1974 (career into the 1990s); died 2010.
Co-discovered 12 elements, americium through seaborgium — the Guinness World Record. He was the gadget man: the detectors, the recoil catch, the HILAC accelerator, the mendelevium counter wired to a fire alarm (Guinness; Physics Today obituary; LBL).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="albert-ghiorso" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="darleane-hoffman-elements" name="Darleane Hoffman" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Darleane Hoffman
> **Who:** the nuclear chemist who proved a "man-made" element occurs in nature. · **When and where:** Los Alamos from 1953; Berkeley from 1984; died 2025, age 98.
In 1971 she detected traces of plutonium-244 in ancient rock from California's Mountain Pass mine — a man-made element found occurring naturally on Earth in tiny amounts. She showed fermium-257 could split spontaneously, led one-atom-at-a-time chemistry of the heaviest elements at Berkeley, was the first woman to lead a Los Alamos scientific division, and won the National Medal of Science (1997) and the ACS Priestley Medal (2000, the second woman ever) (ACS; Physics Today; *Nature* obituary). `science` features her separately.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="darleane-hoffman-elements" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="elements in daily life" -->
- Americium-241 — a Manhattan Project element — sits in household ionization smoke detectors, about a third of a millionth of a gram in each, its alpha particles ionizing the air in a small chamber until smoke trips the alarm (EPA RadTown; LANL). Shared with: `technology` (the device).
- Silicon, one line and no false first (discovered in Sweden, 1824): the transistor age made it the emblem of American technology — "Silicon Valley" is named for the chip element. Shared with: `technology` (the chips) · `economy` (the industry).
- The federal helium program had piled up $1.4 billion in debt; the Helium Privatization Act of 1996 ordered the reserve sold off. Shared with: `economy` (lead).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="elements" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
International teams finished the last row of the periodic table, and the American share is stated honestly: target material, chemistry, detectors, and shared credit — the atoms themselves formed in Russia. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="finishing the seventh row" -->
- Between 1998 and 2010, joint teams at Dubna (JINR) and Livermore (LLNL) — for elements 115 and 117 also Oak Ridge and Vanderbilt — made elements 114–118. IUPAC recognized 113, 115, 117, and 118 on December 30, 2015, completing period 7; the names came November 28, 2016: nihonium (113, Japan's RIKEN — the first element discovered in Asia), moscovium, tennessine, and oganesson. Flerovium (114) and livermorium (116), named May 2012, honor Russia's Flerov Laboratory and the Livermore lab and city. Frame all of it as "made together": IUPAC credits the collaborations, not one country (IUPAC press releases; LLNL).
- Oganesson, element 118, is named for Yuri Oganessian, the Dubna physicist who led the superheavy hunt — only the second element named for a living person, after seaborgium; his colleagues voted after asking him to leave the conference call. He is Russian: the era's emblem in the history prose, not a featured American story (IUPAC; sciencenotes).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="tennessine: Tennessee on the table" -->
- Oak Ridge's HFIR reactor made the only possible target material on Earth: 22 milligrams of berkelium-249, 250 days in the reactor plus 90 days of chemistry. Shipped in June 2009, the package crossed the Atlantic five times because Russian customs twice rejected the paperwork. Six months of calcium-48 beam at Dubna yielded six atoms of element 117 — published April 2010, named tennessine November 28, 2016. Tennessee became the second U.S. state on the table (after californium) — but promethium (Oak Ridge, 1945) is still the only element actually discovered in Tennessee; tennessine's atoms were made in Russia. The collaboration began when Vanderbilt's Joe Hamilton introduced ORNL's Jim Roberto to Yuri Oganessian (ORNL element-117 timeline; "Charmed half-life").
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="clarice-phelps" name="Clarice Phelps" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Clarice Phelps
> **Who:** Oak Ridge nuclear chemist, U.S. Navy veteran, and the first Black woman to help discover a chemical element. · **When and where:** Oak Ridge National Laboratory, from 2009; tennessine target work 2008–09; recognition 2016–19.
Worked on purifying the berkelium-249 used as the element-117 target; the recognition as the first African-American woman on an element-discovery team came after tennessine was confirmed (ORNL staff profile; CNN; Tennessee State University).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="clarice-phelps" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="toward row 8, and the end of federal helium" -->
- In 2024, Berkeley Lab's Heavy Element Group made two atoms of livermorium a new way — a titanium-50 beam on plutonium-244 at the 88-Inch Cyclotron (announced July 23, 2024) — the proof of principle needed to attempt element 120, which would open row 8 and be the heaviest atom ever made. The attempt was under way as of 2026, with no discovery announced (Berkeley Lab News; DOE Office of Science).
- The Federal Helium System — the reserve, the Cliffside field, the 423-mile pipeline — was sold to the industrial-gas company Messer in a sale completed in June 2024; the sale sent about $460 million to the U.S. Treasury (accepted bids totaled $423.35 million), ending nearly a century of federal helium. Helium remains scarce and strategic: MRI machines, rockets, chips (BLM press releases 2024). Shared with: `economy` (lead — the supply story).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<!-- hb-note -->
# Part 4 — Work, Food, and Money
<!-- /hb-note -->


<a id="chapter-14-work-workers"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="14" slug="work-workers" title="Work and Workers" part="4" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 14: Work and Workers

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-07 (all facts web-verified; sources inline in the research bank).
**Angle:** What work actually felt like, and how working people organized — the daily job.
**Keep out:** the companies (`big-business`); the whole economy (`economy`); slavery as a system (`slavery-freedom` — enslaved work touched here only from the work angle, with Shared-with lines).
**Workspace:** `workspace/work-workers.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-work-workers.md` (every date and number below is sourced there).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="work-workers" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Work was organized by season and by household, not by wages or a clock. There were no employers, no set hours, and no job a person could be hired for or fired from — the work is real, but this chapter's subject did not exist here yet.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="household and season" -->
- In Eastern Woodlands communities, women farmed corn, beans, and squash and gathered wild foods; men hunted and fished; everyone joined the big jobs — harvest, maple sugaring, canoe building (Encyclopedia.com; American Yawp).
- Labor gathered into larger groups at planting and harvest; children learned by working alongside adults.
- Where farming supported towns, some people specialized — traders, stoneworkers, religious leaders (American Yawp). Say this plainly and stop; no documented individual survives at story level from this angle.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="work-workers" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first work newcomers organized in this land was forced work, and there is almost nothing else to report from this chapter's angle.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Spanish labor systems" -->
- The encomienda let Spanish settlers take forced labor and tribute from Native people in Florida and the Southwest; the repartimiento (from the mid-1500s) assigned rotating drafts of Native workers, nominally paid, to Spanish projects (Britannica).
- Native people were compelled to build and farm for missions and towns. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the system as enslavement, lead) · `native-nations` (what it did to the nations).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="work-workers" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Most people who worked in the colonies did not work for wages: they were bound — by indenture for a term of years, or, increasingly, for life.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="bound labor and the artisan's shop" -->
- Indentured servitude was the era's labor system: between half and two-thirds of European immigrants arrived under indenture (some estimates run higher — state the range); terms of four to seven years; at the end, "freedom dues" — clothing, corn, tools, sometimes land (EH.net; Oxford Research Encyclopedia).
- Apprenticeship bound children to masters to learn a trade. Household production — spinning, brewing, candle-making — filled the rest of the working day (the household itself is `home-family`'s).
- Enslaved labor begins in the English colonies in this century. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the system, lead — one pointer sentence here only).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="richard-frethorne" name="Richard Frethorne" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Richard Frethorne
> **Who:** an indentured servant boy in early Virginia whose begging letters home survive. · **When and where:** Martin's Hundred, Virginia, 1622–1624.
Arrived December 1622 on the *Abigail*, likely in his early teens. In March–April 1623 he wrote his parents asking them to buy out his indenture or send food — since leaving the ship he had eaten nothing but peas and water gruel, "and when we are sick there is nothing to comfort us." A muster list made by February 1624 records him among the dead at Martin's Hundred (Virtual Jamestown; Encyclopedia Virginia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="richard-frethorne" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="work-workers" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A working world of craft shops, sailors, servants, and enslaved workers — with the enslaved share of the workforce growing fast.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the craft ladder" -->
- Apprentice, then journeyman (a wage-earner paid by the day), then — with luck and savings — master of a shop: the standard path in printing, shoemaking, carpentry, smithing.
- Enslaved men also worked the skilled trades in towns and were "hired out" for wages their owners kept. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the enslaved work day and the system, lead — do not repeat their gang/task detail).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="sailors and the waterfront" -->
- Sailors and dockworkers were the era's big wage-earning workforce, and the navy could seize them: press gangs took men for forced naval service.
- Knowles Riot, Boston, November 17, 1747 — after press gangs seized 46 men, working Bostonians rioted for three days, held naval officers hostage, and forced the pressed men's release (New England Historical Society; Boston 1775).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-franklin-work-workers" name="Benjamin Franklin" movie="Benjamin Franklin (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Franklin
> **Who:** the most famous runaway apprentice in American history — before everything else, a bound teenage print-shop worker. · **When and where:** Boston and Philadelphia, 1718–1723.
> **Movie:** Benjamin Franklin (2022)
Apprenticed at 12 to his brother James's Boston print shop; beaten and bound until 21 by the contract. In September 1723, with about four years left, he ran away — to New York, then Philadelphia, arriving October 6, 1723 nearly penniless — and worked as a journeyman printer before ever owning a shop (Massachusetts Historical Society; UPenn Archives). His other lives belong to other chapters; the runaway apprentice is ours.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-franklin-work-workers" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="work-workers" label="1750 to 1800" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Working people begin acting together as working people — the first authenticated strike, and the first lasting trade union.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first strike and the first union" -->
- Philadelphia journeymen printers, 1786: struck against a wage cut and won a $6-a-week minimum — the first authenticated strike by hired workers against an employer, and the first strike-benefit fund on record (DOL labor-history chronology; ExplorePAhistory). State the dispute: New York journeymen tailors struck in 1768, so say "often called the first."
- Federal Society of Journeymen Cordwainers (shoemakers), Philadelphia, 1794 — the first sustained trade union in the U.S., striking to hold a standard wage (Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia).
- Thin at story level: no verified individual worker's account found for this era; the spans carry it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="work-workers" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The factory arrives, and with it the bell, the clock, and a working day someone else sets.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the law against unions, then for them" -->
- 1806: eight Philadelphia cordwainers convicted of "a conspiracy to raise their wages" — fined $8 each; unions treated as crimes (Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia).
- 1842: Commonwealth v. Hunt (Massachusetts) — unions are not criminal conspiracies as such; organizing and striking can be lawful (Britannica).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
