<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Lowell: the mill girls" -->
- Young New England women lived in company boardinghouses and worked 12 to 14 hours a day, timed by factory bells (Britannica; NPS Lowell).
- February 1834: wage cuts of 12–25% announced; about 800 women "turned out" — and lost. October 1836: about 1,500 struck over a boardinghouse rate hike and partly won (History Matters/GMU).
- Winter 1844–45: Sarah Bagley organized the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association, which petitioned for the ten-hour day and pushed Massachusetts into the first legislative investigation of factory conditions (Britannica; NPS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the ten-hour movement, children, and the gangs" -->
- 1835: the first general strike in the U.S. — Philadelphia coal heavers started it, over forty trades and nearly 20,000 workers joined, and the city granted the ten-hour day (Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia).
- March 31, 1840: President Van Buren ordered a ten-hour day for laborers on federal public works — private workplaces untouched.
- Child labor was normal and legal; children "doffed" bobbins and tended machines. Canal and railroad construction gangs — heavily Irish immigrant labor — dug and graded the routes. Shared with: `transportation` (the canals and lines) · `immigration` (who the diggers were).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="harriet-hanson-robinson" name="Harriet Hanson Robinson" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Harriet Hanson Robinson
> **Who:** a Lowell doffer who walked out in the 1836 strike at age 11 and wrote the mill girls' story down. · **When and where:** Lowell, Massachusetts, 1835–1848.
Began mill work at 10. In the October 1836 turnout, when the girls in her room hesitated, she said she would go out "whether anyone else does or not" — and led them out. Stayed in the mills until 1848; published the memoir *Loom and Spindle* in 1898 (History Matters/GMU; Internet Archive edition).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="harriet-hanson-robinson" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="work-workers" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Industrial work at its harshest — twelve-hour days, child workers, no safety law — and the first national attempts to organize against it, most of them broken by force.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the eight-hour fight: Knights, Haymarket, AFL" -->
- Knights of Labor, founded December 9, 1869 (Uriah Stephens; later Terence Powderly): about 700,000 members by 1886, including women and — unevenly — Black workers (LOC; Britannica).
- May 1, 1886: national strikes for the eight-hour day. May 4, Haymarket Square, Chicago: an unknown hand threw a bomb at police; seven officers and at least four civilians died in the blast and gunfire. Eight anarchists were convicted without proof any threw it; four hanged November 11, 1887; Governor Altgeld pardoned the surviving three in 1893, calling the trial unfair (LOC; Britannica).
- December 8, 1886, Columbus, Ohio: the American Federation of Labor founded — skilled craft unions bargaining for wages and hours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homestead and Pullman" -->
- Homestead, July 6, 1892: 300 Pinkerton agents on barges fought strikers at Carnegie's steel works — seven workers and three Pinkertons killed (some counts more); the state militia followed and the union was broken. Shared with: `big-business` (the company side — Frick, Carnegie, private guards, lead on that half).
- Pullman, 1894: the company cut wages about a quarter to a third but not the rents in its company town. The American Railway Union's national boycott was broken by injunction and federal troops; about 30 people were killed nationwide (counts vary to 34); Debs got six months in jail. Days into the crisis, Congress made Labor Day a federal holiday (June 28, 1894 — the holiday is `holidays`' story). Shared with: `big-business` (the company town and the injunction, from the power side).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what the work was" -->
- Sweatshops in garment lofts and tenements; breaker boys picking slate from coal in the anthracite fields; steel mills on twelve-hour shifts.
- Domestic service was the largest single occupation for women: the 1870 census counted 867,354 servants — about half of all employed women (Women's Bureau via FRASER). Paid housework is ours; the household is `home-family`'s.
- June 25, 1867: several thousand Chinese workers (estimates 2,000–5,000) building the Central Pacific struck for eight days for equal pay and an end to whipping; the company cut off their food and the strike ended without formal concessions (LOC). Shared with: `transportation` (the railroad, lead) · `immigration` (who came).
- Convict leasing put arrested Black men to unpaid work in mines and on railroads. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the system, lead — one sentence here).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="samuel-gompers" name="Samuel Gompers" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Samuel Gompers
> **Who:** cigar maker who built and led the American Federation of Labor for nearly four decades. · **When and where:** London and New York, born January 27, 1850; AFL president 1886–1924 (except 1895).
Rolled cigars from boyhood in London and New York tenement shops, where a reader read aloud to the workers. Built the AFL on "pure and simple" unionism — wages, hours, conditions — from about 140,000 members in 1886 to nearly 3 million at his death (AFL-CIO; Britannica).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="samuel-gompers" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="eugene-debs-work-workers" name="Eugene V. Debs" movie="American Socialist: The Life and Times of Eugene Victor Debs (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Eugene V. Debs
> **Who:** locomotive fireman who founded the first industrial union and went to jail for the Pullman boycott. · **When and where:** Terre Haute, Indiana, and Chicago; ARU founded June 1893.
> **Movie:** American Socialist: The Life and Times of Eugene Victor Debs (2017)
Shoveled coal on locomotives as a young man. His American Railway Union took in all railroad workers, not one craft at a time — the first industrial union. For defying the Pullman injunction he served six months in the Woodstock, Illinois jail (1895). He later ran for president five times as a Socialist — the last time, 1920, from a prison cell, drawing about 900,000 votes (Britannica; EBSCO). `big-business` shows him from the company's side of Pullman.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="eugene-debs-work-workers" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jennie-curtis" name="Jennie Curtis" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Jennie Curtis
> **Who:** the Pullman seamstress whose speech launched the boycott. · **When and where:** Pullman, Illinois, 1894.
Sewed carpets and drapery in Pullman's repair shops. Her pay fell from $1.50–$2.25 a day to about 80 cents, with two cuts in one week in November 1893, while the company kept collecting its rents — including back rent her father owed when he died after 13 years at Pullman. President of the ARU "girls' local" (125 members), she asked the June 1894 ARU convention for help; the delegates voted the boycott. She testified to the U.S. Strike Commission that year (NPS; Strike Commission testimony).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jennie-curtis" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="work-workers" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two disasters, a photographer, and a depression turn the daily job into a matter of federal law: by 1938 the country has a minimum wage, a 40-hour week, and a child-labor ban.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the mines and the mills' children" -->
- 1902 anthracite strike: 147,000 miners and breaker boys out about five months; Theodore Roosevelt's commission — the first federal mediation instead of strikebreaking — heard 558 witnesses, including breaker boys younger than nine; the 1903 award: 10% raise, nine-hour day (PA Center for the Book; LOC).
- Lewis Hine quit teaching in 1908 to photograph child workers for the National Child Labor Committee — thousands of pictures, 1908–1917, of mill children, breaker boys, cannery kids, newsies. The photographs sit in this era by date; the practice's peak came earlier (documentary about him: *America and Lewis Hine*, 1984).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="mother-jones" name="Mother Jones" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Mother Jones
> **Who:** Mary Harris Jones, the miners' organizer a prosecutor called "the most dangerous woman in America" (1902). · **When and where:** born County Cork, Ireland — she claimed 1830; her baptismal record says 1837 (state both); organizing from the 1890s to the 1920s.
A dressmaker who lost her husband and all four children to yellow fever in Memphis (1867) and her home to the Chicago fire (1871), then gave her life to the United Mine Workers' camps. July 1903: she led striking child textile workers on the March of the Mill Children, from Philadelphia toward President Roosevelt's home at Oyster Bay, to make the country look at the mill children's missing fingers (Britannica; Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="mother-jones" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Triangle" -->
- November 22, 1909: shirtwaist maker Clara Lemlich, bruised from a company beating, called the general strike in Yiddish at Cooper Union — the Uprising of the 20,000, eleven weeks of garment strikes (Jewish Women's Archive). Shared with: `rights-movements` (women organizing).
- March 25, 1911: fire in the Triangle Waist Company's top floors killed 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women, some 14 years old; a stairwell door was kept locked; dozens jumped. The owners were acquitted of manslaughter that December. New York then rewrote its factory laws (Cornell ILR Triangle site). Topic documentaries: *Triangle Fire* (PBS, 2011); *Triangle: Remembering the Fire* (HBO, 2011). Shared with: `disasters` (the fire and response) · `government-politics` (the laws) · `rights-movements` (the organizing before and after).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rose-freedman" name="Rose Rosenfeld Freedman" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Rose Rosenfeld Freedman
> **Who:** Triangle survivor who refused to be paid for silence. · **When and where:** New York, March 25, 1911; died 2001.
Two days short of her 18th birthday, she wondered what the executives were doing — and followed them up to the 10th-floor roof, where rescuers pulled survivors across. She said the owners offered money for her silence about the locked doors; she refused, and told the truth for ninety years. Died February 15, 2001, at 107 — the last survivor (Variety obituary; Cornell ILR).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rose-freedman" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frances-perkins-work-workers" name="Frances Perkins" movie="Summoned: Frances Perkins and the General Welfare (2020)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frances Perkins
> **Who:** watched the Triangle fire; became the first woman in a U.S. Cabinet and wrote the fire's lessons into federal law. · **When and where:** New York 1911; Secretary of Labor 1933–1945.
> **Movie:** Summoned: Frances Perkins and the General Welfare (2020)
Having tea near Washington Square when the fire broke out, she ran to the scene and watched workers jump. She investigated factories for New York, then, as FDR's Labor Secretary, drove the Fair Labor Standards Act and Social Security. She later said the New Deal began on March 25, 1911 (Columbia exhibits; DOL history). `economy` features her separately for the New Deal economy.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frances-perkins-work-workers" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="addie-card" name="Addie Card" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Addie Card
> **Who:** the 12-year-old Vermont mill spinner in one of Lewis Hine's most famous photographs. · **When and where:** North Pownal, Vermont, 1910.
Hine photographed her at the spinning frame in 1910, barefoot, and captioned her an "anemic little spinner"; the mill girls said she was ten, and he misspelled her name "Addie Laird." The picture later ran on a 1998 U.S. postage stamp. In 2005–06 researcher Joe Manning traced her real name and long, hard life; she died in 1993 (Met Museum record; LOC; Manning's Mornings on Maple Street).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="addie-card" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the line, the dial painters, and the sit-downs" -->
- The assembly line brought the speed-up: the pace of work set by the machinery, not the worker. Shared with: `technology` (the method as invention) · `big-business` (Ford the company).
- The Radium Girls: dial painters taught to point brushes with their lips, poisoned at work, disbelieved by their employers — Grace Fryer's suit and the Illinois cases established that companies answer for slow occupational poisoning. Shared with: `rights-movements` (the court fight) · `elements` (radium itself) · `health` (the disease).
- Flint sit-down strike, December 30, 1936 – February 11, 1937: autoworkers occupied GM's plants for 44 days; the Women's Emergency Brigade (Genora Johnson, 23) guarded the windows; GM recognized the United Auto Workers (Zinn Education Project; UM-Flint). Topic documentary: *With Babies and Banners* (1979). The CIO organized the mass-production plants; the Wagner Act (1935) made organizing a legal right (shared with `big-business` as regulation).
- Fair Labor Standards Act, June 25, 1938: 25-cent minimum wage, 44-hour week falling to 40 by 1940, most child labor under 16 banned (DOL; LOC). New Deal jobs programs (WPA, CCC) — shared with: `economy` (lead) · `government-politics` (the programs).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="grace-fryer-work-workers" name="Grace Fryer" movie="Radium Girls (2018)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Grace Fryer
> **Who:** dial painter who sued U.S. Radium while dying — and won. · **When and where:** Orange, New Jersey; painting from 1917, suit 1927, settlement June 1928.
> **Movie:** Radium Girls (2018)
Hired at U.S. Radium from 1917, taught to shape the brush with her lips. As the dial painters sickened and died, the company denied everything. Fryer and four dying co-workers — the press called them "the five women doomed to die" — sued in 1927 and won a June 1928 settlement: $10,000 each, a $600-a-year pension, and medical costs (LOC "Living Dead Women"; History.com). The film is a drama inspired by the case, with invented sister characters. Her court fight is also told in `rights-movements`; radium itself in `elements`.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="grace-fryer-work-workers" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="war work" -->
- Women went from 27% of the workforce (1940) to nearly 37% (1945); in 1943 more than 310,000 women built aircraft — about 65% of that industry's workers (Journal of Economic History; wartime records). Documentary about the real "Rosies": *The Life and Times of Rosie the Riveter* (1980).
- After the war: the 1945–46 strike wave, the largest ever recorded — 4,985 stoppages and 4.6 million strikers in 1946 alone (BLS via Encyclopedia.com).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="naomi-parker-fraley" name="Naomi Parker Fraley" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Naomi Parker Fraley
> **Who:** the Navy-yard lathe worker in the 1942 photograph tied to the "We Can Do It!" poster — after seventy years of the credit going to someone else. · **When and where:** Alameda, California, 1942; identified 2015–16; died 2018.
A real war worker photographed at her lathe in 1942. For decades the woman in the photo was misidentified as Geraldine Hoff Doyle; scholar James Kimble found the original captioned print naming Parker. State the rest honestly: the poster itself was little known in the war, became an icon in the 1980s, and even the photo-to-poster link is not proven. She died January 20, 2018, at 96 (Seton Hall; TIME).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="naomi-parker-fraley" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="a-philip-randolph-work-workers" name="A. Philip Randolph" movie="10,000 Black Men Named George (2002)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### A. Philip Randolph
> **Who:** organized the Pullman porters and won the first contract between a major U.S. company and a Black-led union. · **When and where:** union founded August 1925; contract signed August 25, 1937; Washington 1941.
> **Movie:** 10,000 Black Men Named George (2002)
The porters — all Black men, commonly all called "George" — served the sleeping cars for long months of hours. Randolph's Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters fought Pullman for twelve years until the company signed: a sharply shorter working month and $1.25 million in raises (LOC; Britannica). In 1941 his threatened march on Washington made FDR ban discrimination in defense plants (Executive Order 8802, June 25, 1941). Also on film: *A. Philip Randolph: For Jobs and Freedom* (1996, documentary). His 1963 march belongs to `rights-movements`.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="a-philip-randolph-work-workers" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="work-workers" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Union membership peaks at about one worker in three and then falls for the rest of the century; the office replaces the factory; women flood into paid work; and by the end, the mills are closing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the postwar deal" -->
- 1954: union membership peaks at 34.8% of wage and salary workers (NBER/BLS). December 5, 1955: the AFL and CIO merge — about 15 million members, George Meany president.
- By 1956, white-collar workers outnumber blue-collar workers for the first time; the typical job starts moving to a desk (Encyclopedia.com/BLS milestone).
- Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake and Akwesasne — the "skywalkers" — kept walking high steel on bridges and skyscrapers through the century, a Native trade running from the 1920s to the World Trade Center (History.com; 9/11 Memorial Museum). Shared with: `landmarks` (the structures).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="new voices organizing" -->
- Memphis, 1968: sanitation workers Echol Cole and Robert Walker were crushed to death in their truck's compactor on February 1; eleven days later 1,300 Black sanitation men struck under signs reading "I AM A MAN." Dr. King came to stand with them and was assassinated in Memphis April 4; the city then recognized the union (King Institute; AFSCME). Shared with: `rights-movements` (the civil-rights campaign, lead on King).
- 9to5, founded 1973 in Boston by office workers Karen Nussbaum and Ellen Cassedy — women clerical workers organizing over pay, promotion, and harassment (Britannica). Topic documentary: *9to5: The Story of a Movement* (2020).
- OSHA: the job-safety law signed December 29, 1970. In 1970 about 14,000 workers a year — 38 a day — died on the job; by the 2020s about 5,000 a year, roughly 15 a day, in a much larger workforce (OSHA; BLS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="chavez-huerta" name="Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta" movie="Cesar Chavez (2014) · Dolores (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta
> **Who:** organizers who built the farmworkers' union — with Larry Itliong's Filipino strikers, who walked out first. · **When and where:** Delano, California, 1965–1975.
> **Movie:** Cesar Chavez (2014) · Dolores (2017)
September 8, 1965: about 1,500 Filipino American grape pickers of AWOC, led by Larry Itliong, struck the Delano growers; Chavez and Huerta's association voted September 16 to join. The 300-mile march to Sacramento (March 17 – April 11, 1966), Chavez's 25-day fast for nonviolence (1968), and a national grape boycott brought the growers to sign the first contracts on July 29, 1970. The merged union became the United Farm Workers; California's 1975 Agricultural Labor Relations Act made farmworker union rights law for the first time anywhere in the U.S. — federal labor law had excluded farmworkers since 1935. Huerta negotiated the contracts and coined "Sí, se puede" (NPS; UFW). Shared with: `food-farming` (farm labor in the food system) · `rights-movements` (the movement).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="chavez-huerta" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the unraveling" -->
- Manufacturing employment peaked at 19.6 million in June 1979 and fell for forty years (BLS). Plants closed across the industrial Midwest — Youngstown's "Black Monday" (September 19, 1977) alone ended 5,000 steel jobs. Shared with: `big-business` (the corporate decisions) · `economy` (the macro shift).
- August 3, 1981: about 13,000 air traffic controllers struck; President Reagan fired 11,345 of them two days later and their union was decertified — widely read as open season on strikes (Reagan Library; EBSCO).
- Union membership: 20.1% in 1983; about 13% by 2000 (BLS). Women's labor-force participation: 34% in 1950, 60% by 2000 (BLS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="laid-off-industrial-worker" name="(target) a laid-off steel or auto worker" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a laid-off steel or auto worker
Lost a factory job as the plants closed. Documented leads for the writer: Youngstown Black Monday (1977) oral histories; the named interviews in Studs Terkel's *Working* (1974); the Flint workers documented in *Roger & Me* (1989).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="laid-off-industrial-worker" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="work-workers" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Most Americans now work in services; millions work through an app with no boss they can see; and organizing starts again in places nobody expected — coffee shops and warehouses. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the service floor and the app" -->
- Union membership in 2024: 9.9% of wage and salary workers — 14.3 million people — down from one in three at the 1954 peak (BLS).
- Gig work: by August 2021, 16% of U.S. adults had earned money through an online gig platform, 9% within the past year (Pew Research survey). App drivers and couriers are classed as independent contractors, outside most labor law — the legal fights are ongoing (journalism where cited).
- 2020: in May, 35% of employed people were working from home because of the pandemic (BLS) — while "essential" workers in groceries, warehouses, delivery, and hospitals kept reporting in person. Remote and hybrid work stayed for much office work after the emergency.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="organizing returns" -->
- December 9, 2021: baristas at one Buffalo Starbucks voted 19–8 for the first union among the company's roughly 9,000 corporate-owned U.S. stores; hundreds of stores followed (Washington Post — journalism).
- April 1, 2022: workers at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island voted 2,654–2,131 for the independent Amazon Labor Union — the first unionized Amazon warehouse in the U.S. (NLRB count; NPR — journalism).
- State the cutoff plainly: this section is current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="chris-smalls" name="Chris Smalls" movie="Union (2024)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Chris Smalls
> **Who:** the fired Amazon warehouse worker who organized the first Amazon union in the U.S. (journalism-labeled). · **When and where:** JFK8, Staten Island, New York, 2020–2022.
> **Movie:** Union (2024)
A process assistant at JFK8, fired in March 2020 after leading a walkout over COVID safety. He and fellow workers built the independent Amazon Labor Union from a bus-stop table across the road — food, conversations, months of signatures — and won the April 2022 vote (NPR, CNBC — journalism; the vote count is the NLRB's record). The documentary follows the campaign itself.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="chris-smalls" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gig-driver" name="(target) a documented app driver" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a documented app driver
Drives or delivers through an app, with pay set by an algorithm and no employer to face. Needs a named, on-the-record account from major journalism or an oral-history project — label the source when chosen.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gig-driver" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<a id="chapter-15-food-farming"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="15" slug="food-farming" title="Food and Farming" part="4" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 15: Food and Farming

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-07 — all ten eras verified against `research/research-food-farming.md`; every date/number/name in this outline is sourced there.
**Angle:** What Americans ate and how they grew it — from the Three Sisters to fast food. The through-line: skilled Native farming → crops crossing oceans → farming as most people's life → food becoming an industry that reaches from field to distant plate → arguing about what food is and who can reach it.
**Keep out:** farm machinery as invention (`technology`); farm economics and crises as finance (`economy`); farm labor as organizing (`work-workers`); the Dust Bowl soil and exodus (`land-environment`, `migration`); shops and selling (`marketplace`); the 1621 feast as holiday (`holidays`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/food-farming.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-food-farming.md` · **Reference:** `research/research-migration.md` (Homestead figures, cattle drives, Dust Bowl exodus — theirs) · `research/research-economy.md` (cattle business, homestead economics — theirs) · `research/research-land-environment.md` (Three Sisters soil angle, Dust Bowl soil — theirs)
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="food-farming" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Farming here was already old and skilled. Corn had been bred by Native farmers over thousands of years from a wild grass, and it fed towns; each region ate from what its land did best. The crops that would later feed the whole world were already growing in American fields.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Three Sisters" -->
Corn, beans, and squash planted together, each helping the others: the corn stalk is the pole the beans climb; the beans' roots feed nitrogen into the soil all three share; the squash's wide leaves shade the ground, hold water, and crowd out weeds. Eaten together, corn and beans also make a more complete food. Corn itself was bred from teosinte — a grass with a few hard seeds — starting about 9,000 years ago in southern Mexico, then carried and adapted north over millennia. A plant so changed by farmers that it cannot reseed itself without people. (`land-environment` tells the soil side; the food and the technique are ours.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Regional foodways" -->
- The East had invented farming on its own before corn arrived: squash, sunflower, goosefoot, and other local crops domesticated thousands of years ago — the Eastern Agricultural Complex, one of the world's few independent birthplaces of farming.
- Corn fed real towns: Cahokia held roughly 10,000–20,000 people around 1100.
- The Plains ate bison; the Northwest ate salmon; the Great Lakes peoples harvested manoomin — wild rice, "the food that grows on water," gathered by canoe and still central to Ojibwe life today; the coasts ate shellfish; the Northeast tapped maple.
- No named farmer survives from this era at story level, and the book does not invent people; the era carries the wide view and the spans.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="food-farming" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Food crossed the ocean in both directions and changed what the whole world eats — historians call it the Columbian Exchange, after the 1972 book that named it. People here still ate as they had; the century's food story is what got carried, and by whom.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What left, what arrived, who carried it" -->
- Out of the Americas: corn, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, squash, peanuts, peppers, chocolate, vanilla, turkeys — corn and potatoes alone became staple food for much of Europe, Africa, and Asia.
- In: wheat, rice, sugarcane, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens, horses, honeybees. De Soto's expedition landed in Florida in 1539 with a herd of pigs as a walking food supply; escapees became the Southeast's wild hogs. Spanish colonists at St. Augustine (1565) planted wheat and citrus.
- Honest framing: this was not a friendly trade. Europeans carried American crops home from lands they were invading, and sugarcane came to be grown by enslaved people. Africans — most brought in chains — carried okra, watermelon, black-eyed peas, yams, African rice, and the knowledge to grow them; scholars now credit enslaved Africans as the carriers of those crops, not just cargo.
- Thin era for American eating itself, honestly: the exchange is the story, and its harvest lands in every era after.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="food-farming" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
English colonists arrived not knowing how to feed themselves here. Native crops and Native teaching kept the first colonies alive — and then Virginia planted a crop nobody can eat, and grew it instead of food.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Corn saves the colonies" -->
Jamestown's Starving Time, winter 1609–10: with Powhatan food trade cut off, about 500 colonists fell to roughly 61 by spring — they ate horses, dogs, rats, leather, and there is evidence some ate the dead. Corn — bought, seized, and finally grown — kept the colony alive. At Plymouth, the colonists' first corn harvest in autumn 1621 is why there was a second year.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco instead of dinner" -->
John Rolfe's tobacco (first successful crop 1612) paid so well that Virginia planters grew it instead of food, and the colony's own assembly had to force balance — the 1629–30 inspection law capped each family at 2,000 tobacco plants per member, partly so corn would still get planted. The first cash crop, and the first time American farming chased money instead of meals. (The money is `economy`'s; the labor system is `slavery-freedom`'s.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What colonists ate" -->
Corn learned from Native cooks — hominy, samp, johnnycakes — plus beans, pork once hogs multiplied, and cider. Corn dishes stayed on American tables for centuries. (The 1621 harvest gathering as a holiday is `holidays`' story.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="squanto-food-farming" name="Squanto (Tisquantum)" movie="Squanto: A Warrior's Tale (1994)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Squanto (Tisquantum)
> **Who:** Patuxet man who taught the Plymouth colonists to grow corn — after surviving kidnapping and slavery himself. · **When and where:** Patuxet/Plymouth, Massachusetts; kidnapped 1614, returned 1619, taught the colonists spring 1621, died 1622. · **Movie:** *Squanto: A Warrior's Tale* (1994) — Disney, heavily fictionalized; say so.
Kidnapped in 1614 by an English captain to be sold in Spain; got free, learned English, and came home in 1619 to find his whole town dead of an epidemic. In spring 1621 he showed the Plymouth colonists how to plant corn, and interpreted between them and the Wampanoag. The famous detail — burying fish with the seed — is genuinely disputed: he did teach it, but a 1975 study in *Science* argued fish fertilizer may have been a European trick he picked up abroad, not a Native practice, and historians have argued it since. Tell what is sure, and say what is argued.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="squanto-food-farming" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="food-farming" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Farming settled into regions: rice in the Carolina Lowcountry, wheat in the middle colonies, mixed farms in New England, tobacco in the Chesapeake. The richest of those crops stood on African knowledge — carried here by people who had not chosen to come.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rice, built on African skill" -->
Rice made Lowcountry planters some of the richest people in the colonies — the famous strain came to be called Carolina Gold. The fields were built and worked by enslaved Africans, and planters paid more for captives from West Africa's rice coast *because* they knew rice: the record shows embanked tidal fields, seed pressed in with heel and toe, grain winnowed in coiled fanner baskets — African techniques in Carolina mud. How much of the whole industry rests on that knowledge is a real scholarly argument (the "Black Rice" debate): state the documented skills, and state that historians disagree about the share. The enslavement system itself is `slavery-freedom`'s subject.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The breadbasket, and the potato lands" -->
Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey grew wheat past their own needs and shipped flour out through Philadelphia and New York — the "breadbasket colonies." Scots-Irish settlers planted North America's first lasting potato patches at Londonderry, New Hampshire, 1719 — an American plant come home by way of Europe. Most tables held corn, pork, bread, and cider; the rich added imported tea, sugar, and wine.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="eliza-lucas-pinckney" name="Eliza Lucas Pinckney" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Eliza Lucas Pinckney
> **Who:** teenager left running three South Carolina plantations, who made indigo an American crop. · **When and where:** Wappoo plantation near Charleston; experiments from 1739, first successful dye crop 1744.
Her father was posted to Antigua and left her, at about sixteen, managing three plantations. She experimented with indigo seed for years — helped by an indigo maker brought from the Caribbean and by the enslaved workers who did the tending — and in 1744 produced the colony's first successful indigo dye, then shared seed with her neighbors. Exports went from about 5,000 pounds in 1745–46 to 130,000 pounds by 1748. Indigo is a dye, not a dinner — but it shows what colonial farming was: land, weather, borrowed knowledge, and unfree hands.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="eliza-lucas-pinckney" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lowcountry-rice-grower" name="(target) a Lowcountry rice grower" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Lowcountry rice grower
Enslaved rice growers from this era are real but rarely named in surviving records. Honest options: tell the documented skills collectively (fanner baskets, heel-and-toe sowing, tidal-field engineering) rather than invent a person, or draw a named later figure from Lowcountry records if the writer finds one. Do not fabricate.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lowcountry-rice-grower" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="food-farming" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
At the first census in 1790, about nine in ten working Americans farmed. The new country's leaders built an ideal around that fact — the independent family farm as the root of freedom — and its first homegrown cookbook put corn on the printed page.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The farm as an idea" -->
Jefferson in *Notes on the State of Virginia* (printed 1785): "Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people." The belief that family farms make free citizens steered American land law for the next century. Backcountry farmers, meanwhile, turned surplus corn into whiskey because a jug travels where a wagon of corn cannot (`drugs-alcohol` leads on whiskey as money and the 1794 rebellion). Farm tables stayed corn, pork, and cider.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="amelia-simmons" name="Amelia Simmons" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Amelia Simmons
> **Who:** author of *American Cookery* (Hartford, 1796) — the first cookbook written by an American for American kitchens. · **When and where:** Connecticut, 1796.
On her title page she calls herself only "an American orphan." Nothing else about her life is known — say so plainly; it is part of the story that an unknown working woman wrote a founding American book. What the book did is well documented: the first printed recipes using American cornmeal — johnnycake, Indian slapjack, Indian pudding — and the first printed use of pearlash, a wood-ash salt that makes dough rise, the ancestor of baking powder. English cookbooks had ignored corn; hers cooked like America ate.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="amelia-simmons" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="farm-household-daybook" name="(target) a documented farm household" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a documented farm household
Farm daybooks and account books are the documentation for this era's eating — what a family grew, butchered, traded, and put by, season by season. No single household verified yet; find one daybook (New England or Pennsylvania archives are rich in them) and tell one year of food from it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="farm-household-daybook" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="food-farming" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Steel opened the prairie, cotton crowded food out of the South, and for the first time food was preserved and shipped to strangers instead of kept for the family — in cans, and packed in ice.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Breaking the prairie" -->
Prairie sod gummed up iron plows. John Deere's polished steel plow (Grand Detour, Illinois, 1837) scoured itself clean and cut it; Cyrus McCormick's reaper (first demonstrated 1831) let one family harvest many times the wheat that hand-cutting allowed. The machines belong to `technology` (their story: mccormick-deere); what they meant here is the farm itself — the grasslands of Illinois and beyond turned to corn and wheat within a generation, and a family could work far more land than their arms alone allowed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Food for strangers: cans and ice" -->
Canning crossed from France: William Underwood's Boston cannery (1821), Thomas Kensett's American patent for tin cans (1825). Food sealed in metal could be sold far from where it grew — the beginning of food as a shipped, branded thing. And New England began selling winter itself: ice cut from ponds, packed in sawdust, shipped south and abroad.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cotton, and the blight that crossed east" -->
Cotton spread across the Deep South and crowded out food crops; plantations often bought Midwestern corn and pork to eat (`economy` and `slavery-freedom` own cotton's money and labor). And a warning traveled the other way: potato blight broke out around Philadelphia and New York in 1843, crossed the Atlantic by 1845, and destroyed the crop of an Ireland that had nothing else — about 1 million dead in the Great Famine. American farmers lost potatoes too, but had other food. The famine ships are `immigration`'s story.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederic-tudor" name="Frederic Tudor" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frederic Tudor
> **Who:** the Boston "Ice King" — built a business selling New England pond ice around the world. · **When and where:** Boston; first cargo to Martinique 1806, ice to Calcutta 1833.
Boston laughed when he loaded a ship with frozen pond water in 1806 and sailed it to the Caribbean. He kept at it for decades, working out sawdust insulation and ice houses, until in 1833 he landed 180 tons of New England ice in Calcutta, India — still frozen. Ice made the icebox an American kitchen fixture and let fresh food travel; when refrigerated railcars arrive in the next era, they are Tudor's idea on wheels.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederic-tudor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="food-farming" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The government gave farms away by the millions of acres, cattle walked north by the millions of head, and Chicago turned animals into boxed meat for cities a thousand miles off. By the era's end, food was an industry — and farmers had started organizing to survive it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homestead farming" -->
The Homestead Act (May 20, 1862): 160 acres free to anyone who lived on the land and farmed it five years. Over the law's life, about 4 million claims and about 1.6 million completed farms — roughly 270 million acres, near a tenth of the country. Roughly half of claimants failed: drought, grasshoppers, loneliness, debt. The politics and prices are `economy`'s; the journeys `migration`'s; ours is what those families planted, ate, and endured (see the Oblingers below).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The cattle kingdom and the beef machine" -->
About 5.2 million Texas cattle walked north to railheads between 1866 and 1884; Joseph McCoy's yards at Abilene, Kansas (1867) made the market. In Texas as many as one cowhand in four was Black, and many were Mexican or Mexican-American. Chicago's Union Stock Yards (opened December 25, 1865) became the world's largest livestock market, and Gustavus Swift's ice-cooled railcars (engineer Andrew Chase's design, 1878) let beef killed in Chicago reach New York tables — an animal raised, killed, and eaten in three different places. Barbed wire (Glidden patent, 1874 — the invention is `technology`'s) fenced the open range and ended the drives. The cattle business's money is `economy`'s; the drovers as movers are `migration`'s; beef as food is ours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Farmers join together" -->
Oliver Hudson Kelley founded the Grange (1867) — the first great national farmers' organization: meeting halls, cooperative buying, and a shared voice against the railroads and middlemen who set their prices (the rate fights belong to `economy` and `big-business`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="oblinger-family" name="Uriah and Mattie Oblinger" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Uriah and Mattie Oblinger
> **Who:** a homesteading family whose ~3,000 pages of letters record the food life of a Nebraska claim. · **When and where:** Fillmore County, Nebraska; claim filed 1872, Mattie and baby Ella arrived May 1873; letters 1862–1912 (Nebraska State Historical Society / Library of Congress).
Uriah went ahead from Indiana, broke sod, and built a sod house; Mattie's letters home tell the food year from inside it — the garden and corn they planted, what they cooked and lacked, "we will all be poor here together," grasshopper plagues and blizzards and low prices. Mattie died in childbirth in 1880. Their letters are among the best-documented ordinary farm lives in American archives — the homestead story without varnish.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="oblinger-family" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="charles-goodnight" name="Charles Goodnight" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Charles Goodnight
> **Who:** Texas cattleman who invented the chuckwagon — the rolling kitchen of the cattle drives. · **When and where:** Texas, 1866.
Feeding a crew for months on open grassland was the drive's daily problem. In 1866 Goodnight rebuilt a surplus Army wagon with a hinged pantry box on the back that dropped flat into a work table: flour, beans, bacon, coffee, and a cook who ranked second only to the trail boss. (The *Lonesome Dove* characters are fiction partly inspired by him — an inspiration note, not a film about him.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="charles-goodnight" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="food-farming" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A novel forced the government into the packinghouse, tractors pushed the horses off the farm, the plowed-up Plains blew away, and by mid-century Washington was buying pigs, stamping food, and serving school lunch. The government reached the American plate in this era, and it never left.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Jungle and the 1906 laws" -->
On June 30, 1906, Theodore Roosevelt signed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act on the same day — federal inspectors in the packing plants, honest labels required, the beginning of the FDA. The push came from one book (see Sinclair below). The law as law is `government-politics`'s; the packinghouse job is `work-workers`'s; what was in the food is ours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tractors, hybrids, and chickens" -->
In 1920 there were 246,000 tractors on U.S. farms — and about 26 million horses and mules still doing most of the work. The cheap Fordson (1917) and the do-everything Farmall (1924) turned that around within a generation (the machines are `technology`'s). Every retired horse freed about five acres of feed land to grow food for people instead. Henry A. Wallace founded Pioneer Hi-Bred (1926), the first hybrid seed-corn company — the seed that pays off next era. And in Delaware, a mis-shipped box of chicks started the modern chicken industry (see Cecile Steele below).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dust, pigs, and stamps: the New Deal on the farm" -->
On the plowed-up southern Plains, drought from 1931 killed the wheat and the soil blew (the soil is `land-environment`'s telling; the exodus `migration`'s) — farm families lived on gardens, canned goods, government commodities, and jackrabbits. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (May 1933) paid farmers to grow less so prices would rise: about 10 million acres of growing cotton plowed under, about 6 million pigs bought and killed — while people stood in breadlines. Public anger at that contradiction pushed surplus food to relief families and produced the first Food Stamp Program (Rochester, New York, May 16, 1939). Paying farmers became permanent policy (`economy` leads on the money).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Victory gardens, ration books, school lunch" -->
World War II put food on a war footing: sugar rationed from May 1942, coffee that November, meat, cheese, and fats from March 1943 — every person, babies included, carried a ration book of points. Americans answered with about 20 million victory gardens growing about 40 percent of the country's fresh vegetables by 1943–44. Frozen food had already reached stores (Birdseye's first retail case, Springfield, Massachusetts, March 6, 1930; the first supermarket, 1930, is `marketplace`'s story). After the war — pushed partly by how many draftees had been rejected as underfed — Truman signed the National School Lunch Act (June 4, 1946). Territories thread: on annexed Hawaii, sugar plantations ruled and James Dole's Hawaiian Pineapple Company (1901) canned fruit for mainland tables (the workers' arrivals are `immigration`'s; the islands' politics `america-world`'s).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="upton-sinclair-food-farming" name="Upton Sinclair" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Upton Sinclair
> **Who:** novelist whose book about Chicago meatpacking forced the first federal food-safety laws. · **When and where:** Chicago packinghouses (undercover ~7 weeks, 1904); *The Jungle* published February 1906.
He wrote *The Jungle* to show how immigrant packinghouse workers were used up; readers instead fixed on what his pages said was going into the meat. Within months, Congress passed and Roosevelt signed both 1906 food laws. Sinclair's own verdict, written that year: "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach." (`news-communication` tells the muckrakers as journalism; the food is ours.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="upton-sinclair-food-farming" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="george-washington-carver-food-farming" name="George Washington Carver" movie="George Washington Carver: An Uncommon Life (2018)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### George Washington Carver
> **Who:** agricultural scientist who taught worn-out cotton country to feed its own soil and itself. · **When and where:** born enslaved near Diamond, Missouri, about 1864 (exact date unknown); Tuskegee Institute, Alabama, 1896–1943. · **Movie:** *George Washington Carver: An Uncommon Life* (Iowa PBS, 2018).
Cotton had drained Southern soil. Carver taught crop rotation — peanuts, cowpeas, and sweet potatoes to feed nitrogen back, then cotton — through 44 free plain-language bulletins and a mule-drawn demonstration wagon that brought the lessons to farmers who could not come to him. His most famous bulletin (1916) gave 105 ways to cook the peanuts he was asking farmers to grow. Say the true thing and unsay the false one: he did not invent peanut butter — peanut pastes are older than the myth, and the patents belong to others. His real work was soil, self-reliance, and teaching poor farmers, Black and white.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="george-washington-carver-food-farming" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="cecile-steele" name="Cecile Steele" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Cecile Steele
> **Who:** Delaware farm wife whose mis-shipped chick order started the commercial chicken industry. · **When and where:** Ocean View, Delaware, 1923.
She ordered 50 chicks; the hatchery shipped 500. She raised them indoors through the winter and sold them at 16 weeks for 62 cents a pound — and the profit was so good she ordered 1,000 on purpose the next year, 10,000 by 1926. By 1928 some 500 Delmarva farms were raising "broilers." Chicken had been a Sunday luxury; the industry that grew from her accident made it the cheapest meat on the American plate.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="cecile-steele" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ration-book-household" name="(target) a ration-book or victory-garden household" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a ration-book or victory-garden household
A documented WWII household food story — points spent, garden rows, sugar saved for a birthday cake. Leads: National WWII Museum oral histories; Library of Congress folklife collections; Smithsonian victory-garden materials. Left as a target rather than half-verified.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ration-book-household" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="food-farming" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Food got cheaper, faster, and farther from the farm than it had ever been. In 1954, for the first time, tractors outnumbered horses and mules on American farms; farms kept getting fewer and bigger (6.8 million in 1935, falling all era); hybrid corn tripled yields; and dinner came from a drive-through window or a freezer tray. At the era's end came the bill — a farm debt crisis — and the first organized push back toward the local and the organic.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fast food and the freezer" -->
The McDonald brothers rebuilt their San Bernardino stand in 1948 as the "Speedee Service System" — 15-cent hamburgers assembled like factory parts (see Kroc below for what happened next). Swanson's aluminum-tray "TV dinner" went on sale in 1953 at about 98 cents — over 10 million sold in 1954 — and who invented it is honestly disputed: a salesman claimed the idea for decades; the owning family and the company's own scientist said otherwise. Supermarkets, freezers, and highways carried all of it (`marketplace` sells it; `transportation` moves it; the food is ours).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Industrial agriculture, and the people in the rows" -->
Fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation, and hybrid seed pushed yields up era-long; chicken and hogs moved indoors; the Green Revolution carried the same package abroad (see Borlaug below), fed hundreds of millions, and hooked farming on chemicals — both true. The hands that picked the cheap produce organized: Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and the farmworkers' movement are `work-workers`' story (their slug chavez-huerta); this chapter keeps one sentence at the table's edge.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The 1980s farm crisis" -->
After the 1970s export boom came the reckoning: Midwest farmland lost up to 60 percent of its value in the early-to-mid 1980s, farm debt hit about $215 billion by 1984, roughly 300,000 farms defaulted and about 300 rural banks failed. On September 22, 1985, Willie Nelson, John Mellencamp, and Neil Young played Farm Aid to 80,000 people in Champaign, Illinois, raising over $7 million — a concert that has run ever since. The finance is `economy`'s; the lost family tables are ours (see the Jordans below).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Organic, from fringe to federal seal" -->
J.I. Rodale had preached compost-and-soil farming since founding *Organic Farming and Gardening* magazine in 1942; by the 1980s the movement was big enough to regulate, and the Organic Foods Production Act (1990) ordered national standards — the USDA organic seal followed in 2002. Alice Waters put the same idea on a restaurant plate (below).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="norman-borlaug" name="Norman Borlaug" movie="The Man Who Tried to Feed the World (2020)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Norman Borlaug
> **Who:** Iowa-born plant scientist whose wheat is credited with saving hundreds of millions from famine — the "Green Revolution." · **When and where:** Mexico from 1944; India and Pakistan in the 1960s; Nobel Peace Prize 1970. · **Movie:** *The Man Who Tried to Feed the World* (PBS American Experience, 2020).
From 1944 he bred wheat in Mexico for a hunger-fighting program, crossing thousands of strains until he had short-strawed, disease-resistant wheat that yielded several times the old crop. Mexico grew its own bread by 1956; in the 1960s his seed broke famine predictions in India and Pakistan. He won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize — the only farm scientist ever to. He is often credited with saving a billion lives; tell it as the common estimate, not a count — and tell the criticism too: the same seed-fertilizer-irrigation package tied world farming to chemicals and thinned out old crop varieties.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="norman-borlaug" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ray-kroc" name="Ray Kroc" movie="The Founder (2016)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Ray Kroc
> **Who:** milkshake-machine salesman who turned the McDonald brothers' hamburger stand into the world's biggest restaurant chain. · **When and where:** San Bernardino visit 1954; first franchise Des Plaines, Illinois, April 15, 1955; bought the brothers out 1961. · **Movie:** *The Founder* (2016).
Kroc sold the brothers their milkshake machines, saw the line out their door, and became their franchise agent. He opened his own McDonald's in 1955, built the system nationwide, and in 1961 bought the brothers out for $2.7 million. The brothers said a handshake promise of royalties was never honored, and Kroc opened a McDonald's near their original stand — the record supports telling the hard edges plainly; the film dramatizes them.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ray-kroc" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jordan-family-farm" name="Russel and Mary Jane Jordan" movie="Troublesome Creek: A Midwestern (1995)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Russel and Mary Jane Jordan
> **Who:** an Iowa farm couple who sold off their livestock and machinery at auction to pay the bank — filmed by their own daughter. · **When and where:** near Rolfe, Iowa; farm in the family 125 years; auction in the mid-1990s, in the long shadow of the 1980s crisis. · **Movie:** *Troublesome Creek: A Midwestern* (1995) — Sundance Grand Jury Prize; Oscar-nominated documentary about this family.
Carrying about $220,000 in debt out of the crisis years, the Jordans learned their bank wanted its money. Rather than lose everything, they sold the cattle, the machinery, even household goods at auction and rented out the land — keeping the farmhouse and their name on the deed. Their daughter Jeanne Jordan filmed the whole year. One documented family standing for the roughly 300,000 farms the crisis took.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jordan-family-farm" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alice-waters" name="Alice Waters" movie="Alice Waters and Her Delicious Revolution (2003)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Alice Waters
> **Who:** cook who built a restaurant on local farms and put a garden in a public school — the farm-to-table idea's best-known voice. · **When and where:** Chez Panisse, Berkeley, California, opened 1971; Edible Schoolyard founded 1995. · **Movie:** *Alice Waters and Her Delicious Revolution* (PBS American Masters, 2003).
Chez Panisse served whatever local farms had that was ripe — fresh, seasonal, organically grown — and the idea spread from one Berkeley kitchen into a national movement. In 1995 she started the Edible Schoolyard at a Berkeley middle school: students grow, cook, and eat their own food as part of school. The counter-argument to the drive-through, made with a garden.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alice-waters" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="food-farming" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Americans now argue about food the way earlier Americans argued about land: what is in it, who grows it, who profits, and who can reach it. Fewer than 2 million farms remain (1.9 million in the 2022 census, the fewest since before the Civil War), most Americans have never worked one — and food is politics, health, identity, and work all at once. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Eating and reaching food" -->
- Adult obesity reached 41.9 percent (2017–March 2020, CDC), easing to 40.3 percent by 2021–23; diet-linked illness is a leading health burden (`health` leads on the medicine).
- Food deserts, defined: USDA maps low-income areas more than 1 mile from a supermarket in cities or 10 miles in the country — about 19 million people (about 6 percent) by the 2019 count; the number depends on the yardstick used, so state the measure.
- The other direction: farmers' markets grew from 1,755 (1994) to 8,771 (2019); farm-to-table went mainstream; food banks became permanent infrastructure. The COVID year 2020 showed the system's edges — closed packing plants, dumped milk, mile-long food-bank lines.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="GMO arguments and new foods" -->
Over 90 percent of U.S. corn, soybeans, and cotton are genetically engineered. Both truths, stated plainly: the National Academies' 2016 review of about 1,000 studies found no substantiated evidence that approved GE foods harm health — and public argument continued anyway, hard enough that from January 2022 federal law requires "bioengineered" labels. Newer arguments arrived on schedule: plant-based burgers (Impossible 2016; Beyond's 2019 stock debut), the first U.S.-approved lab-grown chicken (June 2023), and vertical farms that boomed on investment and then stumbled (pioneer AeroFarms hit bankruptcy in June 2023, then restructured) — tell the stumble, not just the promise.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Who picks the food" -->
Most hired crop workers are foreign-born. The H-2A seasonal visa grew from about 48,000 certified jobs (2005) to about 385,000 (2024) — roughly 15 percent of crop-farm employment, over 90 percent of the workers from Mexico. The organizing is `work-workers`'; the fields are ours (see Benitez below).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first farmers, still farming" -->
Native food sovereignty is a working movement, not a memory: tribal bison herds, seed banks rebuilding old corn and bean varieties, manoomin harvests defended in court and on the water, Native chefs rebuilding Indigenous cuisine. The circle back to the chapter's first page — the Three Sisters are still being planted, on purpose (`native-nations` leads on sovereignty as sovereignty).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nephi-craig" name="Nephi Craig" movie="Gather (2020)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Nephi Craig
> **Who:** White Mountain Apache/Diné chef cooking Apache foods for his own community — a face of the Native food sovereignty movement. · **When and where:** White Mountain Apache lands, Arizona; 2010s–present. · **Movie:** *Gather* (2020) — documentary featuring him, forager Twila Cassadore, and student scientist Elsie DuBray.
A professional chef who came home to open a café built on Apache-grown and gathered foods, training Native cooks and treating food as recovery — from diet-caused illness and from the history that caused the diet. Documented in the film *Gather* alongside Twila Cassadore, who teaches San Carlos Apache youth to forage, and Elsie DuBray, a Cheyenne River Sioux teenager whose science project compared her nation's traditional buffalo diet with modern beef.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nephi-craig" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lucas-benitez" name="Lucas Benitez" movie="Food Chains (2014)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Lucas Benitez
> **Who:** tomato picker who co-founded the Coalition of Immokalee Workers and helped build the Fair Food Program. · **When and where:** from Guerrero, Mexico, to Immokalee, Florida at 17; CIW founded 1993; Fair Food Program running from 2011. · **Movie:** *Food Chains* (2014) — documentary about the CIW; Benitez appears.
He picked tomatoes in the fields that supply America's winter salads and helped organize the workers who pick them. The Fair Food Program signs up big buyers — McDonald's, Walmart and others — to pay a small premium and buy only from growers who meet a worker-written code: pay floors, shade and water, protection from abuse, checked by audits. The person on the far end of the supply chain from the drive-through window.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lucas-benitez" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<a id="chapter-16-economy"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="16" slug="economy" title="Economy" part="4" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 16: Economy

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-08 — all ten eras verified against `research/research-economy.md`; every date, number, and name below is sourced there.
**Angle:** How the country makes its living — farming → industry → services; booms, panics, depressions.
**Keep out:** currency, banks, and the Fed (`money`); shops, ads, and consumer credit (`marketplace`); the daily job (`work-workers`); the firms and their power (`big-business`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/economy.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-economy.md` (new full bank plus the older parked sections: Gold Rush economics, cotton economy, cattle industry, Homestead economics, Keweenaw copper, aluminum, helium, farm crisis, container costs).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="economy" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The people of this land made their livings by farming, hunting, fishing, and gathering, and they traded what they made and grew across long distances. There was no money here. Goods moved through barter and gift exchange between people and between nations, and some farming towns grew large enough to support full-time craftworkers and traders.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cahokia and the trade routes" -->
- Cahokia, near modern St. Louis (peak about 1050–1150), was the largest city north of Mexico. Corn surpluses fed workers who did not farm — toolmakers, builders, traders (Illinois State Museum; Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site).
- Cahokia controlled the making and movement of hoe blades of Mill Creek chert, quarried in southern Illinois and found more than 400 miles away, from Louisiana to Minnesota (Mill Creek chert studies; Illinois State Museum).
- Sea shells from the Gulf coast, copper from Lake Superior, and obsidian in the West moved along rivers and trails as goods. Wampum as record and exchange is `money`'s subject.
- No named individual is documented from this angle; the spans carry the era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="economy" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
European crowns sent expeditions to this coast looking for gold and silver, and in the land that became the United States they found none. The trades that lasted were plainer ones: fish dried on the northern coasts, and furs bought from Native trappers. There was no colonial economy yet, because there were almost no colonists.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Gold hunts that failed, trades that lasted" -->
- Spanish silver came from mines in Mexico and South America — not from this land. The expeditions that searched here (Coronado, de Soto — `exploration`'s stories) went home without treasure.
- July 1534, Chaleur Bay, north of this land on the Atlantic coast: Mi'kmaq traders held beaver furs up on sticks to Jacques Cartier's crew and traded them for knives and iron goods — the first recorded fur trading between Europeans and Native people on the coast. The fur trade reached the future United States in the next century (Canadian Museum of History).
- European fishing fleets worked the cod waters off the northeast every season; fish, not gold, was the first steady European business in these waters.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="economy" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The colonies each built an economy around what the place could sell: tobacco in the Chesapeake, furs along the northern rivers, fish, timber, and ships in New England. The rules were written in London. Under the idea called mercantilism, colonies existed to supply raw goods to the home country and to buy its finished goods back.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco saves Virginia" -->
- Virginia found no gold and nearly starved. Its cash crop turned out to be a plant: exports of tobacco grew from about 2,300 pounds in 1615–16 to about 20,000 pounds by 1617, about 1.5 million pounds by 1630, and about 22 million pounds a year by 1700 (Encyclopedia Virginia).
- Tobacco also served as money in the Chesapeake — `money` tells that side. Shared with: `money` (commodity money) · `food-farming` (the crop in the fields) · `slavery-freedom` (who was forced to grow it as the century went on).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-rolfe-economy" name="John Rolfe" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Rolfe
> **Who:** the Jamestown settler whose tobacco experiments gave Virginia its cash crop. · **When and where:** Jamestown, Virginia, 1612–1614.
By July 1612 Rolfe was growing tobacco from imported West Indies seed, milder than the local plant, and he worked out how to cure the leaf for shipping. His first shipments reached London in 1614. Within a generation tobacco paid for the colony (Encyclopedia Virginia; Historic Jamestowne). His marriage to Pocahontas is told in `native-nations`; no documentary film about him exists.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-rolfe-economy" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Furs, and rules from London" -->
- One Dutch ship, the *Arms of Amsterdam*, carried 7,246 beaver skins to Amsterdam in a single 1626 cargo — recorded in the same letter that reports the purchase of Manhattan. Beaver felt hats in Europe drove the demand (New York State Library, Schaghen letter). The trading companies themselves are `big-business`'s story.
- Navigation Acts: from 1651, colonial trade had to travel in English or colonial ships; from 1660, "enumerated" goods — tobacco, sugar, cotton, indigo — could be shipped only to England or its colonies (Britannica).
- New England ships ran Atlantic circuits: goods and rum to West Africa, enslaved people across the ocean, sugar and molasses back north. The buying and selling of human beings was part of how these colonies made money — said plainly. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (lead — the Middle Passage and the system).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="economy" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Farming was most colonists' living, but the colonies also built ships, traded across the Atlantic, and sold tobacco, rice, indigo, wheat, and fish. Economic historians Peter Lindert and Jeffrey Williamson calculated in 2016 that free colonists had higher average incomes than the people of England by 1774. Much of that wealth, especially in the South, was produced by enslaved people who were paid nothing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What the colonies sold" -->
- Tobacco from the Chesapeake; rice and indigo from the South Carolina Lowcountry, grown and processed by enslaved workers; wheat and flour from the middle colonies; fish, rum, and ships from New England (research bank; colonial-economy scholarship).
- Shipbuilding: colonial timber made ships cheaper than English-built ones, and by the Revolution about one-third of the British merchant fleet was American-built (Encyclopedia.com).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="London's rules tighten" -->
- Molasses Act, 1733: a sixpence-a-gallon duty on molasses from non-British islands, widely dodged by smuggling (Encyclopedia.com).
- Iron Act, 1750: colonial raw iron could enter Britain duty-free, but building new colonial mills to finish iron into goods was banned. Colonists built them anyway (Britannica).
- The point of the rules, stated simply: Britain wanted the colonies' raw materials and the colonies' shopping, and wanted the profitable finishing work kept at home.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="eliza-lucas-pinckney-economy" name="Eliza Lucas Pinckney" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Eliza Lucas Pinckney
> **Who:** the sixteen-year-old who ran three plantations and built South Carolina's second cash crop. · **When and where:** near Charleston, South Carolina, 1739–1744.
Left in charge of her father's three plantations at 16, she spent five years testing indigo, the plant behind blue dye. The 1744 crop produced 17 pounds of good dye, and she shared seed with neighboring planters. Exports went from about 5,000 pounds in 1745–46 to about 130,000 pounds by 1748, and indigo became second only to rice in the colony's trade. The dye was made by enslaved workers, and skilled dye-makers brought from the Caribbean carried much of the knowledge — the profit went to planter families like hers (South Carolina Encyclopedia; Britannica).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="eliza-lucas-pinckney-economy" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="economy" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Independence was won on borrowed money. The paper dollars Congress printed to pay its soldiers lost almost all their value, and the new government began life owing about 79 million dollars. Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury, built the plan that paid the debts and established the country's credit.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The war's bill" -->
- Congress could not tax, so it printed Continental dollars from 1775. By the end of 1777 it took about 4 paper dollars to equal 1 silver dollar; by 1781, about 100 — "not worth a Continental" (Harvard American Currency collection; NY Fed history). The currency itself is `money`'s lead; the debt is ours.
- Hamilton's count in January 1790: about 54 million dollars of national debt, plus about 25 million owed by the states (First Report on Public Credit).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The whiskey tax" -->
- 1791: a federal excise tax on distilled spirits — 7 cents a gallon — to help carry the war debt. Frontier farmers moved their corn to market as whiskey, and the tax fell hard on them.
- 1794: western Pennsylvania farmers attacked tax collectors; Washington called up about 13,000 militia and marched west; the rebellion dissolved without a battle (Mount Vernon; TTB). Shared with: `drugs-alcohol` (whiskey as drink and money, and the rebellion's people) · `government-politics` (federal power proven).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alexander-hamilton-economy" name="Alexander Hamilton" movie="Alexander Hamilton (American Experience, 2007)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Alexander Hamilton
> **Who:** the first Secretary of the Treasury, who made the new country's debts into the foundation of its credit. · **When and where:** New York and Philadelphia, 1789–1795.
> **Movie:** Alexander Hamilton (American Experience, 2007)
His plan, laid out in the First Report on Public Credit (January 1790): pay the war debts in full, and have the federal government take over the states' debts too, so every creditor would trust the new government. The assumption plan was losing in Congress until a June 1790 dinner with Jefferson and Madison produced the trade — the debt plan passed, and the permanent capital went south to the Potomac. His December 1791 Report on Manufactures argued the country should grow its own industry with tariffs and subsidies; Congress never voted on it, but the argument ran through the next two centuries (National Archives; Gilder Lehrman). His arrival as an immigrant is `immigration`'s story; the Mint and the national bank are `money`'s.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alexander-hamilton-economy" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="economy" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In 1800 most American families grew and made most of what they used. By 1850 far more of them raised crops and made goods to sell, and bought what they needed with the money — historians call the change the market revolution. Canals and steamboats cut the cost of moving goods to a tenth of what wagons charged, cotton grown by enslaved people became the country's largest export, and a panic in 1837 was followed by six years of closed banks, failed businesses, and lost work.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="From household to market" -->
- After the Erie Canal opened in 1825, freight from Buffalo to New York City fell from about 100 dollars a ton by road to about 10 dollars by canal, and the trip dropped from about twenty days toward ten (EBSCO; Britannica). The canal itself is `transportation`'s; the price collapse is what changed farming.
- The first big factories: New England textile mills hired farm daughters for cash wages — money entering households that had rarely handled it. The mills' working day and the mill girls' strikes are `work-workers`' (their Harriet Hanson Robinson story).
- California gold (found January 1848): about 80,000 people went in 1849 and about 300,000 by 1855. Most miners found little; the merchants who sold them food, tools, and clothes made the steadier money. Shared with: `migration` (lead — the crowds) · `elements` (the metal).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="King Cotton" -->
- Cotton was 51.6 percent of the value of all U.S. exports in 1840, and stayed above half nearly every year until the Civil War. Between 1820 and 1860 about 80 percent of the world's cotton came from the United States (OpenStax U.S. History).
- The crop was planted, picked, and processed by enslaved people. The country's biggest business ran on forced, unpaid labor — said plainly, in the same sentence. Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (lead — the system and the people) · `food-farming` (cotton crowding out food crops).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Panic of 1837" -->
- A panic, explained simply: too many people trying to get their money out, or sell what they own, at the same time — and finding that nobody is buying.
- Years of borrowed money had gone into western land and cotton. When cotton prices fell and British lenders pulled back, New York banks stopped paying out gold and silver on May 10, 1837 (the bank side is `money`'s). Of about 850 banks in the country, roughly 4 in 10 closed entirely or partly failed, and hard times lasted until about 1843 (Lumen/US history surveys).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="philip-hone-economy" name="Philip Hone" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Philip Hone
> **Who:** a New York merchant whose diary recorded the Panic of 1837 day by day. · **When and where:** New York City; diary kept 1828–1851.
A carpenter's son who got rich in the auction business and served one term as mayor (1826–27), Hone wrote in his diary nearly every day for 23 years. In the spring of 1837 he recorded the city's business stopping around him: "No goods are selling, no business stirring, no boxes encumber the sidewalks of Pearl Street." His own fortune shrank in the crisis years. The diary, published after his death, is one of the fullest firsthand records of the era's money life (The Diary of Philip Hone, 1889 edition).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="philip-hone-economy" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="economy" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Between 1850 and 1900 the United States became an industrial country. Railroad track grew from about 9,000 miles to about 193,000. By 1890 American mills made more steel than Britain's, and by 1900 more than Britain's and Germany's combined. The same half century brought panics in 1873 and 1893 that each turned into years of failed businesses and men out of work, and it made the largest private fortunes the country had seen. Mark Twain named the era in an 1873 novel: the Gilded Age — a thin layer of gold over the problems underneath.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
