<!-- hb-chapter id="24" slug="slavery-freedom" title="Slavery and Freedom" part="6" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 24: Slavery and Freedom

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** **MAJOR.** Slavery as a system and the long fight out of it — how it worked, what it did, how it ended, and **what freedom actually looked like** (full detail, not a closing paragraph). **Owns the Middle Passage.**
**Keep out:** later civil rights campaigns (`rights-movements`, from Reconstruction's end onward — the handoff sits at 1877).
**Workspace:** `workspace/slavery-freedom.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-slavery-freedom.md` — all ten eras verified with inline sources (2026-08-07); every date and number below is sourced there. Registry rulings honored: 1 (Kossola and the *Clotilda* live here; `immigration` hands off in a sentence), 2 (domestic slave trade: this chapter leads on the system and the families; `migration` tells the journey), 9 (the legacy prejudice bank split is done).
**Director's standing instruction (2026-07-23):** the freedom half gets as much room as the slavery half — 1850–1900 is the longest section in the book. Emancipation is not one document and one date; it is a process with people in it.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Captive-taking existed in some Native societies, and in most of them it was different in kind from lifelong inherited chattel slavery. Say the difference plainly — and carry the honest exception.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="captive-taking, not chattel slavery" -->
- Captives taken in raids could be adopted into families and nations to replace the dead (the Haudenosaunee "mourning war" pattern is the best-described case); enslavement was a status that could end, and it did not automatically pass to children.
- **The honest exception:** on the Northwest Coast (Tlingit, Haida, and neighbors), slaves were property, were traded, and slave status was hereditary (Donald, *Aboriginal Slavery on the Northwest Coast*). Do not flatten in either direction.
- No documented named individual survives from this era's practice — no story block; say so rather than invent.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first enslavement in this land was Spanish, and its first victims were Native people. The first enslaved Africans arrived in 1526 — and rebelled the same year.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Spanish slavery — and the first rebellion" -->
- Spanish raiders took Native captives from the Florida and Carolina coasts from the early 1500s; the encomienda forced Native labor and tribute (the 1542 "New Laws" curbed it on paper; forced labor continued).
- **San Miguel de Gualdape, 1526:** Ayllón's failed colony (Georgia or Carolina coast; exact site unknown) included about 100 enslaved Africans among 600–700 colonists. In October 1526 the enslaved Africans rebelled and escaped — the first documented rebellion of enslaved Africans in what became the United States; the escapees likely found refuge with nearby Native communities.
- **St. Augustine, founded 1565,** counted Africans, free and enslaved, among its first residents; Spanish law recognized certain rights that later English law would not.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="estevanico-slavery-freedom" name="Estevanico" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Estevanico
> **Who:** an enslaved North African who survived the Narváez disaster and crossed the continent's south on foot. · **When and where:** from Azemmour, Morocco; shipwrecked near Texas 1528; reached Mexico 1536; killed at a Zuni town 1539.
His journey belongs to `exploration` (slug cabeza-de-vaca-estevanico); his status — an enslaved man doing the advance work of empire — is this chapter's. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="estevanico-slavery-freedom" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A system that did not exist in English law is built here piece by piece over about fifty years — and then written into statute so it passes from mother to child.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="1619 and the Middle Passage — the full telling lives here" -->
- **Late August 1619:** the English privateer *White Lion* landed "20. and odd Negroes" (John Rolfe's words) at Point Comfort, Virginia — people taken from a Portuguese slave ship, originally from the Ndongo/Kongo region of West Central Africa. The exact date is disputed (late August / August 20 / about August 25) — state the range. Whether the 1619 arrivals were treated as servants or slaves the records do not settle — say so.
- **The Middle Passage, the numbers (SlaveVoyages database):** about 12.5 million Africans embarked on Atlantic slave ships over the whole trade; about 10.7 million survived the crossing — roughly 1.8 million people died at sea. Fewer than 4 percent of survivors came to mainland North America (about 305,000 directly from Africa; close to 388,000 counting the Caribbean route); most captives went to the Caribbean and Brazil.
- **The conditions:** chained below decks in spaces too low to stand; voyages of one to three months; disease, dehydration, and suicide killed steadily; the dead were thrown overboard.
- Shared with: `immigration` (hands off in one sentence — forced arrival is told here).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="from servitude to hereditary slavery — the legal hinge" -->
- **John Punch, 1640:** three servants ran away together; the two European men got added years of service; Punch, an African, got life — the first documented lifetime slavery sentence in Virginia (story below).
- **Johnson v. Parker, 1654–55:** a Virginia court ruled John Casor a servant for life — the first civil ruling in the English mainland colonies that a person who had committed no crime could be held for life. The man who won the case, Anthony Johnson, was himself a free African landowner; tell that complexity honestly.
- **Massachusetts Body of Liberties, 1641:** the first English mainland colony to give slavery statutory recognition. Slavery was a New England institution too.
- **Virginia, 1662 — *partus sequitur ventrem*:** a child's status follows the mother, a deliberate break from English common law. Slavery now reproduced itself.
- **Virginia, 1705:** the consolidated slave code — enslaved people as real property; baptism frees no one; no penalty for a master who kills while "correcting."
- **The anti-literacy thread starts later:** no colony banned teaching enslaved people in the 1600s; the first statute is South Carolina's, 1740 (next era). The 1600s codes controlled bodies and status, not yet books.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-punch" name="John Punch" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### John Punch
> **Who:** the first African documented as sentenced to lifetime slavery in Virginia. · **When and where:** Virginia, July 1640 — three runaways, two sentences of years, one of life.
The court record survives; the racial line is drawn in a single sentence. (A 2012 genealogy study tying him to a president is a claim, not a fact — leave it out of prose.)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-punch" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Slavery spreads and hardens by law; rice wealth is built on African knowledge; the first mass revolt marches toward Spanish Florida — the one place people could run *to*.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="rice and the Lowcountry" -->
- South Carolina's rice economy was built on the knowledge and labor of West Africans from rice-growing coasts; planters paid premiums for captives from those regions. Charleston became the largest mainland arrival port.
- Sullivan's Island in Charleston harbor was the quarantine station for arriving slave ships. The claim that about 40 percent of enslaved arrivals passed over the island specifically is disputed by Charleston historians — carry Charleston's leading role, flag the island percentage.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Stono, 1739, and the Negro Act of 1740" -->
- **September 9, 1739:** about 20 enslaved men led by Jemmy (described in a contemporary account as Angolan) seized weapons at the Stono River and marched south toward Spanish Florida, gathering recruits, with banners and drums. About 25 white colonists were killed; the militia killed roughly 35 to 50 of the rebels (counts vary — state the range). The largest slave uprising in the mainland colonies before the Revolution.
- **The Negro Act of May 10, 1740** answered it: no assembling, no growing food, no earning money, no moving freely — and the first anti-literacy statute in the future United States, banning teaching an enslaved person **to write** (reading was not named; the distinction matters and runs to 1865).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fort Mose, 1738 — freedom by running south" -->
- Spain had promised (1693) freedom to enslaved people escaping British colonies who reached Florida, accepted Catholicism, and served in the militia. In 1738, Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose — Fort Mose — rose about two miles north of St. Augustine: the first legally sanctioned free Black town in what is now the United States, roughly 100 people. Destroyed in the 1740 British siege, rebuilt 1752, evacuated to Cuba with the Spanish in 1763. Today a Florida state park.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Native people were enslaved too" -->
- English Carolina ran a large trade in enslaved Native people: an estimated 24,000 to 51,000 Native people of the Southeast enslaved between 1670 and 1715 (Gallay's range); in that period more Native slaves were exported from Charleston than Africans were imported there.
- Shared with: `native-nations` (what the trade did to the nations). The plain point here: the system enslaved Native people as well as Africans.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="francisco-menendez" name="Francisco Menéndez" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Francisco Menéndez
> **Who:** Mandinga-born captain of the free Black militia at Fort Mose, the first free Black town. · **When and where:** born in the Gambia region; enslaved in Carolina; escaped to Florida; led Mose from 1738.
Documented in Spanish colonial records — the best-documented named resident. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="francisco-menendez" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A country declares that all men are created equal while holding hundreds of thousands of people as property. The first Americans to attack the contradiction are enslaved people themselves — in the courts, in the army lines, and on foot.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Revolution's two promises" -->
- **Crispus Attucks**, a sailor of African and Wampanoag descent, was the first person killed at the Boston Massacre, March 5, 1770. Whether he was legally free or a fugitive from slavery is disputed — say so.
- **Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775:** freedom for enslaved men of rebel masters who joined the British; the "Ethiopian Regiment" grew to about 800. Over the whole war an estimated 20,000 Black people sided with or fled to the British; an estimated 9,000 served the Patriot side (about 5,000 in combat). Both promises of freedom were kept unevenly.
- **Freedom suits:** enslaved people sued. Elizabeth Freeman's case (story below) and the Quock Walker cases (1781–83) ended slavery in Massachusetts through its own courts, using the 1780 constitution's "all men are born free and equal."
- Shared with: `war` (the fighting and the armies); this chapter's slice is the freedom bargain.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first abolitions — gradual, partial, real" -->
- Vermont's 1777 constitution banned holding adults in slavery — the first constitutional ban. Pennsylvania's gradual-abolition act (March 1, 1780) was the first abolition statute passed by an elected legislature anywhere: children born after it freed at 28. Massachusetts by court decision (1781–83); Connecticut and Rhode Island 1784; New York 1799 (fully free 1827); New Jersey last, 1804. Gradual meant slow — people remained enslaved in the North for decades.
- The **Northwest Ordinance (1787)** banned slavery north of the Ohio River.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Constitution's compromises, 1787" -->
- Three protections for slavery without using the word: the **three-fifths clause** (representation), the **fugitive clause** (escapees "held to Service or Labour" must be delivered up), and the bar on ending importation before **1808**. The 1808 clock mattered — it runs out in the next era.
- Shared with: `government-politics` (the Constitution as law and government).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elizabeth-freeman" name="Elizabeth Freeman (&quot;Mum Bett&quot;)" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Elizabeth Freeman ("Mum Bett")
> **Who:** sued for freedom under Massachusetts's brand-new constitution and won. · **When and where:** Sheffield and Great Barrington, Massachusetts; jury verdict August 1781; died 1829.
*Brom and Bett v. Ashley* helped end slavery in Massachusetts; she chose the name Freeman and worked for wages the rest of her life. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elizabeth-freeman" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="phillis-wheatley-slavery-freedom" name="Phillis Wheatley" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Phillis Wheatley
> **Who:** kidnapped from West Africa as a child of about seven; the first African American to publish a book of poetry. · **When and where:** landed Boston 1761 on the slave ship whose name she was given; book published London, September 1, 1773; freed weeks later; died in poverty 1784, about age 31.
Her book is `art`'s (slug phillis-wheatley); her enslavement, manumission, and poverty in freedom are this chapter's. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="phillis-wheatley-slavery-freedom" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ona-judge" name="Ona Judge" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Ona Judge
> **Who:** escaped from President George Washington's household and was never caught; her own interviews survive. · **When and where:** walked out of the Philadelphia President's House May 21, 1796; lived free in New Hampshire; died 1848.
The runaway advertisement offering ten dollars for her ran three days later — an ordinary life documented by the people trying to recapture her. She told her own story in 1840s interviews: poor, she said, but free. No film (the 2017 book *Never Caught* is the standard account).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ona-judge" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The import ban takes effect January 1, 1808 — and cotton makes slavery bigger, richer, and more brutal anyway. Growth now comes by birth, and by a domestic trade that moves more than a million people away from everyone they know.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the scale" -->
- Census counts: 697,624 enslaved people in 1790; 3,953,760 by 1860 — growth mainly by birth after the 1808 ban. By 1860 the South grew about 75 percent of the world's cotton, more than half of U.S. exports by value.
- Shared with: `economy` (the cotton economy) · `technology` (the gin as machine) · `food-farming` (the crop).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the domestic slave trade — people as property, families broken" -->
- More than 1 million people moved from the Upper South to the Deep South between about 1790 and 1860 — roughly 200,000 a decade from 1820 — overland in chained coffles and by coastwise ship to New Orleans, the country's largest slave market.
- **Our lead — what sale did to families:** the trade separated nearly half of the people it moved from a spouse or a parent (EJI's accounting); about one enslaved marriage in three was destroyed by forced sale. Children were sold away from mothers. The "Information Wanted" ads of the 1860s–1900s (next era) are the after-record of these separations.
- Shared with: `migration` (leads on the forced journey — routes, coffles, ships, conditions; ruling 2).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="daily life under slavery" -->
- **Labor:** sunup to sundown, six days a week — the gang system on cotton and sugar, the task system in Lowcountry rice.
- **Food and clothing, from a primary source:** Douglass's *Narrative* (1845) records his plantation's monthly allowance — eight pounds of pork or the equivalent in fish, one bushel of corn meal — and a clothing issue so thin that young children often had only a long shirt. People stretched rations with gardens, fishing, and trapping where allowed.
- **Housing:** one-room cabins, dirt floors, board beds — described from memory in the WPA narratives (era 8).
- **Family under the auction block:** marriages had no legal standing; sale could end any family any day — the fact that organized daily life more than any other.
- **Worship and music:** Richard Allen, born enslaved, founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church (Philadelphia, organized 1816) — the first Black denomination; in the slave states, worship out of the owners' sight in brush arbors ("hush harbors"); the spirituals carried faith and coded meaning.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="reading made a crime" -->
- After Nat Turner's rebellion and the rise of the abolition press, states tightened or newly passed anti-literacy laws: Georgia 1829, Louisiana and North Carolina 1830, Virginia 1831, Alabama 1832, South Carolina tightened again 1834. Most, but not all, slave states had such laws. Penalties differed: fines for white teachers (North Carolina $200), fines and jail elsewhere; the whip for Black teachers and learners (North Carolina 39 lashes; Virginia up to 20). Several laws covered free Black people too.
- **Why a slaveholding state feared literacy:** passes could be forged, abolition newspapers read, the Bible read without an owner's editing; after 1831, the fear was organized revolt. **Say it plainly: the schooling itself was the crime.**
- **People learned anyway:** historians estimate roughly 5 to 10 percent of enslaved people could read by 1860 (some late-period estimates run to 20 percent — state the spread). Verified methods only: Douglass's trades of bread for lessons (story below); Milla Granson's midnight school in Natchez (story below); Susie King Taylor's secret Savannah schools (era 7 story). The "pit school" claim could not be verified and is dropped.
- Shared with: `education` (the schooling side — ruling 7) · `government-politics` (the statutes as law).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="resistance and revolt" -->
- Everyday resistance: slowed work, broken tools, feigned illness, food taken — and above all running away. The runaway advertisements filling Southern newspapers are the system's own record of it (Freedom on the Move is digitizing thousands); ads often note the person "can read" or "can write and may forge a pass."
- **Gabriel's conspiracy, 1800 (Richmond):** betrayed hours before; 26 men hanged, Gabriel among them.
- **Denmark Vesey, 1822 (Charleston):** a free Black carpenter's planned rising, betrayed; 35 executed; Charleston's independent AME church torn down — the congregation that later became Mother Emanuel.
- **Nat Turner, August 21–23, 1831 (Southampton County, Virginia):** the deadliest slave revolt in U.S. history — at least 55 white people killed; in the panic afterward, militias and vigilantes killed more than 100 Black people, many with no part in it (some estimates run to 200 — state the range); 19 of those convicted were executed; Turner hanged November 11, 1831. The anti-literacy and anti-assembly wave above was the answer.
- **The *Amistad*, 1839–41:** kidnapped Mende captives seized the schooner at sea, led by Sengbe Pieh; jailed in Connecticut; the Supreme Court freed them in 1841; 35 survivors sailed home to Sierra Leone in 1842. Never enslaved on U.S. soil — the story here is the freedom fight in U.S. courts.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Underground Railroad and the abolitionists" -->
- The network of guides, safe houses, and above all Black communities and churches; the current estimate is about 100,000 people helped over its decades — label it an estimate, and say many more tried and were caught.
- **Harriet Tubman:** escaped September 1849; returned about 13 times and brought out about 70 people, mostly family and friends. **The old "19 trips, 300 people" figure is a legend — state the correction** (NPS).
- **Frederick Douglass:** escaped 1838; *Narrative* 1845; the *North Star* 1847 — the century's most photographed and most heard abolitionist voice.
- **Free Black institutions:** *Freedom's Journal* (1827), the first Black-owned U.S. newspaper; the AME church; the vigilance committees that made the Railroad work.
- **Sojourner Truth:** walked to freedom in New York, 1826; when her five-year-old son was illegally sold south, she sued — and won his return (1828).
- Shared with: `news-communication` (the Black press as press; Douglass as publisher).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="harriet-tubman" name="Harriet Tubman" movie="Harriet (2019)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Harriet Tubman
> **Who:** escaped, then returned about 13 times to lead about 70 people out; later a Union scout (era 7). · **When and where:** Maryland's Eastern Shore; escaped September 1849; died 1913.
> **Movie:** Harriet (2019)
Feature film verified (Cynthia Erivo, Oscar-nominated); a PBS documentary, *Harriet Tubman: Visions of Freedom* (2022), also exists — note in text if wanted. Use the corrected 13-trips/70-people numbers.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="harriet-tubman" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederick-douglass-slavery-freedom" name="Frederick Douglass" movie="Becoming Frederick Douglass (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frederick Douglass
> **Who:** taught himself to read against the law, escaped, and became the century's most famous abolitionist. · **When and where:** born Talbot County, Maryland, February 1818 (exact date unrecorded; he kept February 14); escaped September 3, 1838, by train in a sailor's clothes; died 1895.
> **Movie:** Becoming Frederick Douglass (2022)
His *Narrative* (1845, chs. 6–7) is the best-known first-person account of learning to read: Sophia Auld taught him the alphabet until forbidden — a prohibition he called his first antislavery lecture — then bread traded for lessons, and *The Columbian Orator* at about twelve. The film is a PBS documentary about him specifically. His newspaper life is `news-communication`'s (slug frederick-douglass-publisher).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederick-douglass-slavery-freedom" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nat-turner" name="Nat Turner" movie="The Birth of a Nation (2016)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Nat Turner
> **Who:** enslaved preacher who led the deadliest slave revolt in U.S. history. · **When and where:** Southampton County, Virginia, August 1831; hanged November 11, 1831.
> **Movie:** The Birth of a Nation (2016)
The 2016 feature is about Turner — not the 1915 film of the same name; the title reuse was deliberate. His jailhouse account was published as *The Confessions of Nat Turner* (1831).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nat-turner" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sojourner-truth-slavery-freedom" name="Sojourner Truth" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sojourner Truth
> **Who:** walked to freedom with her infant daughter, then sued to recover her son sold south — and won. · **When and where:** Ulster County, New York; walked free 1826; won Peter's return 1828; died 1883.
Per the Historical Society of the New York Courts, the first Black woman to win such a suit against a white man in a U.S. court. Her 1851 women's-rights speech belongs to `rights-movements` (slug sojourner-truth); here she is the woman who sued slavery for her son. No known feature film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sojourner-truth-slavery-freedom" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="solomon-northup" name="Solomon Northup" movie="12 Years a Slave (2013)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Solomon Northup
> **Who:** a free New Yorker kidnapped into twelve years of slavery; his memoir named names. · **When and where:** drugged and kidnapped in Washington, D.C., 1841; freed January 4, 1853; after about 1857 he disappears from the record — where and when he died is not known, say so.
> **Movie:** 12 Years a Slave (2013)
The film won Best Picture. His kidnappers were never convicted.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="solomon-northup" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sengbe-pieh" name="Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué)" movie="Amistad (1997)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué)
> **Who:** led the *Amistad* rising and won freedom in the U.S. Supreme Court. · **When and where:** Mende country (Sierra Leone region); revolt July 1, 1839; freed 1841; home 1842.
> **Movie:** Amistad (1997)
Argued in part by former president John Quincy Adams.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sengbe-pieh" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="milla-granson" name="Milla Granson (Lilly Ann Granderson)" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="candidate" -->
### Milla Granson (Lilly Ann Granderson)
> **Who:** ran a midnight school in Natchez — about twelve pupils at a time, taught between roughly midnight and 2 a.m.; accounts credit her with about 200 students, some of whom wrote their own passes and escaped. · **When and where:** Kentucky, then Natchez, Mississippi, mid-1800s.
Candidate, honestly: the account traces mainly to one primary source (Laura Haviland's 1881 memoir) — tell it with that caveat. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="milla-granson" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The system reaches its legal peak, then breaks — and four million people become free, which turns out to be the beginning of the work, not the end of it. **The freedom half in full: this is the longest section in the book, by the director's instruction.**
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the crisis" -->
- **Fugitive Slave Act, September 18, 1850:** federal commissioners, no jury, the accused barred from testifying; the commissioner was paid 10 dollars for ruling a person a slave and 5 for ruling them free; bystanders could be compelled to help. It reached into the free states — free Black Northerners fled to Canada.
- **Anthony Burns, 1854:** arrested in Boston; on June 2, 1854, federal troops marched him through the city to a ship back to Virginia, past crowds draped in mourning black.
- ***Dred Scott v. Sandford*, March 6, 1857:** 7–2 against Dred and Harriet Scott — Black Americans were not and could never be citizens; Taney: Black people "had no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="freedom taken, not merely given" -->
- **Fort Monroe, May 1861:** three enslaved men — Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory, James Townsend — rowed to the Union fort at Old Point Comfort (the same ground as 1619) rather than build Confederate batteries; General Butler called them "contraband of war" and refused to return them. Word spread; by war's end roughly half a million people had freed themselves by reaching Union lines. The freedom-seekers' name for the fort: "Freedom's Fortress."
- **Emancipation Proclamation, January 1, 1863** — what it did: freed the enslaved in the states in rebellion, made the Union army an army of liberation wherever it advanced, opened enlistment to Black men. What it did NOT do: exempted the loyal border states (Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri), Tennessee, and Union-held parts of Virginia and Louisiana — freedom there waited for state action or the 13th Amendment.
- **About 180,000 Black soldiers served in the U.S. Colored Troops** — roughly one Union soldier in ten by war's end — plus about 19,000 in the navy. Fourteen Black soldiers earned the Medal of Honor in a single battle (New Market Heights, September 29, 1864).
- **Harriet Tubman at Combahee Ferry, June 2, 1863:** guided Union gunboats up the river; more than 700 enslaved people carried to freedom in one night.
- **Juneteenth — June 19, 1865:** General Granger's General Order No. 3 at Galveston: "all slaves are free." More than 250,000 people were still enslaved in Texas, two and a half years after the Proclamation, because the army had not been there to enforce it. The date became the freedom anniversary.
- **The 13th Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865:** slavery abolished everywhere — "except as a punishment for crime." The exception clause matters; convict leasing walked through it (below).
- **The *Clotilda*'s people:** about 110 Africans smuggled into Mobile in July 1860, 52 years after the ban, were freed five years later; unable to afford passage home, about 30 founded Africatown (Kossola's story below).
- **The Five Tribes too:** the Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole nations had also held enslaved Black people; their 1866 treaties freed them and promised the Freedmen citizenship — a promise still being fought over in era 10.
- Shared with: `war` (leads on the armies and the fighting; ours is the freeing) · `government-politics` (the amendments as law) · `native-nations` (the Five Tribes and sovereignty).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="freedom, day to day — the searches, the marriages, the names, the churches" -->
- **Searching for family:** freedpeople placed "Information Wanted" newspaper ads for decades, hunting for mothers, children, husbands, wives sold away; the Last Seen project (Villanova) has digitized more than 5,000. Reunions were rare and recorded with joy when they happened. (Thornton Copeland's ad, story below.)
- **Legalizing marriages:** the Freedmen's Bureau recorded thousands of marriages slavery had refused to recognize — couples married for decades stood up to be married in law. The registers survive at the National Archives.
- **Choosing surnames:** some kept a former owner's name to stay findable by sold-away family; others chose new ones — Freeman among them.
- **Churches:** hush-harbor congregations built their own buildings; the AME and AME Zion churches spread across the South within a decade. The church became the freedpeople's school hall, meeting hall, and political hall.
- **The Freedman's Savings Bank — a promise broken early:** chartered 1865 for freedpeople's savings; wrecked by mismanagement and speculation; failed June 1874 with about 3 million dollars belonging to some 61,000 depositors.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="schools, the moment freedom came" -->
- The demand arrived with freedom, immediately: schools opened in churches, army camps, and confiscated buildings as soon as Union lines arrived — Susie King Taylor was openly teaching freed children on St. Simons Island, Georgia, in 1862, at age 14, while the war still ran (story below). Grandparents and grandchildren learned in the same rooms; adults filled night classes after full workdays.
- Freedpeople paid for it themselves where they could — school fees out of first wages, land and labor for schoolhouses — alongside Northern aid societies (the American Missionary Association foremost), whose teachers, many women and a growing number of them Black, came south by the thousands.
- **The Freedmen's Bureau's count: by 1870, more than 2,600 day and night schools with about 150,000 pupils** (broader counts that include every kind of school run higher — state the count and its scope).
- **The first Black colleges of the emancipation wave:** Fisk (opened January 1866), Howard (chartered 1867), about 25 institutions for freedpeople by 1872. (Cheyney's forerunner, Lincoln, and Wilberforce predate the war — `education` carries them as institutions.)
- **Schools burned:** in the Memphis Massacre (May 1–3, 1866) mobs and police killed 46 Black residents and burned every Black church and school in the city — 91 homes, 4 churches, 8 schools, by the congressional committee's count. Attacks on schools and teachers recur through Bureau records.
- **Freedpeople wrote schooling into law:** the Reconstruction state constitutions of 1868–69 — drafted by the first public bodies in U.S. history with substantial Black membership — created the South's first statewide free public school systems, open to white children too.
- Shared with: `education` (leads on the schools as schools — ruling 7; the point here is that people forbidden to read made schooling one of freedom's first acts) · `rights-movements` (the later school campaigns).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Black political power" -->
- After the 15th Amendment (ratified February 3, 1870), 16 Black men served in Congress within the decade — 14 representatives and 2 senators, all Southern Republicans. Hiram Revels was sworn in as the first Black U.S. senator February 25, 1870; Joseph Rainey became the first Black U.S. representative that December; Blanche K. Bruce served the first full Senate term (1875–81). Robert Smalls served five terms in the House.
- Across the South, about 2,000 Black men held office during Reconstruction; Foner's *Freedom's Lawmakers* documents more than 1,500 by name — give both the estimate and the documented count.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the promises broken" -->
- **"Forty acres":** Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 (January 16, 1865) set aside about 400,000 acres for freedpeople in forty-acre plots; about 40,000 people settled. President Johnson reversed it that fall and returned the land to the former owners.
- **Black Codes:** Mississippi first, November 1865 — vagrancy laws requiring proof of employment, apprenticeship laws binding Black children, arrest and hired-out labor for violators. Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment (ratified 1868).
- **Sharecropping:** without land, freedpeople farmed shares against advances at plantation-store prices — debt that rolled over year after year and bound families to the land.
- **Convict leasing:** through the 13th's crime exception, states arrested Black men under the new codes and leased them to planters, mines, and railroads — labor without wages, profitable to the states for decades.
- **Terror:** the Ku Klux Klan (founded December 1865, Pulaski, Tennessee) ran whipping, arson, and murder campaigns; the Colfax Massacre (April 13, 1873) killed between 62 and 153 Black men, most after surrender — the count itself is uncertain, state the range. The Enforcement Acts briefly broke the Klan; the will to enforce faded.
- ***Plessy v. Ferguson*, May 18, 1896** (7–1, Harlan alone in dissent): "separate but equal" — the decision's date sits in this era, its shadow over the next.
- **The end:** the disputed 1876 election; the Compromise of 1877; federal troops withdrawn from the last Southern statehouses that April. The amendments stayed on paper; the power to enforce them was surrendered. **From this point the campaigns to win the rights back belong to `rights-movements`.**
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dred-harriet-scott" name="Dred and Harriet Scott" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Dred and Harriet Scott
> **Who:** the couple whose freedom suit the Supreme Court turned into slavery's biggest legal victory — reversed within a decade by war and amendment. · **When and where:** suit filed St. Louis 1846; decision March 6, 1857; freed by Taylor Blow that May; Dred died September 17, 1858.
No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dred-harriet-scott" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="robert-smalls" name="Robert Smalls" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Robert Smalls
> **Who:** enslaved harbor pilot who sailed himself, his family, and his crew out of slavery on a Confederate ship, then served five terms in Congress. · **When and where:** Charleston, before dawn May 13, 1862, past Fort Sumter in the captain's straw hat; later Beaufort, South Carolina; died 1915.
"First Black captain" phrasings vary by source — use the safe verified line: he became a ship's captain in U.S. service, then a legislator and five-term congressman. No film released.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="robert-smalls" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="william-harvey-carney" name="William Harvey Carney" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### William Harvey Carney
> **Who:** born enslaved, escaped north, and carried the flag at Fort Wagner with the all-Black 54th Massachusetts — the first Black American whose actions earned the Medal of Honor. · **When and where:** born Norfolk, Virginia, 1840; Fort Wagner July 18, 1863; medal awarded May 23, 1900.
The documented Black soldier story (the 54th was a state regiment; the 180,000-man USCT figure sits in the span). The assault appears in *Glory* (1989) — a topic film, not about Carney; mention in text only, no Movie line.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="william-harvey-carney" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="susie-king-taylor" name="Susie King Taylor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Susie King Taylor
> **Who:** learned in secret Savannah schools, escaped at 13, and became the first Black teacher to openly teach freedpeople in Georgia — at 14, while the war ran. · **When and where:** born Georgia, August 6, 1848; St. Simons Island 1862; nurse with the 33rd USCT; memoir 1902; died 1912.
Her own memoir documents the whole arc: forbidden learner, then teacher of the freed. Fills the Freedmen's-school teacher slot. No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="susie-king-taylor" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="oluale-kossola" name="Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis)" movie="Descendant (2022)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis)
> **Who:** among the last survivors of the last known slave ship; a founder of Africatown. · **When and where:** born about 1841 in present-day Benin; carried on the *Clotilda* to Mobile about July 8, 1860; freed 1865; interviewed by Zora Neale Hurston in 1927 (*Barracoon*, published 2018); died 1935; the wreck confirmed 2019.
> **Movie:** Descendant (2022)
Lives here per registry ruling 1; `immigration` hands off in one sentence. Finished prose exists at `_reference/manuscript-v1/ch02-migration-MERGED-draft/` to re-angle.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="oluale-kossola" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thornton-copeland" name="Thornton Copeland" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Thornton Copeland
> **Who:** placed an 1865 newspaper ad searching for his mother Betty, from whom he was sold away in 1844. · **When and where:** ad in the *Colored Tennessean* (Nashville), October 1865; he had been sold in Richmond to Samuel Copeland.
Verified in the Last Seen database (item 918). Whether he found her is not recorded — do not invent an ending. The Information-Wanted ad writer, by name.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thornton-copeland" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="revels-bruce" name="Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce
> **Who:** the first Black U.S. senators — Revels first (sworn February 25, 1870), Bruce the first to serve a full term (1875–81). · **When and where:** both Mississippi, during Reconstruction.
No known film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="revels-bruce" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Slavery is gone and a system built to replace it runs at full strength, with the law behind it — while the last people born enslaved put their memories on the record.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Jim Crow as slavery's successor" -->
- Segregation ordered daily life — schools, railroad cars, waiting rooms, water fountains, courtrooms, cemeteries — under *Plessy*'s shelter. This chapter tells the system as slavery's successor; the campaigns against it are `rights-movements`'.
- **Disfranchisement by design:** Mississippi's 1890 constitution wrote the model (poll tax, literacy test, understanding clause); Louisiana 1898 added the grandfather clause. Louisiana's registered Black voters fell from 130,344 in 1896 to 1,342 by 1904.
- **Lynching as terror:** the Equal Justice Initiative documents more than 4,400 racial terror lynchings between 1877 and 1950 — counts differ by period and definition, so name the source with the number. The terror drove the Great Migration (`migration` tells the journey).
- **Forced labor continued:** convict leasing and debt peonage ran deep into the 20th century (Blackmon, *Slavery by Another Name*; PBS film 2012).
- Shared with: `rights-movements` (leads on the fight against Jim Crow) · `migration` (the Great Migration).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the last survivors speak" -->
- The **WPA Federal Writers' Project (1936–38)** interviewed formerly enslaved people across 17 states — more than 2,300 first-person accounts and 500 photographs, held at the Library of Congress as "Born in Slavery."
- Separately, the Library of Congress holds **actual sound recordings** of people born in slavery ("Voices Remembering Slavery," recorded 1932–1975) — among them Fountain Hughes (story below).
- Zora Neale Hurston interviewed Kossola in 1927; *Barracoon* waited until 2018 for publication.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="fountain-hughes" name="Fountain Hughes" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Fountain Hughes
> **Who:** born in slavery near Charlottesville; one of the few people born enslaved whose actual voice survives on tape. · **When and where:** born 1848 by his own account (reference works also give 1854, and some scholars argue later — state the uncertainty); grandson of Wormley Hughes, enslaved head gardener at Monticello; recorded by the Library of Congress in Baltimore, June 11, 1949.
The named narrator for the recorded-voices thread; the recording itself is at LOC. No film.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="fountain-hughes" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The century-long job of making the amendments mean what they say — and the beginning of finding the families.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="emancipation's unfinished business" -->
- *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954, unanimous) overturned *Plessy*'s doctrine in schooling; the **Civil Rights Act (1964)** and **Voting Rights Act (1965)** finally gave the 14th and 15th Amendments enforcement machinery — ninety-nine years after the 13th.
- Mississippi's legislature voted to ratify the 13th Amendment only in **1995** — and the paperwork was never filed; the omission stood for another 18 years (finished in the next era).
- **Keep the frame:** the movement's own story belongs to `rights-movements`; this chapter's angle is the unfinished business of emancipation.
- Shared with: `rights-movements` (leads on the movement) · `government-politics` (the laws as laws) · `education` (Brown as schooling).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="finding the families — Roots" -->
- Alex Haley's *Roots* (1976; Pulitzer special award 1977) and the ABC miniseries (January 1977, watched by an estimated 130 million people) set off a national boom in Black family genealogy.
- **The disputes, told honestly:** Haley settled Harold Courlander's plagiarism suit for 650,000 dollars (1978), and genealogists have challenged links in the family's documentary chain. The book's power and its problems are both part of the record.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alex-haley" name="Alex Haley" movie="Roots (1977)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Alex Haley
> **Who:** traced his family from an enslaved ancestor and set off a national genealogy boom; the record includes a plagiarism settlement and challenged genealogy. · **When and where:** *Roots* published 1976; miniseries January 1977; Courlander settlement 1978; died 1992.
> **Movie:** Roots (1977)
The miniseries dramatizes the family story he traced — an adaptation, not a documentary about Haley; say so in text. Fills the descendant-tracing-a-family-line slot with a documented (and honestly disputed) case.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alex-haley" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="slavery-freedom" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
How the country remembers, argues about, and documents what it did. Current through 2026 — state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="memory built in stone" -->
- The Smithsonian's **National Museum of African American History and Culture opened September 24, 2016**; its history galleries begin with the slave trade and hold a preserved slave cabin. The **International African American Museum opened June 27, 2023**, in Charleston at Gadsden's Wharf, a principal disembarkation site.
- **Juneteenth became a federal holiday June 17, 2021.** Shared with: `holidays` (how the country marks it); ours is what is being remembered.
- Mississippi's 1995 ratification of the 13th Amendment was finally **officially recorded February 7, 2013**, after two residents discovered the paperwork had never been filed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="repair debated" -->
- **H.R. 40** (a reparations study commission, named for the forty acres) has been introduced every Congress since 1989; the House Judiciary Committee advanced it for the first time in 2021.
- **Evanston, Illinois** created the first city-funded reparations program (2019 resolution; first 25,000-dollar housing grants approved 2021 from a 10-million-dollar fund, for victims of the city's 1919–1969 housing discrimination).
- **California's task force** delivered its final report June 29, 2023 — more than 115 recommendations, including a formal apology.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the ledgers and the records opened" -->
- **The GU272:** in 1838 the Maryland Jesuits sold 272 enslaved people to Louisiana plantations, partly to keep Georgetown College solvent — among the best-documented mass sales in U.S. history. Georgetown announced descendant admissions preference and renamings in 2016; more than 8,000 descendants identified; in 2021 the Jesuits and descendant leaders created the Descendants Truth & Reconciliation Foundation with a 100-million-dollar pledge.
- **The records opened:** volunteers indexed about 1.8 million names from the Freedmen's Bureau records (searchable at discoverfreedmen.org) — for millions of Black Americans, the first documents where ancestors appear by name.
- **The *Clotilda* found:** the wreck was confirmed in the Mobile River in 2019; Africatown's descendant community is the subject of *Descendant* (2022).
- **The Freedmen of the Five Tribes:** a 2017 federal ruling (*Cherokee Nation v. Nash*) held the Cherokee Nation to its 1866 treaty — Freedmen descendants are entitled to full tribal citizenship; the nation's supreme court struck "by blood" language in 2021. Shared with: `native-nations` (leads on sovereignty and citizenship politics).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="melisande-short-colomb" name="Mélisande Short-Colomb" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Mélisande Short-Colomb
> **Who:** descendant of the Mahoney and Queen families sold in the 1838 Jesuit sale; enrolled at Georgetown at 63. · **When and where:** New Orleans family; Georgetown class entry 2017; performer of the one-woman show "Here I Am."
A documented life tracing directly to a documented sale — the genealogist/family-historian slot, by name. No film released.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="melisande-short-colomb" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="africatown-descendant" name="(target) an Africatown descendant" movie="Descendant (2022)" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) an Africatown descendant
> **Movie:** Descendant (2022)
Traces a family line to a specific ship and a specific year. Documented descendants appear throughout the film (community figures named in its coverage include Joycelyn Davis and Emmett Lewis — journalism; verify and confirm consent framing before naming one in prose).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="africatown-descendant" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

# Chapter 25: Rights and Movements

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** **MAJOR.** Americans organizing to win rights denied them — women, civil rights, disability, LGBTQ.
**Keep out:** slavery itself (`slavery-freedom`); the laws as laws (`government-politics`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/rights-movements.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-rights-movements.md` · **Reference:** `control/RESTRUCTURE-PLAN.md` §4 (ten-era seed, transcribed below) · `research/research-ch17-prejudice.md` (**the non-slavery half of the old prejudice bank**: the 1790 racial citizenship bar, the Page Act and Chinese Exclusion, Angel Island detention, the 1924 quotas as racial policy, the MS *St. Louis*, Mexican Repatriation, the Great Migration's push and pull, anti-"Okie" hostility, the Radium Girls' court fight, the Ontonagon Boulder repatriation refusal, and credit-denied figures from `exploration` — York, Matthew Henson, Jim Beckwourth, Katherine Johnson).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="rights-movements" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Rights and authority were arranged very differently across hundreds of nations — and in some of them, women held formal political power that no European country gave them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="women's political power in some nations" -->
Haudenosaunee clan mothers choosing and removing chiefs; women's control of fields and stores in some farming nations; the range across nations, so no single "Native" pattern is claimed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="rights-movements" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A thin era for organized rights claims; what exists is individual resistance and the first colonial legal statuses.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="resistance and Spanish legal categories" -->
Native resistance to mission and encomienda rule; Spanish law's categories for Native and African people.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="rights-movements" label="The 1600s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
English law arrives with a rule that erases a married woman's legal existence — and the first person to argue publicly against colonial authority is a woman.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="coverture and religious dissent" -->
Coverture and colonial women's legal status; women's work without legal ownership; religious dissent as an early rights fight; Anne Hutchinson tried and banished, 1638 [VERIFY the date — trial 1637, banishment 1638].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="anne-hutchinson-rights-movements" name="Anne Hutchinson" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Anne Hutchinson
Banished from Massachusetts for preaching her own reading of scripture.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="anne-hutchinson-rights-movements" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="rights-movements" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Rights claims in this era are mostly about worship, and they are made by people the established churches did not want.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="dissent and early antislavery conscience" -->
Dissenting congregations; Quakers, including their early antislavery statements; the beginnings of a public argument about conscience.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="rights-movements" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A revolution built on "all men are created equal" leaves out most of the people who live here, and some of them say so at once.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="who the Revolution left out" -->
Abigail Adams's "remember the ladies" letter, 1776; women's part in boycotts and the war effort; petitions from free Black communities; the first antislavery societies (**the slavery half belongs to `slavery-freedom`**).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="abigail-adams" name="Abigail Adams" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Abigail Adams
Told her husband to "remember the ladies" while the country was being written.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="abigail-adams" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="rights-movements" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Women who organize against slavery and drink learn how to organize for themselves — and the first American movements for disabled people begin.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Seneca Falls and the first disability reforms" -->
Temperance and abolition as women's political training; the Seneca Falls Convention, 1848, and its Declaration of Sentiments; deaf education from 1817 [VERIFY the American School for the Deaf's founding] and the growth of a signing community; Dorothea Dix and asylum reform; married women's property acts beginning.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the schoolroom door" -->
Getting girls into school at all is one of the first organized demands of this era. Female academies and seminaries founded to teach girls the subjects boys were taught [VERIFY named founders, schools, and dates]; the first college in the country to admit women alongside men [VERIFY the college and the year — Oberlin is the name usually given]; the argument used against it, that study would damage a girl's health [VERIFY a real quoted example]; free Black children shut out of the new common schools, and the schools their communities built instead [VERIFY named examples]; a school for Black girls attacked and closed by its own town [VERIFY the teacher's name, the town, and the year — Prudence Crandall is the name usually given]. `education` leads on the schools as schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="stanton-mott" name="Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott
Called the Seneca Falls Convention, 1848.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="stanton-mott" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dorothea-dix" name="Dorothea Dix" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Dorothea Dix
Forced states to see how they treated people with mental illness.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dorothea-dix" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sojourner-truth" name="Sojourner Truth" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Sojourner Truth
Abolitionist and women's-rights speaker; her best-known 1851 speech sits in the next era by the boundary rule — check placement.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sojourner-truth" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="teacher-driven-out" name="(target) a teacher prosecuted for teaching Black or female pupils" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a teacher prosecuted for teaching Black or female pupils
Prosecuted or driven out for teaching pupils the law or the town would not allow [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="teacher-driven-out" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="rights-movements" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The end of slavery splits the movement that fought it, and the campaign for the vote becomes a fifty-year fight.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the suffrage split and Chinese exclusion" -->
The split over the 15th Amendment (which enfranchised Black men and not women); the two rival suffrage organizations and their eventual merger; Western states and territories granting women the vote first (Wyoming, 1869 [VERIFY]); Ida B. Wells's anti-lynching campaign and her data; Chinese Exclusion (1882) and the Page Act (1875) as racial exclusion; the beginnings of Native rights advocacy.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="schools as a rights fight" -->
Women's colleges founded, and state universities opened to women one by one [VERIFY dates]; the first women to earn degrees in medicine and law and the fights to be admitted [VERIFY names and years]; Black parents suing over separate and unequal schools long before *Brown* [VERIFY the earliest cases — a Massachusetts case in the 1840s and a California case over a Chinese American girl in the 1880s are the ones usually named]; parents and nations resisting the taking of children to Indian boarding schools (**`native-nations` leads**).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="susan-b-anthony" name="Susan B. Anthony" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Susan B. Anthony
Campaigned for the vote for fifty years and was arrested for voting.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="susan-b-anthony" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ida-b-wells-rights-movements" name="Ida B. Wells" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Ida B. Wells
Investigated and published the facts of lynching.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ida-b-wells-rights-movements" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sarah-winnemucca-rights-movements" name="Sarah Winnemucca" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Sarah Winnemucca
Early Native rights advocate and author (shared with `native-nations`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sarah-winnemucca-rights-movements" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="parent-who-sued-school-board" name="(target) a parent who sued a school board" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a parent who sued a school board
Sued over separate and unequal schools before *Brown* (documented court record).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="parent-who-sued-school-board" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="rights-movements" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Women win the vote, disabled people are legally sterilized, and 120,000 Japanese Americans are imprisoned without charge — all in the same fifty years.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="suffrage, eugenics, internment, and the Radium Girls" -->
The suffrage endgame — parades, pickets, arrests, force-feeding — and the 19th Amendment, 1920, which in practice left many Black women disfranchised in the South; the eugenics movement and *Buck v. Bell*, 1927, as disability injustice; Japanese American internment from 1942 and the court cases; the 1924 quota laws as racial policy; the Radium Girls' court fight — Grace Fryer and four dying co-workers sued in 1927 and won a settlement in June 1928 ($10,000 each, a $600-a-year pension, and medical costs), and Catherine Wolfe Donohue collapsed while testifying and won her Illinois case in 1938, months before her death; early civil rights litigation.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the long campaign to open the schoolhouse" -->
The NAACP's legal campaign works upward from graduate and professional schools toward the elementary classroom over about twenty years [VERIFY the sequence of cases and their years]; Mexican American families win a school desegregation case in California in the 1940s, before *Brown* [VERIFY the case name and year — *Mendez* is the name usually given]; children with disabilities are simply refused enrolment in this period, lawfully, and parents begin organizing about it [VERIFY what the state laws actually permitted].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alice-paul" name="Alice Paul" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Alice Paul
Picketed the White House for suffrage and was jailed and force-fed.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alice-paul" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="grace-fryer" name="Grace Fryer" movie="Radium Girls (2018)" kind="ordinary" status="candidate" -->
### Grace Fryer
Radium dial painter who sued while dying and won.
> **Movie:** Radium Girls (2018)
<!-- hb-story:end slug="grace-fryer" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="carrie-buck" name="Carrie Buck" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Carrie Buck
Sterilized under the ruling in *Buck v. Bell*, 1927 [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="carrie-buck" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="fred-korematsu" name="Fred Korematsu" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Fred Korematsu
Refused internment, lost in court, and was vindicated decades later.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="fred-korematsu" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="pre-brown-school-family" name="(target) a family in the pre-Brown school cases" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a family in the pre-Brown school cases
Documented by name in the court record.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="pre-brown-school-family" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="rights-movements" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The era when movements changed the country: civil rights, women's rights, disability rights, and gay rights, each with its own campaigns and its own victories.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="four movements at once" -->
The civil rights movement — Montgomery, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, Birmingham, the March on Washington, Selma; the women's movement and the ERA fight; Stonewall, 1969, and gay rights organizing; the disability rights movement — the 504 sit-in of 1977, the Capitol Crawl, and the Americans with Disabilities Act, 1990; the American Indian Movement (shared with `native-nations`); farmworker organizing (shared with `work-workers`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="desegregating the schools — as a campaign" -->
*Brown*, 1954, as the end of a twenty-year legal campaign rather than a single day; what happened next — a state closing its schools rather than integrating them [VERIFY which county and for how long], soldiers escorting nine students into a high school in 1957 [VERIFY the details], a six-year-old walking past a crowd in 1960 [VERIFY], universities desegregated under federal order, and busing fights in Northern cities in the 1970s [VERIFY named cities]. The children and parents who volunteered, and what it cost them. **`education` tells the classroom; this chapter tells the campaign.**
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="girls, Title IX, and disabled children" -->
Title IX, 1972 — the campaign behind it, what it changed in courses, admissions, and school sport, and what it did not change [VERIFY the sponsors and the wording]; the Education for All Handicapped Children Act, 1975, later IDEA, won by parents who had sued to get their children admitted at all [VERIFY the two 1971–72 cases usually named]; deaf students' Gallaudet protest of 1988 [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rosa-parks-mlk" name="Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King Jr." movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King Jr.
The boycott and the movement it started.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rosa-parks-mlk" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="bayard-rustin" name="Bayard Rustin" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Bayard Rustin
Organized the March on Washington as a gay Black man kept in the background.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="bayard-rustin" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="judy-heumann" name="Judy Heumann" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Judy Heumann
Led the 504 sit-in and the campaign that produced the ADA; she was refused a teaching licence and sued [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="judy-heumann" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="fannie-lou-hamer" name="Fannie Lou Hamer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="candidate" -->
### Fannie Lou Hamer
Sharecropper who testified on national television about being beaten for registering to vote.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="fannie-lou-hamer" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="student-who-desegregated-a-school" name="(target) a student who desegregated a school" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a student who desegregated a school
Documented by name; `education` shares this person — agree who leads.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="student-who-desegregated-a-school" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="rights-movements" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
New movements, new tools, and arguments over rights that earlier movements thought were settled.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="new movements and the schools again" -->
Same-sex marriage recognized nationwide in 2015; Black Lives Matter; #MeToo; disability access arguments; trans rights debates; voting-rights fights after *Shelby County v. Holder* (2013) [VERIFY]. Schools are again a main site of argument — how segregated schools are now compared with 1970 [VERIFY the measure and its source year], disabled students' services, English-learner services, trans students and school sport and facilities, and disputes over which books a school library holds. `education` covers what this does inside schools. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="26" slug="health" title="Health, Disease, and Medicine" part="7" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 26: Health, Disease, and Medicine

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** SEED — awaiting deep research · *(agent changes to: RESEARCHED <date>)*
**Angle:** Illness and healing — epidemics, doctors, hospitals, medical advances, **and public health as policy**.
**Keep out:** general science (`science`); sudden calamities (`disasters`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/health.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-health.md` → re-point to `research/research-health.md` · **Reference:** `research/research-health.md` (parked and sourced: radium poisoning and what it did to bone, the "radium jaw," how the dial painters' bodies set later radiation-safety limits; Radithor and Eben Byers's death in 1932, with a caution that the famous "jaw came off" headline is a 1990 retrospective; technetium-99m as the workhorse imaging isotope; Oak Ridge medical radioisotopes) · `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §18 Health.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="health" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Native medicine was a body of practical knowledge — plants, setting bones, wound care, midwifery — and populations here were free of the crowd diseases that had swept Europe and Asia.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Plant medicine and no crowd diseases" -->
Plant medicine and healers; sweat lodges and other treatments; illness and injury that did exist; no smallpox, measles, or influenza.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="health" label="The 1500s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The deadliest event in this land's history is a wave of disease that arrives before most Europeans do.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Great Dying" -->
Smallpox, measles, and influenza spreading ahead of the newcomers along trade routes; the population collapse and how badly the size of it is disputed; whole towns emptied before any European saw them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="health" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonists brought their diseases with them and had almost no medicine to answer them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Colonial epidemics and folk medicine" -->
Smallpox epidemics in the colonies; the Starving Time and malnutrition; folk medicine, midwives, and household remedies; almost no trained doctors.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="colonial-midwife" name="(target) a colonial midwife" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a colonial midwife
Research target — midwives appear in colonial diaries and court records.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="colonial-midwife" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="health" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A public argument over the first real preventive treatment, and an enslaved man is at the center of it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The 1721 smallpox inoculation controversy" -->
The Boston smallpox inoculation controversy, 1721 — Cotton Mather learned the practice from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man, and Zabdiel Boylston tried it against fierce opposition; the first American medical writing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="onesimus" name="Onesimus" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Onesimus
Enslaved man who described inoculation and changed American medicine.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="onesimus" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="zabdiel-boylston" name="Zabdiel Boylston" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Zabdiel Boylston
Boston physician who tried inoculation against fierce opposition in 1721.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="zabdiel-boylston" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="health" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first hospitals and medical schools open, and a city loses a tenth of its people in one summer.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="First hospitals and the 1793 yellow fever" -->
Pennsylvania Hospital [VERIFY 1751]; the first medical school [VERIFY 1765]; the Philadelphia yellow-fever epidemic of 1793 and the Free African Society's members who nursed the sick when others fled.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-rush" name="Benjamin Rush" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Rush
Philadelphia doctor at the center of the 1793 yellow-fever epidemic.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-rush" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jones-and-allen" name="Absalom Jones and Richard Allen" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Absalom Jones and Richard Allen
Organized nursing during the 1793 yellow-fever epidemic (their church work belongs to `religion`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jones-and-allen" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="health" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Cholera arrives in the growing cities, and surgery becomes survivable.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cholera, ether, and the first women doctors" -->
Cholera epidemics of the 1830s and 1840s and what cities did about water; ether anesthesia, 1846; heroic medicine — bleeding and purging — still standard; the first women admitted to medical schools [VERIFY Elizabeth Blackwell, 1849].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elizabeth-blackwell" name="Elizabeth Blackwell" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Elizabeth Blackwell
First woman to earn a medical degree in the United States.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elizabeth-blackwell" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="health" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Doctors learn that germs cause disease, and cities learn that clean water saves more lives than doctors do.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Germ theory, nursing, and sanitation" -->
Germ theory and antiseptic surgery; nursing as a trained profession after the Civil War; the Civil War's field hospitals; public sanitation, water filtration, and milk inspection; medical licensing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="clara-barton-health" name="Clara Barton" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Clara Barton
Battlefield nurse who founded the American Red Cross.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="clara-barton-health" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="civil-war-nurse" name="(target) a Civil War nurse" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Civil War nurse
Kept a diary of what a field hospital was actually like (many did).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="civil-war-nurse" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="health" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The century when infectious disease stops being the main way Americans die — but not before the worst epidemic in the country's history.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The 1918 flu, antibiotics, and Tuskegee" -->
The 1918 influenza pandemic; antibiotics; vitamins and nutrition; X-rays; the growth of hospitals and health insurance; the Tuskegee syphilis study begun in 1932 (**tell it plainly**); radium poisoning and the radiation-safety limits it produced; the FDA and drug regulation [VERIFY 1938].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="1918-flu-nurse-or-survivor" name="(target) a 1918 flu nurse or survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a 1918 flu nurse or survivor
Research target — a documented nurse or survivor of the 1918 influenza pandemic.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="1918-flu-nurse-or-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="tuskegee-study-participant" name="(target) a Tuskegee study participant" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Tuskegee study participant
Denied treatment for decades so doctors could watch a disease (documented by name).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="tuskegee-study-participant" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="health" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Vaccines, transplants, and scans change what medicine can do, and paying for it becomes a permanent political argument.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Polio, Medicare, and AIDS" -->
The polio vaccine, 1955, and the mass trials that tested it; Medicare and Medicaid, 1965 [VERIFY]; heart surgery and cancer treatment; technetium-99m imaging; HIV/AIDS from 1981 and the response to it; the Indian Health Service (**Native continuity past 1900**).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jonas-salk" name="Jonas Salk" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Jonas Salk
Developed the polio vaccine and did not patent it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jonas-salk" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="polio-survivor" name="(target) a polio survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a polio survivor
Lived with a disease a vaccine then ended (many documented accounts exist).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="polio-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="aids-activist-or-patient" name="(target) an AIDS activist or patient" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) an AIDS activist or patient
Research target — a documented AIDS activist or patient from the 1980s–90s response.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aids-activist-or-patient" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="health" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Medicine gets more precise and more expensive at once, and a pandemic tests everything the chapter has described.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Genomic medicine, opioids, and COVID-19" -->
Genomic medicine after the 2003 genome; the opioid crisis; COVID-19 from 2020 — the disease, the vaccines, and the public-health fights; mental health care; rural hospital closures. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="covid-19-nurse-or-patient" name="(target) a COVID-19 nurse or patient" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a COVID-19 nurse or patient
Worked a hospital ward through the pandemic — a documented, on-the-record account.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="covid-19-nurse-or-patient" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="27" slug="disasters" title="Disasters and Rescue" part="7" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 27: Disasters and Rescue

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** SEED — awaiting deep research · *(agent changes to: RESEARCHED <date>)*

**Research bank:** `research/research-disasters.md`
