<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="disasters" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Floods, droughts, earthquakes, and storms are older than any record here, and Native nations carried memory of them and planned around them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Drought and remembered quakes" -->
Drought as a factor in the dispersal of Chaco and Cahokia; flood-aware settlement; oral traditions that record real events, including a Pacific Northwest earthquake and tsunami [VERIFY the 1700 Cascadia event — it falls in the 1700–1750 era by date].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="disasters" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
For newcomers, the first American disasters were at sea and in the first winters.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Wrecked fleets and burned outposts" -->
Hurricanes wrecking Spanish fleets; shipwrecks along the coasts; the destruction of St. Augustine in 1566.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-shipwreck-survivor" name="(target) a 1500s shipwreck survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a 1500s shipwreck survivor
Survivors' accounts exist, including Cabeza de Vaca's.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-shipwreck-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="disasters" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonies were fragile enough that a bad season was a catastrophe.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Starving Time and town fires" -->
The Starving Time at Jamestown, 1609–10; hurricanes; town fires in wooden settlements; early fire regulations (buckets, ladders, chimney rules).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="disasters" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Towns burn, storms come, and communities start organizing the first firefighting on purpose.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Cascadia quake and the first fire companies" -->
Town fires; the 1700 Cascadia earthquake and tsunami, recorded in Native oral history and in Japanese tide records [VERIFY]; volunteer fire companies from 1736 [VERIFY Franklin's Union Fire Company].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-franklin-fire-company-disasters" name="Benjamin Franklin" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Benjamin Franklin
The fire company (the city angle belongs to `city-building`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-franklin-fire-company-disasters" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="disasters" label="1750 to 1800" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Disasters begin to produce organized relief instead of only private charity.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Great Hurricane and fire insurance" -->
The Great Hurricane of 1780 in the Caribbean and its effects [VERIFY the U.S. connection]; early fire insurance companies; city fire companies spreading.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="disasters" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
New machines bring new ways to die suddenly, and the country gets its first federal safety law because of them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="New Madrid and the Steamboat Acts" -->
The New Madrid earthquakes, 1811–12, which rang church bells hundreds of miles away; steamboat boiler explosions and the Steamboat Acts [VERIFY 1838/1852]; city fires; the loss of ships on the Great Lakes.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-steamboat-explosion-survivor" name="(target) a steamboat-explosion survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a steamboat-explosion survivor
Documented in newspapers and inquest records.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-steamboat-explosion-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="disasters" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The worst decades yet for fire and flood — and the country begins to build organizations whose job is to show up afterward.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Peshtigo, Chicago, Johnstown, and the Red Cross" -->
The Peshtigo fire and the Chicago fire, both October 8, 1871 — Peshtigo killed far more people and is far less remembered; the Johnstown Flood, 1889, and the private dam that failed; the founding of the American Red Cross, 1881 [VERIFY]; mine disasters.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="clara-barton-disasters" name="Clara Barton" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Clara Barton
Founded the American Red Cross and ran relief at Johnstown.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="clara-barton-disasters" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-johnstown-survivor" name="(target) a Johnstown survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Johnstown survivor
Lived through a wall of water released by a private dam.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-johnstown-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="disasters" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The half-century of the most famous American disasters, and of the safety rules written in their aftermath.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Galveston, San Francisco, Triangle, and the Hindenburg" -->
**The Galveston hurricane, September 1900** — the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history, and the seawall and grade raising afterward [moved here from 1850–1900; v1 had the era wrong]; the San Francisco earthquake and fire, 1906; the *Titanic*, 1912, and the lifeboat rules that followed; the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, 1911; the Dust Bowl storms; the Hindenburg, 1937; the Texas City explosion, 1947 [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-galveston-survivor" name="(target) a Galveston survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Galveston survivor
Survived the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history (documented accounts exist).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-galveston-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-sf-earthquake-survivor" name="(target) a San Francisco earthquake survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a San Francisco earthquake survivor
Lived through the 1906 quake and the fire after.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-sf-earthquake-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-triangle-shirtwaist-survivor" name="(target) a Triangle Shirtwaist survivor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Triangle Shirtwaist survivor
Escaped a fire behind locked doors.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-triangle-shirtwaist-survivor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Warning systems, building codes, and a federal agency for emergencies — and disasters that are watched live on television.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Warnings, FEMA, and disasters on TV" -->
Hurricanes and the National Hurricane Center; tornado warning systems; the 1964 Alaska earthquake [VERIFY]; Three Mile Island, 1979; the *Challenger*, 1986; the founding of FEMA, 1979 [VERIFY]; Hurricane Andrew, 1992.

Bigger storms, bigger fires, and a hard public argument about who gets rescued and who pays to rebuild.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="9/11 responders, Katrina, and Maria" -->
The September 11 response and its responders' later illnesses; Hurricane Katrina, 2005; Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, 2017 (**territories thread**); western megafires; the pandemic as an emergency-management event. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.

<!-- hb-chapter id="28" slug="drugs-alcohol" title="Drugs and Alcohol" part="7" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 28: Drugs and Alcohol

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** SEED — awaiting deep research · *(agent changes to: RESEARCHED <date>)*
**Angle:** Intoxicants over time — alcohol and Prohibition, tobacco, other drugs, their use and control.
**Keep out:** the law itself (`government-politics`); organized crime (`crime-justice`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/drugs-alcohol.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-drugs-alcohol.md`
**Reference material:** `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §25 Drugs and Alcohol (ten-era seed) · `research/research-health.md` (patent medicines and Radithor as unregulated "cures" — the health effects stay there).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Some plants were used ceremonially and with rules about who used them and when; alcohol was rare or unknown across most of the continent.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ceremonial plant use" -->
Ceremonial tobacco (a different plant use from later smoking for pleasure); other ceremonial plants in specific regions; fermented drinks in the Southwest [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two intoxicants change places: tobacco goes to Europe, and distilled alcohol arrives here.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco out, distilled drink in" -->
Tobacco carried to Europe and becoming a craze there; Spanish wine and brandy in the missions; alcohol used deliberately in trade with Native nations.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Tobacco becomes the first colonial fortune, and everyone drinks — including children — because the water is not trusted.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cash-crop tobacco, rum, and taverns" -->
Tobacco as the Chesapeake's cash crop; cider, beer, and rum; rum distilling in New England and its link to the Atlantic trade; ordinaries and taverns licensed by towns.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-tavern-keeper" name="(target) a tavern keeper" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a tavern keeper
Named in tavern licenses and court records.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-tavern-keeper" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The tavern is the town's meeting hall, courtroom, post office, and newsroom.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rum, taverns, and politics" -->
Rum consumption per person at levels far above today's [VERIFY the figures — commonly cited and worth checking]; taverns as political spaces; drink as part of elections and militia musters.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Whiskey becomes the drink of the backcountry, a form of money — and the cause of the first test of federal taxing power.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Whiskey as money, and the Rebellion" -->
Corn distilled into whiskey because a jug travels and a wagon of corn does not; the whiskey excise and the Whiskey Rebellion, 1794.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-whiskey-rebellion-farmer" name="(target) a Whiskey Rebellion farmer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Whiskey Rebellion farmer
Distilled his corn and refused the tax on it (participants are documented in court records).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-whiskey-rebellion-farmer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Americans drink more than at almost any other time, and the first mass movement against it begins.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Peak drinking and temperance" -->
Consumption peaking in the 1830s [VERIFY]; the temperance movement, pledges, and temperance societies; Maine's statewide ban, 1851 [VERIFY — just outside this era]; drink and the working day.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-temperance-pledge-signer" name="(target) a temperance pledge signer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a temperance pledge signer
A reformed drinker who left a published account.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-temperance-pledge-signer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Anything could go in a bottle and be sold as medicine, and the saloon becomes the target of an organized national campaign.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Patent medicines and the saloon fight" -->
Patent medicines containing opium, morphine, and cocaine, sold without labels; cocaine in early soft drinks [VERIFY]; morphine addiction after the Civil War; the saloon; the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="carry-nation" name="Carry Nation" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Carry Nation
Temperance campaigner who smashed saloon bars with a hatchet [VERIFY the spelling of her name and the dates].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="carry-nation" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-patent-medicine-buyer" name="(target) a patent-medicine buyer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a patent-medicine buyer
Took a "tonic" that turned out to be opium.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-patent-medicine-buyer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The country writes a ban on drink into the Constitution, discovers what that does, and takes it back out thirteen years later.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Labels, Prohibition, and cigarettes" -->
The Pure Food and Drug Act, 1906, forcing labels; the Harrison Narcotics Act, 1914 [VERIFY]; Prohibition, 1920–33 — speakeasies, home stills, bootlegging, and the enforcement that could not keep up; repeal in 1933 and the state-by-state patchwork after it; cigarettes becoming a mass habit, helped by the wars.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-prohibition-agent-or-speakeasy-operator" name="(target) a Prohibition agent or speakeasy operator" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Prohibition agent or speakeasy operator
Worked one side of a law nobody could enforce.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-prohibition-agent-or-speakeasy-operator" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Cigarettes are proved deadly, drugs become a political issue, and the drinking age goes up.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The smoking report, the War on Drugs, and MADD" -->
The 1964 Surgeon General's report on smoking [VERIFY] and the long fight over tobacco advertising and warning labels; marijuana in the 1960s; the War on Drugs from the 1970s; crack cocaine in the 1980s and the sentencing disparity; the drinking age raised to 21 [VERIFY 1984]; Mothers Against Drunk Driving.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-person-in-recovery-late" name="(target) a person in recovery" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->

<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-person-in-recovery-late" -->

### (target) a tobacco company whistleblower
[VERIFY] a documented insider who exposed the industry.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-tobacco-whistleblower" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two directions at once: a legal cannabis industry, and an overdose crisis that kills more Americans than car crashes.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The opioid crisis and legal cannabis" -->
The opioid crisis — prescription painkillers, then heroin, then fentanyl; overdose deaths; treatment and naloxone; cannabis legalization state by state from 2012 [VERIFY]; vaping and teenagers; falling teen drinking and smoking. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="29" slug="religion" title="Religion" part="8" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 29: Religion

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** Faith in America — the many religions, freedom of worship, revivals, congregations.
**Keep out:** religious refugees arriving (`immigration`); religious holidays (`holidays`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/religion.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-religion.md` · **Reference:** `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §20 Religion (ten-era seed, transcribed below) · `research/research-immigration.md` (verified: the 1654 Jewish refugees at New Amsterdam; Puritan, Quaker, Catholic, and Jewish arrivals — the arrival angle stays in `immigration`).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="religion" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Hundreds of nations with their own spiritual traditions — tied to place, season, and community rather than to a book or a building.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="traditions tied to place and season" -->
Ceremonies tied to harvest, hunt, and solstice; sacred places on the land; specialists and societies within nations; the range across nations, so no single "Native religion" is claimed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="religion" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first organized religion newcomers brought here came with soldiers, and conversion was not optional.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the missions and forced conversion" -->
Spanish missions in Florida and New Mexico; forced conversion and the suppression of ceremonies; Native people practicing in secret. Teaching doctrine was the mission's main instrument — the first European schooling in this land was religious instruction, and its purpose was conversion (`education` covers it as schooling).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="mission-convert-or-resister" name="(target) a mission convert or resister" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a mission convert or resister
Mission records name individual converts and resisters; say whose records survive.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="mission-convert-or-resister" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="religion" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Several colonies are founded as religious projects — and most of them do not extend their own freedom to anyone else.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="religious colonies and their limits" -->
Pilgrims and Puritans; Massachusetts's established church and its punishments; Quakers persecuted, then Pennsylvania founded on toleration; Maryland's Catholics and its 1649 Toleration Act [VERIFY]; Roger Williams and Rhode Island; the first Jewish community at New Amsterdam, 1654; the Pueblo Revolt, 1680, as a religious as well as political rising.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="reading for God" -->
New England makes children's schooling a legal duty for a religious reason: so that every child can read scripture. The Massachusetts laws of 1642 and 1647 are church-minded laws, and the 1647 act's stated purpose names Satan as the enemy of a reading public [VERIFY the wording and both dates]. Harvard, 1636, is founded largely to keep a supply of ministers [VERIFY]. The first schoolbooks are religious ones [VERIFY the New England Primer's first printing]. `education` leads on the schools themselves.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="roger-williams" name="Roger Williams" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Roger Williams
Banished from Massachusetts; founded a colony on religious liberty.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="roger-williams" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="anne-hutchinson-religion" name="Anne Hutchinson" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Anne Hutchinson
Preached her own reading of scripture and was banished (shares with `rights-movements`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="anne-hutchinson-religion" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="religion" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A wave of revival preaching sweeps the colonies and creates something new: a religious event that crosses colony lines.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the First Great Awakening" -->
The First Great Awakening; George Whitefield's preaching tours and the crowds; churches splitting into "New Light" and "Old Light"; enslaved people beginning to be converted, and what Christianity became in their hands. The split also builds colleges — several of today's oldest were founded by one side or the other to train its own ministers [VERIFY which, and the dates] (`education` leads on them as colleges).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jonathan-edwards" name="Jonathan Edwards" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Jonathan Edwards
Preacher whose sermons defined the First Great Awakening.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jonathan-edwards" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="george-whitefield" name="George Whitefield" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### George Whitefield
Drew crowds of thousands across the colonies.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="george-whitefield" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="religion" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The new country makes an unusual decision: no national church, and no religious test for office.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="disestablishment and the first Black congregations" -->
Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom, 1786 [VERIFY]; the First Amendment, 1791; disestablishment state by state (Massachusetts last, 1833 [VERIFY]); the first independent Black congregations, including Richard Allen's church in Philadelphia [VERIFY dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="richard-allen" name="Richard Allen" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Richard Allen
Founded an independent Black church and denomination.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="richard-allen" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="absalom-jones" name="Absalom Jones" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Absalom Jones
Led an early independent Black congregation alongside Richard Allen.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="absalom-jones" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="religion" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A second wave of revivals remakes American religion into something enthusiastic, popular, and endlessly dividing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Second Great Awakening" -->
The Second Great Awakening; camp meetings; circuit riders; Methodists and Baptists becoming the largest denominations; new faiths founded here, including the Latter-day Saints; churches splitting north and south over slavery; Shakers and other communal groups; Sunday schools spreading as a way to teach both reading and religion [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Bible in the new public schools" -->
The common schools call themselves nonsectarian and then read the King James Bible and say Protestant prayers. Catholic families object, ask for their own version or for none, and are refused; the argument turns violent in at least one city in the 1840s [VERIFY the city, the year, and what actually happened before writing it]. Out of that refusal comes the decision to build a separate Catholic school system. `education` leads on the schools; this chapter leads on the faith argument.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="charles-grandison-finney" name="Charles Grandison Finney" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Charles Grandison Finney
Revivalist preacher of the Second Great Awakening [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="charles-grandison-finney" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-smith" name="Joseph Smith" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Joseph Smith
Founded a religion in western New York.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-smith" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="religion" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Immigration makes the country far more Catholic and more Jewish, and freedpeople build churches of their own by the thousand.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a second school system, and the Black church" -->
Catholic parishes and the parochial school system built in earnest — an 1884 council instruction that every parish build a school, and nuns and brothers teaching for almost no pay, which is what made a second school system affordable [VERIFY the council, the year, the wording, and the staffing]; synagogues and the growth of American Judaism, with Hebrew schools alongside them [VERIFY]; anti-Catholic and antisemitic hostility, including arguments over public money for church schools [VERIFY]; the Black church after emancipation as the center of community life, and the schools that congregations founded and paid for; the Social Gospel; suppression of Native ceremonies, including the Ghost Dance and the ban on the Sun Dance [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="churches and the boarding schools" -->
Much of the Indian boarding-school system was run by churches under contract or on their own [VERIFY which denominations, and the years of the contract-school arrangement]. This chapter's angle is what the churches said they were doing and what they actually did. `native-nations` leads on the damage; `education` covers them as schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="freedpeoples-minister" name="(target) a freedpeople's minister" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a freedpeople's minister
Built a congregation out of a people just freed (a freedpeople's congregation and its founding minister, documented).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="freedpeoples-minister" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="religion" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
American Protestantism splits over how to read the Bible, and the argument reaches a courtroom in Tennessee.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="fundamentalism, modernism, and Scopes" -->
Fundamentalism and modernism; the Scopes trial, 1925 — a fight over what a public school may teach, told here as the faith argument; state laws against teaching evolution [VERIFY which states and when they were passed and repealed]; Pentecostalism from the Azusa Street revival [VERIFY 1906]; the Great Migration carrying Southern churches north; radio preachers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the right to a church school" -->
The 1925 Supreme Court decision that a state cannot require every child to attend a public school [VERIFY the case name and year] is what secures the parochial and private school; it began as a fight over a state law aimed at Catholic schools [VERIFY the state and the law]. `education` covers the schools, `government-politics` the ruling as law.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="aimee-semple-mcpherson" name="Aimee Semple McPherson" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Aimee Semple McPherson
Pentecostal preacher and radio evangelist [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aimee-semple-mcpherson" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="religion" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A postwar religious boom, then a country that is both more evangelical and more diverse than before.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the postwar boom and a wider faith" -->
Church membership peaking in the 1950s; Billy Graham's crusades; churches at the center of the civil rights movement; the rise of the evangelical political movement; growing Muslim, Hindu, and Buddhist communities after 1965; the American Indian Religious Freedom Act, 1978 (**Native continuity past 1900**).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="prayer leaves the classroom" -->
For most of American history a public-school day opened with a prayer or a Bible reading. In 1962 and 1963 the Supreme Court held that official school prayer and official Bible reading were not allowed [VERIFY both case names and years]. Tell it from the faith side: what families and teachers felt had been taken away, what defenders of the rulings said had been protected, and what schools did instead — released time, a moment of silence, student-led prayer, religion taught *about* rather than practiced [VERIFY each]. `education` leads on what changed in the school day; `government-politics` on the rulings as law.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="objecting to the curriculum" -->
Creation and evolution back in court [VERIFY the 1968 and 1987 cases]; textbook protests, including a county-wide fight in the 1970s [VERIFY where and when]; sex education; the 1972 ruling letting Amish families end schooling early [VERIFY]; religious families as one of the two roots of the modern homeschooling movement, with `home-family` leading on the household side and `education` on the schooling side.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billy-graham" name="Billy Graham" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Billy Graham
Filled stadiums and advised presidents.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billy-graham" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="civil-rights-congregation" name="(target) a congregation that housed a civil rights campaign" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a congregation that housed a civil rights campaign
A church that became a movement base (documented).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="civil-rights-congregation" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="curriculum-objector-parent" name="(target) a parent who objected to or defended a school's teaching" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a parent who objected to or defended a school's teaching
Objected to what a school taught, or defended it, with an on-the-record account (documented).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="curriculum-objector-parent" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="religion" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The fastest-growing religious group in the country is people who claim no religion, while the country's religions themselves become more varied.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the rise of the nones" -->
The rise of the "nones"; declining membership in mainline denominations; growing pluralism; religion in politics; congregations arguing over LGBTQ inclusion; worship online after 2020. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="faith and school now" -->
Public money reaching religious schools through vouchers and tax-credit programs, and the court cases about it [VERIFY the cases, the years, and which states]; a 2022 ruling on a coach praying at a school game [VERIFY the case name]; state laws about religious texts or displays in classrooms [VERIFY which states, and give the source year]; objections to particular books and lessons; parochial school enrollment now compared with its peak [VERIFY]; religious homeschooling's share [VERIFY]. Say plainly where the law is unsettled rather than describing it as settled.

<!-- hb-chapter id="30" slug="education" title="School and Education" part="8" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 30: School and Education

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** SEED — awaiting deep research · *(agent changes to: RESEARCHED <date>)*
**Angle:** How people learned — schools, literacy, public education, colleges, reforms.
**Keep out:** school desegregation as a campaign (`rights-movements`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/education.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-education.md`
**Reference material:** `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §21 School and Education (ten-era seed) · `research/research-ch17-prejudice.md` (school segregation and desegregation as a rights campaign — that half goes to `rights-movements`).
**Director ruling 7 (2026-07-23) — this chapter carries the school-system spine.** Every item below has to land somewhere in this chapter and none may be dropped: the one-room schoolhouse and what a school day was actually like · discipline and punishment · dame schools, Latin grammar schools, and academies · the common-school movement · public vs. private vs. parochial vs. charter vs. magnet · homeschooling · the rise of the high school and compulsory attendance · teaching as a job · curriculum, textbooks, testing, and the school year. The placement of each is marked **[R7]** in the era sections so the researcher can tick them off.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="education" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Children learned by watching, doing, and listening — teaching was a family and community job, not a building. There were no schoolhouses, no grades, no set school year, and no teachers who did only that.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Learning by watching and doing" -->
Stories carrying law, history, and geography; apprenticeship in skills; ceremonies marking stages of learning; memory as the storage system. Learning followed the seasons and the work that had to be done. (Documented individuals are scarce this far back; do not invent one.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="education" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
There were no schools in this land in the sense the rest of this chapter means. The only European schooling was religious instruction attached to Spanish missions, aimed at conversion rather than at learning to read for its own sake. Native teaching went on as before.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mission teaching" -->
Mission teaching of doctrine and Spanish; literacy for a few Native converts [VERIFY who was taught, and what mission records actually show].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-mission-pupil" name="(target) a mission pupil" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a mission pupil
Mission records may name individual pupils; if none can be verified, say so and keep the era short.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-mission-pupil" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="education" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
New England makes schooling a legal duty within a generation of landing — mostly so children can read the Bible. Elsewhere, learning stays a family and apprenticeship matter.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The laws" -->
The Massachusetts school laws of 1642 and 1647 (the "Old Deluder Satan" act); Harvard, 1636; apprenticeship indentures requiring reading instruction; laws in the South that forbade teaching enslaved people (**`slavery-freedom` leads**).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The kinds of school [R7 dame schools and Latin grammar schools]" -->
The dame school: a woman teaching a handful of small children letters in her own kitchen for a small fee, often while doing her own work. The town Latin grammar school for the boys headed to college — Boston Latin [VERIFY founding date] is the standard example. Hornbooks and, later, the New England Primer [VERIFY first printing date and what was in it].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline [R7 discipline]" -->
The schoolmaster's rod as normal equipment; "spare the rod and spoil the child" as a household and schoolroom rule, with its wording traced to a proverb and to Proverbs 13:24 [VERIFY the phrase's actual origin and first printed use — do not assert it without a source].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-schoolmaster-1600s" name="(target) a colonial schoolmaster" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a colonial schoolmaster
Town records name schoolmasters, their pay, and sometimes their contracts.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-schoolmaster-1600s" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="education" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Most learning still happens at home or on the job, and the schools that exist mostly serve boys whose families can pay.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Apprenticeship, tutors, and charity schools" -->
Apprenticeship as the main training system; tutors; charity schools [VERIFY which societies ran them]; women teaching in dame schools; literacy rates varying sharply by colony and by sex [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The academy appears [R7 academies]" -->
The academy appears: a private school between the town school and the college, teaching practical subjects as well as Latin. Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia academy [VERIFY date and what it taught] is the school-history example.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The school day [R7 one-room school day]" -->
Where a school existed it was normally one room, one master, all ages together, no grades, and a term that stopped when the work in the fields started [VERIFY how well documented this is for this early].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-schoolmaster-1700-1750" name="(target) a colonial-era schoolmaster" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a colonial-era schoolmaster
Schoolmasters' contracts and town minutes are the likeliest source.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-schoolmaster-1700-1750" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="education" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A republic decides it needs educated citizens, and starts arguing about who pays.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Educated citizens and who pays" -->
Jefferson's proposals for public schooling in Virginia [VERIFY]; new colleges founded before and after the Revolution; schoolbooks and Noah Webster's speller [VERIFY]; the 1785 Land Ordinance reserving a section of every township for schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Schools for girls" -->
Academies for girls begin to appear after the Revolution [VERIFY named examples and dates] — the first argument that a republic needs educated mothers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching as a job [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Teaching is still mostly a man's job and often a short-term one, taken between other work, with pay and lodging arranged by the town [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="noah-webster" name="Noah Webster" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Noah Webster
Wrote the speller and dictionary that standardized American English.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="noah-webster" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="education" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The common-school movement: free, tax-supported schools open to all white children, taught increasingly by women, in a one-room building most readers have seen a picture of.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The common-school movement [R7 common-school movement, public school]" -->
Horace Mann and the Massachusetts board; the spread of free schools in the North; school taxes and the argument over them; who was left out — enslaved children by law (**`slavery-freedom` leads**), free Black children by custom or into separate schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The one-room school and the school day [R7 one-room schoolhouse]" -->
One room, one teacher, and pupils from about four years old to nearly twenty in the same room. Recitation: a class came to the front and said its lesson aloud while the rest worked. Slates and slate pencils instead of paper. A wood stove in the middle, with the children nearest it too hot and the ones by the door cold. Children walking to school, sometimes miles, and the older ones only attending in winter when there was no farm work. The teacher "boarding round" — living a week or two at a time in each family's house as part of the pay. [VERIFY each of these details against schoolhouse-museum and state-archive sources; they are widely repeated and need real citations.]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline and punishment [R7 discipline]" -->
The switch cut from a tree and the hickory stick kept in the corner; the ruler across the knuckles; the dunce cap and the dunce stool; standing in the corner; punishment recorded in the teacher's book. [VERIFY the dunce cap's origin and how commonly it was actually used, the survival of punishment records, and how much of this picture comes from later storybooks rather than from records.]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching becomes women's work [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Normal schools — schools that trained teachers — begin [VERIFY the first state normal school, its town and year]; Catharine Beecher's campaign to recruit women as teachers; women hired because they could be paid far less than men [VERIFY the pay comparison and its source]; many teachers were teenagers with only a few more years of schooling than their pupils [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Books and curriculum [R7 curriculum and textbooks]" -->
The McGuffey readers [VERIFY]; Webster's speller; reading, writing, arithmetic, spelling bees, and memorized recitation as the whole program; the beginning of deaf education, 1817, and schools for blind students [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A second school system starts [R7 parochial]" -->
Catholic families object to the King James Bible and Protestant prayers in schools that call themselves nonsectarian; the first Catholic parish schools follow [VERIFY dates and the specific disputes — `religion` leads on the faith argument].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="horace-mann" name="Horace Mann" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Horace Mann
Built the case for free public schools paid for by taxes.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="horace-mann" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="catharine-beecher-education" name="Catharine Beecher" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Catharine Beecher
Campaigned to make teaching a job women could take (training women as teachers — shares with `home-family`).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="catharine-beecher-education" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-boarding-round-teacher" name="(target) a boarding-round teacher" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a boarding-round teacher
Lived a week at a time with each pupil's family as part of her pay; wrote a diary while boarding round [VERIFY — several are said to survive; find one that genuinely does].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-boarding-round-teacher" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="education" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Several enormous changes at once: schooling becomes compulsory, colleges open to farmers' children, four million freedpeople demand schools, and Native children are taken from their families to schools built to erase them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The law [R7 compulsory attendance]" -->
Compulsory attendance laws state by state, starting with Massachusetts in 1852 and finishing with the last state in the 1910s [VERIFY both ends]; truant officers; the Morrill Act, 1862, and the land-grant colleges.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Kinds of school [R7 public vs private vs parochial]" -->
Public common schools; private academies turning into private high schools; Catholic parochial school systems built in earnest, including the 1884 council instruction that every parish build a school [VERIFY the council, the year, and the wording]; segregated schools North and South.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Freedmen's schools" -->
**Lead as schools:** the buildings, the teachers who came south, pupils of every age in one room, adults in night classes after work, and the first Black colleges. (`slavery-freedom` leads on what the schools meant to people just freed.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Boarding schools" -->
Carlisle from 1879 [VERIFY], "kill the Indian, save the man," hair cut on arrival, uniforms, English only and punishment for speaking one's own language, the half-day work system [VERIFY its name and how it ran]. **`native-nations` leads;** this chapter covers them as schools — who ran them, what was taught, how the day was organized.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The school day and the rod [R7 discipline]" -->
Recitation, slates, and the stove continue; the switch is still standard; the first serious arguments against school beatings appear, and at least one state bans them in this era [VERIFY which state and what year — New Jersey is the name usually given].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Teaching becomes majority women [VERIFY the share and the year it crossed]; normal schools spread; rules teachers had to live by, including districts that fired women teachers who married [VERIFY how widespread the marriage bar was and when].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The school year [R7 school year and summer break]" -->
Where the long summer break came from — the usual "so children could work the harvest" explanation is disputed by historians, and city schools once ran far more days a year than country schools [VERIFY, and state the disagreement rather than picking a side].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="booker-t-washington" name="Booker T. Washington" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Booker T. Washington
Founded Tuskegee and argued for a particular kind of Black education.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="booker-t-washington" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-freedmens-bureau-teacher" name="(target) a Freedmen's Bureau teacher" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a Freedmen's Bureau teacher
Taught in a school built by people just freed.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-freedmens-bureau-teacher" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="zitkala-sa-education" name="Zitkala-Ša" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="candidate" -->
### Zitkala-Ša
A boarding-school student sent far from home to a school meant to erase their language (documented; the featured slot is "a boarding-school student — to name").
<!-- hb-story:end slug="zitkala-sa-education" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="education" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The high school becomes normal, the one-room school is closed down by the thousand, and a bill for returning soldiers turns college into a mass experience.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The high school [R7 rise of the high school]" -->
High school enrollment rising sharply [VERIFY the figures and the years]; the comprehensive high school with subjects, periods, and a bell; graduating becoming an ordinary thing rather than a rare one.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The one-room school ends [R7 one-room schoolhouse]" -->
Tens of thousands of one-room schools still running in 1900 [VERIFY the count and its source]; consolidation into bigger schools; the school bus as the thing that made consolidation possible; what was gained and what was lost.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Progressive education [R7 curriculum]" -->
John Dewey and learning by doing; the argument over what school is for — citizens, workers, or both; desks bolted to the floor giving way to movable ones [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Testing and textbooks [R7 testing]" -->
Intelligence testing entering schools after the army's wartime tests [VERIFY]; the college entrance test first given in 1926 [VERIFY name and date]; textbook adoption fights, and what the textbooks said about slavery, Native nations, and the West (ties to the `how-we-know` Afterword).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Private and parochial schools get a right to exist [R7 private, parochial]" -->
The 1925 Supreme Court case holding that a state cannot require every child to attend a public school [VERIFY the case name and year — *Pierce v. Society of Sisters* is the name usually given]. `government-politics` carries it as law.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline [R7 discipline]" -->
The paddle in the principal's office; corporal punishment normal, written into school rules, and rarely questioned [VERIFY what district rulebooks of the period actually say].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Normal schools becoming teachers' colleges [VERIFY]; the marriage bar weakening during the Second World War when teachers were short [VERIFY]; pay, and the first teacher organizations.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The G.I. Bill" -->
The G.I. Bill, 1944, and who was and was not able to use it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-dewey" name="John Dewey" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Dewey
Argued that children learn by doing.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-dewey" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-one-room-schoolhouse-teacher" name="(target) a one-room schoolhouse teacher" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a one-room schoolhouse teacher
Taught eight grades in one room, often at eighteen years old (many left memoirs; verify one).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-one-room-schoolhouse-teacher" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-first-in-family-graduate" name="(target) a first-in-the-family high school graduate" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a first-in-the-family high school graduate
Documented account of graduating when few did.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-first-in-family-graduate" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="education" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The courts, the Cold War, and Congress all reach into the classroom — and the number of *kinds* of school multiplies.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The courts" -->
*Brown v. Board of Education*, 1954, and what desegregation looked like in practice, including busing and the first days (**`rights-movements` leads on the campaign**); the rulings that ended official prayer and Bible reading in public schools, 1962 and 1963 [VERIFY the case names and years — *Engel v. Vitale* and *Abington v. Schempp* are the names usually given] (**`religion` leads on the faith argument**); the 1972 ruling on Amish families and compulsory schooling [VERIFY — *Wisconsin v. Yoder*].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline ends, slowly [R7 discipline]" -->
The Supreme Court holds in 1977 that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution [VERIFY the case name and year — *Ingraham v. Wright* is the name usually given], so the ending happens state by state instead: the first state ban in the 1800s, the first modern ban in 1971 [VERIFY the state], and most states following over the next thirty years [VERIFY the sequence]. Say plainly that it did not end everywhere.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Kinds of school [R7 magnet, charter, private]" -->
Magnet schools created from the 1960s and 1970s as a way to desegregate by attracting families rather than assigning them [VERIFY the first one and the year]; private schools founded in the South specifically to avoid desegregation [VERIFY the term used by historians and named examples]; parochial school enrollment peaking and then falling [VERIFY the peak year and figures]; the first charter school law in Minnesota in 1991 and the first charter school opening the following year [VERIFY both dates and the school's name].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homeschooling [R7 homeschooling]" -->
Teaching your own children at home was illegal or effectively illegal in most states into the 1980s, and parents were taken to court over it [VERIFY named prosecutions and the states]; two separate roots for the movement, one secular and one religious [VERIFY the leading figures usually named]; state-by-state legalization finishing in the early 1990s [VERIFY the last state and the year]. (**`home-family` leads on what homeschooling is like as household life.**)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Federal money, testing, and access [R7 curriculum and testing]" -->
The push for science and math after Sputnik [VERIFY the 1958 act's name]; federal school aid and Head Start, 1965 [VERIFY]; Title IX, 1972, in schools (**`rights-movements` leads**); the Education for All Handicapped Children Act, 1975, later IDEA — the point at which children with disabilities had a legal right to a classroom; bilingual education and the 1974 ruling on English-only instruction [VERIFY — *Lau v. Nichols*]; the 1983 report that started the modern standards argument [VERIFY — *A Nation at Risk*]; the higher-education boom and the start of student debt.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Teacher unions and the first large teacher strikes [VERIFY]; teacher pay measured against other jobs that need a degree [VERIFY the comparison and the source].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ruby-bridges" name="Ruby Bridges" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Ruby Bridges
Walked into a school that did not want her [VERIFY the details before writing them].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ruby-bridges" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-special-education-student-or-parent" name="(target) a special-education student or parent" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a special-education student or parent
Got a classroom because a law said they had to have one.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-special-education-student-or-parent" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-homeschooling-family-prosecuted" name="(target) a homeschooling family taken to court" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->

Prosecuted for teaching their own children at home [VERIFY the documented court record].

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="education" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Testing, choice, technology, and cost define school now, and a pandemic sent everyone home to find out what school was for.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Testing and the law [R7 testing]" -->
No Child Left Behind, 2001 [VERIFY], and the testing era; its replacement in 2015 [VERIFY the name]; what a testing week actually looks like for a child.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

Charter schools and the share of pupils in them [VERIFY the current figure and its year]; magnet schools; vouchers and education savings accounts [VERIFY]; parochial and private enrollment now [VERIFY].

Homeschooling's growth, including the jump during and after 2020 and how much of it stayed [VERIFY the figures and the source year]; how states check it, which varies enormously [VERIFY].

One laptop or tablet per child; the school calendar and experiments with changing it [VERIFY]; school start times; the school bus, school lunch, and what a day contains.

Remote schooling in 2020 and what it revealed; teacher shortages and pay; college cost and debt. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.

<!-- hb-chapter id="31" slug="news-communication" title="News and Communication" part="8" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 31: News and Communication

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** How Americans learned what was happening — messengers, the post, the press, radio, TV, the feed.
**Keep out:** the inventions themselves (`technology`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/news-communication.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-news-communication.md` · **Reference:** `control/RESTRUCTURE-PLAN.md` §4 (ten-era seed, transcribed below) · `research/research-technology.md` (the machines themselves stay there). New chapter.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="news-communication" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
News moved on foot, by fire, and along trade routes, and it moved reliably over long distances.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="runners, signal fires, and wampum" -->
Runners carrying messages; signal fires and smoke; wampum belts as record and message; news traveling with traders; council protocol for delivering it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="news-communication" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
For newcomers, news crossed the ocean at the speed of a ship, and could be a year out of date on arrival.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="letters and printed accounts by ship" -->
Letters and reports carried by ship; printed accounts of the Americas published in Europe and read as news.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="news-communication" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The colonies get a post route and their first newspaper — which is shut down after one issue.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first post route and the first newspaper" -->
Letters by ship and by rider; the first colonial post route, 1673 [VERIFY]; *Publick Occurrences*, Boston, 1690, suppressed after a single issue; the first printing press at Cambridge, 1638 (the press as a machine belongs to `technology`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="news-communication" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Newspapers become a normal part of colonial town life, and a jury decides that printing the truth is not a crime.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Boston News-Letter and the Zenger trial" -->
The *Boston News-Letter*, 1704, the first continuously published colonial newspaper; the Zenger trial, 1735, and the argument that truth is a defense against libel; Franklin as printer, newspaper owner, and later postmaster.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-peter-zenger-news-communication" name="John Peter Zenger" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### John Peter Zenger
Printer acquitted of libel for printing the truth.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-peter-zenger-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-franklin-news-communication" name="Benjamin Franklin" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Benjamin Franklin
Printer, newspaper owner, and postmaster.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-franklin-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="news-communication" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Printed words organize a revolution, and the new country writes the post office and a free press into its founding documents.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="pamphlets, the Post Office, and the First Amendment" -->
Committees of Correspondence; pamphlets, including *Common Sense*, 1776; the Post Office written into the Constitution; the First Amendment, 1791; partisan newspapers appearing at once.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-paine" name="Thomas Paine" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Thomas Paine
Wrote the pamphlet that argued a country into existence.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-paine" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="news-communication" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
News gets cheap enough for anyone to buy, and then it gets faster than a horse.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the penny press and the telegraph" -->
The penny press from 1833; the growth of the post; abolitionist papers, including Garrison's *Liberator* and Douglass's *North Star*, 1847 [VERIFY]; the telegraph, 1844, breaking the link between news and travel; foreign-language and Native-language newspapers, including the *Cherokee Phoenix*, 1828 [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederick-douglass-publisher" name="Frederick Douglass" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Frederick Douglass
Published his own newspaper, the *North Star*, after escaping slavery.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederick-douglass-publisher" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elias-boudinot" name="Elias Boudinot" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Elias Boudinot
Editor of the *Cherokee Phoenix* [VERIFY], the first Native-language newspaper.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elias-boudinot" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="news-communication" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
War reporting, wire services, and photographs — plus newspapers that will print nearly anything to sell copies.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the wire, yellow journalism, and investigative reporting" -->
The Associated Press; Civil War correspondents and photographs; the rise of big-city papers and yellow journalism; rural free delivery [VERIFY 1896]; the immigrant-language press; Ida B. Wells's investigative reporting on lynching.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nellie-bly" name="Nellie Bly" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Nellie Bly
Reporter who got herself committed to expose an asylum.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nellie-bly" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ida-b-wells-news-communication" name="Ida B. Wells" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->

Investigated lynching and published the numbers.

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="news-communication" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Reporting becomes a profession that investigates, and a voice in a box reaches every kitchen at once.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the muckrakers and the radio age" -->
The muckrakers, including Ida Tarbell and Upton Sinclair; radio from KDKA, 1920; Roosevelt's fireside chats; the *War of the Worlds* broadcast, 1938; newsreels; wire photographs; television beginning.

<!-- /hb-zoom -->

Murrow and the McCarthy broadcasts; Cronkite; civil rights and Vietnam shown in living rooms; Watergate reporting; the growth of cable and CNN, 1980; talk radio; local newspapers still profitable.
