<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="art" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The oldest art made in this land that still survives was made to be used. Pots held food and water. Baskets carried it. Robes and blankets were worn. Carved and painted objects belonged to ceremonies. Almost none of the makers' names survive, because these nations kept their records in speech, in song, and in the objects themselves rather than in writing. The traditions did not stop: people are working in them today, and those living artists are named and documented.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pottery, weaving, and carving" -->
Regional traditions to name with dates and places [VERIFY each]:
- Ancestral Puebloan black-on-white painted pottery in the Southwest.
- Mississippian shell gorgets and hammered copper plates from Cahokia and Etowah.
- Northwest Coast cedar carving, bentwood boxes, and painted house fronts.
- Southeastern river-cane double-weave basketry.
- Great Lakes and Northeast porcupine-quill embroidery.
- Effigy pipes and carved stone from the Ohio valley.

Say who holds these objects now and how they got them — the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian and the university collections [VERIFY holdings; `how-we-know` leads on the taking].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rock art and earthworks" -->
Petroglyphs pecked into stone and pictographs painted on it, across the Southwest, the Great Basin, and the Columbia Plateau [VERIFY sites and date ranges]. The Ohio and Mississippi valley earthworks are built form as well as engineering [VERIFY; `landmarks` leads on the mounds as places].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-tradition-bearer-artist" name="(target) a named living artist in a continuing tradition" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a named living artist in a continuing tradition
The before-1500 makers are unnamed and stay unnamed. A named, documented artist working today in one of these same traditions — a Pueblo potter, a Cherokee basketmaker, a Tlingit carver — can carry this cell honestly. Find one with a published interview or museum record, and use their own account of what the tradition is. Do not invent a pre-1500 maker.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-tradition-bearer-artist" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="art" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Almost no Europeans lived in this land in the 1500s, so almost no European art was made here. What survives from them is a set of drawings and watercolors made to show people back in Europe what the place and its people looked like, and painted and carved decoration inside the first Spanish mission churches. Native artists went on working. Where Spanish missionaries took hold, they destroyed religious objects and forbade some ceremonies; this outline needs the documented cases, places, and dates rather than a general statement [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="John White's watercolors, 1585" -->
John White sailed with the English expedition to Roanoke in 1585 and painted watercolors of Algonquian towns, people, plants, fish, and birds on the Carolina coast [VERIFY the count, the dates, and where the originals are held]. They were made for English readers and investors deciding whether to pay for a colony, not for the people in them, and the engravings later made from them in Europe changed what the pictures showed [VERIFY what changed].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mission church decoration" -->
Painted and carved decoration in the first Spanish mission churches in Florida and New Mexico, much of it made by Native hands under mission rule. Do not write "workers": the labour system the missions ran on is documented, and this outline needs it named — who was made to work, under what law or requirement, and what happened to those who refused [VERIFY the labour system in the Florida and New Mexico missions, and the earliest surviving examples and their dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-white-roanoke-art" name="John White" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### John White
> **Who:** English painter, and later governor of the Roanoke colony. · **When and where:** the Carolina coast, 1585; England after.

The watercolors are the earliest detailed European pictures of people and places in what is now the United States [VERIFY that claim precisely, and his dates]. `exploration` leads on the Roanoke colony itself.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-white-roanoke-art" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="art" label="The 1600s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial painting in the 1600s was mostly plain portraits of people who could pay for them, and most of those painters' names were never written down. The other body of work that survives is the carved gravestones in New England burying grounds, and most of those carvers are unnamed too.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Limners and gravestone carvers" -->
Traveling painters were called limners. The portrait known as *Mrs. Elizabeth Freake and Baby Mary*, painted in Massachusetts about 1671 to 1674, is by a painter whose name is not known [VERIFY dates and holding museum]. Slate headstones carved with winged skulls and soul effigies; needlework samplers stitched by girls; joined furniture and painted chests.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first books printed and written here" -->
The *Bay Psalm Book* was printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1640, the first book printed in the English colonies [VERIFY]. Anne Bradstreet's *The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America* was published in London in 1650, the first published book of poems by a colonist [VERIFY]. `music` takes the psalm singing itself; `news-communication` takes the printing trade.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="anne-bradstreet" name="Anne Bradstreet" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Anne Bradstreet
> **Who:** Poet in the Massachusetts Bay colony. · **When and where:** Massachusetts, 1630s to 1672 [VERIFY].

Her brother-in-law took the poems to London and had them printed in 1650 [VERIFY whether she knew or consented, which is a documented question, and what the title page actually says].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="anne-bradstreet" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="art" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Painting became a trade. A painter who could get a likeness right made a living from merchants and landowners who wanted their faces on a wall, and the same workshops painted signs, coach doors, and clock faces. Prints made in Europe hung in colonial houses and were copied by painters here.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Portrait painting as a trade" -->
John Smibert arrived in Boston in 1728 and opened a studio and print shop [VERIFY the claim that it was the first]. Gustavus Hesselius in Philadelphia; Robert Feke in Newport; Justus Engelhardt Kuhn in Maryland [VERIFY each]. Find what a portrait cost and who could afford one, in money a reader can compare with a worker's pay [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Prints, signs, and almanacs" -->
Imported engravings; painted trade signs; almanacs bought by households that owned few other books, including *Poor Richard's Almanack* from 1732 [VERIFY]. The printing business itself belongs to `news-communication` and `marketplace`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-smibert" name="John Smibert" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### John Smibert
> **Who:** Scottish-trained painter who settled in Boston. · **When and where:** Boston, from 1728 [VERIFY his dates].

His studio held copies and casts of European work, and later colonial painters came to look at them [VERIFY who came, and what they said].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-smibert" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="henrietta-johnston" name="Henrietta Johnston" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Henrietta Johnston
> **Who:** Pastel portraitist in Charleston, South Carolina. · **When and where:** Charleston, from about 1707 [VERIFY].

Often described as the first woman working as a professional painter in the colonies [VERIFY the claim, her dates, and how many of her portraits survive].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="henrietta-johnston" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="art" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A new country wanted pictures of itself. The men who signed the documents and led the armies sat for portraits, and the painters who made them built careers on it. In the same years the first books by writers living here were printed, including a book of poems by a woman who was still enslaved on the day it was published.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Portraits of the founding" -->
Charles Willson Peale painted George Washington from life more than once [VERIFY how many sittings and how many portraits]. Gilbert Stuart's unfinished 1796 portrait of Washington, called the Athenaeum head, is the face printed on the one-dollar bill [VERIFY]. John Singleton Copley painted Boston merchants before leaving for London; Benjamin West trained a line of American painters in London [VERIFY who]. Patience Wright modeled portraits in wax [VERIFY dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first American books" -->
Phillis Wheatley's *Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral* was published in London in 1773 [VERIFY]. Before it could be printed, a group of Boston men examined her in person, because a book of poems by an enslaved African woman was not believed to be her own work; their signed statement was printed at the front of the book [VERIFY the wording, the number of men, and the date]. Say that plainly. Do not call it an endorsement.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Peale's museum, 1786" -->
Charles Willson Peale opened a museum in Philadelphia in 1786 that hung his portraits alongside mounted animals and, later, a mastodon skeleton he dug up himself [VERIFY dates and the admission price]. `science` leads on the mastodon.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="phillis-wheatley" name="Phillis Wheatley" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Phillis Wheatley
> **Who:** Poet, enslaved in Boston, published in London in 1773. · **When and where:** West Africa to Boston in 1761; London in 1773; died in Boston in 1784 [VERIFY every one of these].

Research targets: her age when she was taken and when the book appeared; who taught her to read and write; the examination by the Boston men; when and how she was freed; how she lived and died after freedom. `slavery-freedom` leads on her enslavement; this chapter leads on the book.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="phillis-wheatley" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="charles-willson-peale" name="Charles Willson Peale" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Charles Willson Peale
> **Who:** Painter of the Revolution's leaders; founder of an early American museum. · **When and where:** Maryland and Philadelphia, 1770s to 1820s [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="charles-willson-peale" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gilbert-stuart" name="Gilbert Stuart" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Gilbert Stuart
> **Who:** Portrait painter; made the Washington likeness Americans still handle every day. · **When and where:** Rhode Island, London, Philadelphia, Boston [VERIFY dates].

Research target: how many copies of the Washington portrait he made and sold, and whether the dollar-bill engraving is taken from the 1796 unfinished head.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gilbert-stuart" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="art" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
American painters found a subject of their own: the land. Large landscape paintings of the Hudson valley, the Catskills, and the western mountains sold to city buyers who would never stand in those places. Photography arrived in 1839, and within about ten years a portrait was something an ordinary family could pay for.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Hudson River School" -->
Thomas Cole painted *The Oxbow* in 1836 [VERIFY]; Asher B. Durand followed him. The paintings mostly show land with no people in it. In the same decades the nations who lived on that land were being removed by federal law, and the two facts belong in the same paragraph [VERIFY; `native-nations` leads on removal, `land-environment` on the parks argument these paintings later fed].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Painters working farm to farm" -->
Traveling painters made portraits for a fixed fee in country towns, and some painted the body in advance and added the face on arrival [VERIFY that practice]. Ammi Phillips and Edward Hicks are documented names [VERIFY dates]. Quilts, weathervanes, painted furniture, and scrimshaw carved by whalers at sea.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Photography arrives, 1839" -->
The daguerreotype was announced in France in 1839 and was being made in American studios within months [VERIFY]. Find what a portrait cost by the 1850s and how many studios were operating [VERIFY]. Frederick Douglass sat for photographs on purpose and often, and is described as the most photographed American of the 1800s [VERIFY the count and who counted].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Writers, and what the record also holds" -->
Washington Irving, James Fenimore Cooper, Edgar Allan Poe, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Ralph Waldo Emerson; the *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass*, 1845 [VERIFY sales]. John James Audubon's *The Birds of America* was issued in parts between 1827 and 1838 [VERIFY]. Audubon also bought and sold enslaved people and wrote against abolition; that is documented and goes in the same passage as the birds [VERIFY the record and cite it].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-cole" name="Thomas Cole" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Thomas Cole
> **Who:** Landscape painter; the Hudson River School formed around his work. · **When and where:** England to Ohio to the Catskills, 1818 to 1848 [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-cole" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederick-douglass-art" name="Frederick Douglass" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Frederick Douglass
> **Who:** Writer and speaker who used photography deliberately. · **When and where:** Maryland, Massachusetts, Rochester, 1838 to 1895 [VERIFY].

This chapter's slice is the writing and the photographs, and his argument that a photograph could not lie about what a Black American looked like the way a drawing could [VERIFY the lecture and its date]. `slavery-freedom` leads on his escape and his life; `news-communication` leads on his newspaper. Do not repeat either.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederick-douglass-art" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="art" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Painting, sculpture, and photography all became careers a person could train for and live on. The Civil War was photographed while it happened, and magazines carried pictures into towns that had no museum.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Painting after the war" -->
Winslow Homer covered the war for a magazine and then painted the sea and country life for forty years [VERIFY]. Thomas Eakins taught in Philadelphia and was dismissed from the Pennsylvania Academy in 1886 over a nude model in a class that included women [VERIFY the year and the account]. Mary Cassatt worked in Paris and showed with the Impressionists [VERIFY]. Henry Ossawa Tanner left for Paris in 1891 and afterward said why he did not stay in America [VERIFY the quotation and its source, and print what he actually said].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Sculpture" -->
Augustus Saint-Gaudens's memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts was unveiled in Boston in 1897 after about fourteen years of work [VERIFY]. Edmonia Lewis, Mississauga Ojibwe and African American, worked in marble in Rome; her *The Death of Cleopatra*, shown in 1876, was lost for roughly a century and is now in the Smithsonian [VERIFY the dates and where it was found].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Photography as evidence" -->
Mathew Brady's name is on the Civil War photographs; most were taken by the men he employed, and several left him over the credit [VERIFY the names and the dispute]. Timothy O'Sullivan photographed the dead at Gettysburg; whether a body was moved for one of those pictures is documented and argued over, so state the argument rather than settling it [VERIFY]. Carleton Watkins and William Henry Jackson photographed the West for surveys and railroads [VERIFY; `land-environment` leads on the parks argument]. Jacob Riis published *How the Other Half Lives* in 1890 [VERIFY; `city-building` leads].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Writers and cheap books" -->
Harriet Beecher Stowe's *Uncle Tom's Cabin*, 1852, and what it sold in its first year [VERIFY the figure and the source]. Mark Twain, Herman Melville, Walt Whitman. Emily Dickinson wrote roughly 1,800 poems and published almost none while she lived; the rest were found after she died in 1886 [VERIFY both numbers]. Dime novels sold by the hundred thousand [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="winslow-homer" name="Winslow Homer" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Winslow Homer
> **Who:** Painter and war illustrator. · **When and where:** Boston, New York, Virginia during the war, then Maine [VERIFY dates].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="winslow-homer" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="edmonia-lewis" name="Edmonia Lewis" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Edmonia Lewis
> **Who:** Sculptor, Mississauga Ojibwe and African American, working in marble in Rome. · **When and where:** New York state, Oberlin College, Boston, Rome, London [VERIFY dates; sources give different birth years — state the range].

Research targets: what was done to her at Oberlin in 1862 and the trial that followed, told plainly and not glossed; how she paid for Rome; the century *The Death of Cleopatra* spent lost and where it turned up.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="edmonia-lewis" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="henry-ossawa-tanner" name="Henry Ossawa Tanner" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Henry Ossawa Tanner

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="art" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Painters stopped agreeing about what a picture was supposed to look like. Photographers argued that a photograph was art. For eight years the federal government paid artists and writers a wage to work. And for about a decade a few streets in Harlem held more Black painters, sculptors, and writers working together than anywhere else in the country.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Armory Show, 1913" -->
A New York exhibition in 1913 showed modern European painting to a large American audience for the first time [VERIFY the attendance figure and the newspaper reaction]. The Ashcan painters, including Robert Henri and George Bellows, painted street life and boxing matches. Alfred Stieglitz ran a gallery and a magazine arguing that photography was art [VERIFY dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Harlem Renaissance" -->
Aaron Douglas's murals; Langston Hughes and the poets; Zora Neale Hurston's novels and folklore collecting; James Van Der Zee's studio portraits of Harlem [VERIFY]. Augusta Savage taught, and the large sculpture she made for the 1939 World's Fair was destroyed after the fair closed because there was no money to cast it in bronze or to store it [VERIFY]. `migration` leads on the Great Migration that brought people north; `rights-movements` on what the work meant politically; `music` on the jazz.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Art paid for by the government, 1935 to 1943" -->
The Works Progress Administration's Federal Art Project put artists on a payroll [VERIFY how many, and the weekly wage in dollars]. The Federal Writers' Project sent interviewers to record more than 2,300 people who had been enslaved [VERIFY the count; `slavery-freedom` leads on the narratives themselves and on the problems with how they were taken]. Post office murals were painted in hundreds of towns and many are still hanging [VERIFY the count].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Depression photographed" -->
Farm Security Administration photographers were paid to photograph rural poverty. Dorothea Lange's 1936 photograph of a mother in a California pea-pickers' camp became the best-known American photograph of the decade. The woman in it was Florence Owens Thompson, Cherokee, and she was not publicly named for about forty years; she said afterward that she received nothing for it and had not wanted it used [VERIFY her words, the dates, and the family's account].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="American modernism and regionalism" -->
Georgia O'Keeffe; Edward Hopper; Grant Wood's *American Gothic*, 1930 [VERIFY]. Jacob Lawrence painted the *Migration Series*, sixty panels, in 1940 and 1941, while in his early twenties [VERIFY his age and the panel count].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Native artists after 1900" -->
Maria Martinez and Julian Martinez at San Ildefonso Pueblo worked out the black-on-black pottery finish and taught it to others in the pueblo [VERIFY the dates and how the money was shared]. The painting studio at the Santa Fe Indian School opened in 1932 and set rules about what students were allowed to paint and in what style [VERIFY those rules — they are the honest part of the story].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="georgia-okeeffe" name="Georgia O'Keeffe" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Georgia O'Keeffe
> **Who:** Painter of flowers, bones, and the New Mexico landscape. · **When and where:** Wisconsin, Texas, New York, Abiquiu, 1887 to 1986 [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="georgia-okeeffe" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dorothea-lange" name="Dorothea Lange" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Dorothea Lange
> **Who:** Photographer employed by the federal government. · **When and where:** California and the West in the 1930s; the Japanese American incarceration camps in 1942 [VERIFY].

Research target: the 1942 photographs she made of the incarceration, which the Army impounded and did not release for decades [VERIFY; check whether `rights-movements` or `migration` leads on the camps before writing them here].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dorothea-lange" -->

Research targets: the 1923 French scholarship withdrawn after the selection committee learned she was Black, and what was said at the time [VERIFY the account and quote the record]; the school she ran and who studied there; the destruction of the 1939 World's Fair sculpture.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="augusta-savage" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="zora-neale-hurston" name="Zora Neale Hurston" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->

> **Who:** Novelist and folklorist. · **When and where:** Florida, Harlem, Haiti, 1891 to 1960 [VERIFY].

She interviewed Kossola, also called Cudjo Lewis, in 1927; `slavery-freedom` leads on that interview. This chapter takes her books and the folklore collecting, and the fact that she died with her books out of print and was buried in an unmarked grave [VERIFY both].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="zora-neale-hurston" -->

> **Who:** Potter at San Ildefonso Pueblo, New Mexico. · **When and where:** San Ildefonso, about 1887 to 1980 [VERIFY her birth year — sources give it differently].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="maria-martinez" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="art" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
After 1945 the buyers, the galleries, and the arguments about painting were in New York rather than Paris. Paintings got very large and stopped showing recognizable things; then they went back to showing soup cans and comic panels. Artists who were kept out of galleries painted on walls instead.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Abstract Expressionism" -->
Jackson Pollock laid canvas on the floor and poured and flung paint onto it [VERIFY when he began and what he called the method]. Lee Krasner, Willem de Kooning, Mark Rothko. Find who first said the center of the art world had moved to New York, and when [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pop Art and the price of a painting" -->
Andy Warhol printed the same image over and over and called his studio a factory [VERIFY dates]. Roy Lichtenstein painted enlarged comic panels. Give real auction figures with dates and the works they were paid for, rather than saying prices rose [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Art made as protest" -->
The Black Arts Movement of the 1960s. The Chicano mural movement, including the murals painted on the bridge pillars at Chicano Park in San Diego from 1970 [VERIFY]. Faith Ringgold's story quilts. Judy Chicago's *The Dinner Party*, 1979, and the argument over it [VERIFY]. The AIDS Memorial Quilt was first shown on the National Mall in October 1987; give the number of panels then and the number now, and say what each panel is [VERIFY both figures]. The 1989 and 1990 fights in Congress over public money for art, and what was actually at issue [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Native and Asian American artists" -->
Fritz Scholder and T. C. Cannon painted Native subjects in ways that were argued about inside Native art circles; state both sides of that argument rather than one [VERIFY]. The Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 made it illegal to sell work as Native-made when it was not [VERIFY the penalties]. Maya Lin won the competition for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in 1981 with an anonymous entry, one of 1,421, and she was twenty-one [VERIFY every number; `landmarks` leads on the memorial as a place and on what was said about her afterward].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Photographs and books" -->
Robert Frank's *The Americans* was published in France in 1958 and in the United States in 1959 [VERIFY]. Gordon Parks photographed for Life magazine [VERIFY his years there]. Ralph Ellison's *Invisible Man*, 1952; James Baldwin; Toni Morrison, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993 [VERIFY]; Maya Angelou.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jackson-pollock" name="Jackson Pollock" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Jackson Pollock
> **Who:** Painter. · **When and where:** Wyoming, New York, Long Island, 1912 to 1956 [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jackson-pollock" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="andy-warhol" name="Andy Warhol" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Andy Warhol
> **Who:** Printmaker and painter; ran a studio called the Factory. · **When and where:** Pittsburgh and New York, 1928 to 1987 [VERIFY].

His films belong to `storytelling-evolution`, not here.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="andy-warhol" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gordon-parks" name="Gordon Parks" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Gordon Parks
> **Who:** Photographer; described as the first Black photographer on the Life magazine staff [VERIFY]. · **When and where:** Kansas, Washington, New York, 1912 to 2006 [VERIFY].

Keep this block on the photographs, including the 1942 Washington portrait he titled *American Gothic* [VERIFY]. His films go to `storytelling-evolution`.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gordon-parks" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="faith-ringgold" name="Faith Ringgold" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Faith Ringgold
> **Who:** Painter and quilt maker; also wrote children's books. · **When and where:** Harlem and New Jersey, 1930 to 2024 [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="faith-ringgold" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="toni-morrison" name="Toni Morrison" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Toni Morrison
> **Who:** Novelist and editor. · **When and where:** Ohio, New York, Princeton, 1931 to 2019 [VERIFY].

Research target: the years she worked as an editor publishing other Black writers before her own novels sold [VERIFY which books she acquired].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="toni-morrison" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="art" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Almost everyone carries a camera. Anyone can put a picture in front of strangers without a gallery. The money for art concentrated in a small number of names and auction rooms anyway, and museums were made to account for how they got what they hold — including Native human remains and funerary objects taken from graves, which a 1990 federal law requires them to give back. This chapter is current through 2026; say the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Who is in the picture" -->
Kehinde Wiley's portrait of Barack Obama and Amy Sherald's portrait of Michelle Obama were unveiled at the National Portrait Gallery in February 2018 [VERIFY the date and how the painters were chosen]. Kara Walker's cut-paper silhouettes of slavery, and the arguments about them among Black artists and critics [VERIFY, and state both sides].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What museums hold, and what goes back" -->
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act passed in 1990. A rule change that took effect in 2024 required museums to consult tribes and led many to cover or remove Native displays [VERIFY the rule, the date, and how many museums closed exhibits]. Confederate monuments were taken down in large numbers after 2015 and again after 2020; give the counts and say who counted them [VERIFY; `how-we-know` leads on the monuments argument].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Digital work, tokens, and machine-made pictures" -->
A digital work by the artist known as Beeple sold at auction in March 2021 for about $69.3 million [VERIFY the exact figure and how it was paid]. Image generators became widely usable from 2022, and artists sued over the use of their work to train them; say where those cases stood at the cutoff rather than predicting an outcome [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Books" -->
Self-publishing and audiobooks changed who could publish and what sold [VERIFY figures]. Challenges to books in school and public libraries rose sharply after 2020. PEN America and the American Library Association both count them and their totals differ because they count different things; give both numbers and say why they differ [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="amy-sherald" name="Amy Sherald" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Amy Sherald
> **Who:** Painter; made the National Portrait Gallery portrait of Michelle Obama. · **When and where:** Georgia, Baltimore, 2018 onward [VERIFY her dates].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="amy-sherald" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="kehinde-wiley" name="Kehinde Wiley" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Kehinde Wiley
> **Who:** Painter; made the National Portrait Gallery portrait of Barack Obama. · **When and where:** Los Angeles, New York, Dakar [VERIFY dates].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="kehinde-wiley" -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="33" slug="music" title="Music" part="9" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 33: Music

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** SEED — awaiting deep research · *(agent changes to: RESEARCHED <date>)*
**Angle:** The music Americans made and listened to — who made it, where it came from, how it was recorded and sold, and who was paid.
**Keep out:** painting, sculpture, photography, and writing (`art` — this chapter was split off from `art-music` by Jon's ruling, 2026-09-06) · film, television, and theater, including movie musicals and Broadway staging (`storytelling-evolution`, being built in parallel; song and score can be named here only where the music itself is the point) · the phonograph, the radio, and the streaming server as machines (`technology`) · records as a retail product and the label business (`marketplace`, `big-business`) · dance as fashion (`styles`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/music.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-music.md` — **does not exist yet.** Nothing in this file is verified. Every story is `target` or `candidate` on purpose.
**Reference material:** `_reference/retired-art-music-2026-09-06/art-music-outline.md` (the seed this was split out of, retired by the director) · `_reference/retired-art-music-2026-09-06/research-art-music.md` (covers both halves).
**Standing instruction for this chapter:** minstrelsy, the music made under slavery, and the record business's treatment of Black artists are all central here and all get told plainly, per Jon's ruling of 2026-09-06. No euphemism, no gist-summary, no leaving the reader to guess what happened.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="music" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Music here was not something a person sat and watched. It belonged to ceremonies, to healing, to games, to work, to war, and to putting children to sleep, and in many nations particular songs belonged to particular families or societies and could not be sung by anyone else. Nobody wrote the music down, and no composers' names survive from before 1500. The traditions continued, and singers and drum groups working in them today are named and documented.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Voices, drums, flutes, and rattles" -->
Instruments to name with places and dates [VERIFY each]: hand drums and large frame drums; water drums; gourd and turtle-shell rattles; notched-stick rasps; cane and wooden flutes, including flutes recovered from dry caves in the Southwest that are more than a thousand years old. Say what is known about the archaeology and what is not.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Songs that belong to someone" -->
In many nations a song was property: it was received, given, or inherited, and singing another person's song without the right was a real offence [VERIFY with a specific documented tradition rather than a general claim]. This matters later in the book, when songs from these traditions were recorded and sold by people who had no right to them [VERIFY the twentieth-century cases and park the strong ones in `native-nations`].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-native-singer-tradition" name="(target) a named living singer or drum group in a continuing tradition" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a named living singer or drum group in a continuing tradition
No pre-1500 musician's name survives, and none will be invented. A named, documented singer, flute maker, or drum group working today in one of these traditions can carry this cell, using their own published account. Look for museum and tribal-archive interviews.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-native-singer-tradition" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="music" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Almost no Europeans lived in this land in the 1500s, so there was almost no European music being made here. What there was came with Spanish soldiers and priests: church singing at the missions in Florida and, at the very end of the century, New Mexico. Native music continued everywhere else.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mission singing" -->
Spanish missionaries taught plainchant and simple polyphony to Native singers and used the singing as part of conversion [VERIFY the earliest documented mission choirs, where, and in what year]. Where missionaries banned Native ceremonies, they were banning the songs with them; find the documented orders and quote them rather than describing them [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="music" label="The 1600s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In the English colonies of the 1600s, most music was singing in church, and most of it was psalms. Many New England meetinghouses had no instruments at all. There were no concerts to buy tickets for and no music printed here except psalm books.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Psalm singing and the Bay Psalm Book, 1640" -->
The *Bay Psalm Book*, printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1640, was the first book printed in the English colonies; it held the words, not the tunes [VERIFY, including which later edition first carried printed music]. Congregations sang by lining out: one person called a line and everyone sang it back, which is how people who could not read music sang together [VERIFY the term and the practice]. That call-and-response habit stayed in American church singing for centuries.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What arrived with enslaved Africans" -->
The first Africans sold into slavery in Virginia arrived in 1619 [VERIFY the number and the ship; `slavery-freedom` leads]. They came from societies with their own instruments, tunings, and ways of singing together, and those did not stop at the dock. What can actually be documented about music in the 1600s colonies, as opposed to inferred from later evidence, is thin — say which is which [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="music" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two kinds of music grew at once. In New England, ministers who thought congregational singing had gone bad started singing schools to teach it, and those schools became the first music lessons most colonists ever had. In the plantation colonies, enslaved people were making music that white owners used at their dances and feared at every other time.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Singing schools" -->
Singing schools spread through New England from the 1720s: an itinerant teacher, a few weeks in a town, shape-note or letter methods, a fee per pupil [VERIFY the earliest documented school and the fee]. They were also one of the few places young men and women could gather in the evening, which is part of why they took hold [VERIFY that this is documented and not folklore].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fiddles, banjos, and dance tunes" -->
Fiddle and dance music at taverns and in houses. The banjo descends from West African gourd-and-skin instruments, brought and rebuilt here by enslaved people; the earliest colonial descriptions of it are documented and should be quoted [VERIFY the sources and dates]. Enslaved musicians were made to play at white weddings and balls, and colonial newspapers advertised runaways by naming them as fiddlers, which is how some of their names survive at all [VERIFY with actual advertisements].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The 1740 South Carolina law against drums" -->
After the Stono Rebellion of 1739, South Carolina passed the Negro Act of 1740, which among other things made it illegal for enslaved people to beat drums, blow horns, or use other loud instruments, on the stated ground that they could be used to signal [VERIFY the wording of the section and quote it]. Say plainly what that law did: it made a kind of music a crime, and the reason given was that the music could carry a message. `slavery-freedom` leads on Stono itself.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-named-enslaved-fiddler" name="(target) an enslaved fiddler named in a colonial newspaper" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) an enslaved fiddler named in a colonial newspaper
Colonial runaway advertisements name individual enslaved people and often say that a man played the fiddle or the French horn. Those advertisements are the record, and the name in one is a real name. Find a specific advertisement, quote it, name the person, and say what the advertisement was for. Do not build a composite and do not invent a name.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-named-enslaved-fiddler" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="music" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first American composers published their own music, and it was mostly written for people who could not read music to sing in a room together. Armies moved to fifes and drums. In the port towns, free and enslaved Black musicians played for a living, and a few of them ran their own schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="William Billings and the singing masters" -->
William Billings, a Boston tanner, published *The New-England Psalm-Singer* in 1770 and several more collections after it, including the tune known as Chester [VERIFY the dates, the printer, and whether he made money from them — the answer to the last one is part of the story]. His music was sung in meetinghouses and by soldiers [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The music of the Revolution" -->
Fifes and drums as the army's signal system, not decoration: specific calls meant specific orders [VERIFY the calls]. Yankee Doodle was sung at the Americans by British troops first [VERIFY the account and its date]. Ballads and broadsides printed on single sheets and sold in the street [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Black musicians in the port towns" -->
Free and enslaved Black musicians played at dances, taverns, and militia musters in Newport, Philadelphia, and Charleston [VERIFY specific documented cases]. In some New England towns, Black communities held their own election-day celebrations with their own music and parades [VERIFY where, when, and what the day was called].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="william-billings" name="William Billings" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### William Billings
> **Who:** Tanner and singing master; among the first Americans to publish his own compositions. · **When and where:** Boston, 1746 to 1800 [VERIFY].

Research targets: how many collections he published and when; whether he died poor, which is commonly said and needs a source; how his tunes travelled without copyright.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="william-billings" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="newport-gardner" name="Newport Gardner" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="candidate" -->
### Newport Gardner
> **Who:** Also known by the name Occramer Marycoo; taken from West Africa as a boy and enslaved in Newport, Rhode Island; became a singing master and composer. · **When and where:** Newport, from about 1760 [VERIFY his dates and the spelling of both names].

Research targets: how he learned music; the lottery winnings said to have bought his freedom and his family's; the singing school he ran and who attended it; his emigration to Africa late in life. Every one of these is commonly repeated and needs a real source before it is written.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="newport-gardner" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="music" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two things happened in these fifty years that shaped everything after. Enslaved people made a body of song — the spirituals, the work songs, the field hollers — that later became the root of most American popular music. And white performers built the country's most popular entertainment out of pretending to be Black people and making them look stupid.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The music made under slavery" -->
Spirituals, work songs, field hollers, and ring shouts. What is documented: the songs themselves, collected and printed from 1867 onward in *Slave Songs of the United States*, and the descriptions written by observers before then [VERIFY]. What is disputed: the claim that particular spirituals carried coded escape directions. Historians disagree about it, and the book states the disagreement rather than choosing [VERIFY who argues what]. Owners banned drums but not singing, and singing was used to set the pace of work and to say things that could not be said plainly [VERIFY specific documented cases]. `slavery-freedom` leads on worship and on survival; this chapter leads on the music as music.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Blackface minstrelsy, from the 1830s" -->
Tell this plainly, at a young reader's level, without softening. White men blacked their faces with burnt cork, put on ragged clothes, and performed as Black characters who were lazy, greedy, stupid, and happy to be enslaved. Audiences paid to laugh at that. Thomas D. Rice's Jump Jim Crow act dates from about 1830, and the Virginia Minstrels put the full show together in 1843 [VERIFY both]. Within a decade it was the most popular stage entertainment in the country, playing in the North far more than the South [VERIFY]. Two facts to carry: the segregation laws later called Jim Crow took that name from a minstrel character [VERIFY the path of the name], and much of the music the shows used was taken from Black musicians who were paid nothing [VERIFY documented cases]. Stephen Foster wrote songs for minstrel shows, including songs still sung today, and the original words of several are racist caricature; say so and say what he changed later [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hymns, shape notes, and camp meetings" -->
Camp-meeting songs of the revivals; shape-note singing books, ending with *The Sacred Harp* in 1844 [VERIFY]. Shape notes let people who could not read standard notation sing four-part music from a book; the tradition is still practiced [VERIFY where]. `religion` leads on the revivals themselves.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Concert halls, brass bands, and singing families" -->
Town brass bands. Touring European performers, and the money Americans paid to hear them [VERIFY figures for the 1850 Jenny Lind tour, which is in the next era]. The Hutchinson Family Singers toured with antislavery songs and were attacked for it [VERIFY specific incidents].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="francis-johnson" name="Francis Johnson" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Francis Johnson
> **Who:** Black bandleader, composer, and bugler in Philadelphia; led one of the best-known bands in the country. · **When and where:** Philadelphia, about 1792 to 1844 [VERIFY].

Research targets: how many pieces he published; the 1837 tour of England and the report that he performed for Queen Victoria; whether his band was attacked by white mobs, which is documented and belongs in plainly [VERIFY each].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="francis-johnson" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="stephen-foster" name="Stephen Foster" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Stephen Foster
> **Who:** Songwriter whose songs were written for and sold to minstrel shows. · **When and where:** Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, New York, 1826 to 1864 [VERIFY].

Research targets: which songs were written for minstrel performance and what their original words were; what he was paid and how he died; the later rewriting of his lyrics and who did the rewriting. Do not present him as separate from minstrelsy, and do not print the original slurs — say what they were.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="stephen-foster" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="music" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Music became something that could be sold as an object. Printed sheet music went into millions of parlors with pianos in them, and by the 1890s a machine could hold a performance and play it back. In the same years, the songs made under slavery went on tour, and the blues and ragtime took shape in the South.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Fisk Jubilee Singers, from 1871" -->
Fisk University in Nashville was nearly out of money, and in 1871 a group of its students, most of them born enslaved, went on tour singing spirituals to raise it [VERIFY the number of singers and the amount raised]. They sang in northern cities and then in Britain, and were refused hotels and meals along the way [VERIFY documented incidents]. Their tour is how most white audiences first heard this music sung straight rather than in a minstrel show.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="War songs and brass bands" -->
Songs both armies sang, and the ones each side wrote about the other [VERIFY]. The Battle Hymn of the Republic, words written by Julia Ward Howe in 1861 and published in 1862, set to a tune already in use [VERIFY the dates and the tune's origin]. Regimental bands; John Philip Sousa led the Marine Band from 1880 and then his own band [VERIFY dates and the marches].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ragtime" -->
Ragtime published as sheet music from the 1890s. Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag was published in 1899 and sold in numbers no piano piece had sold before [VERIFY the sales figure and the royalty arrangement]. Ragtime was played by Black musicians for years before it was printed, and the printing is what made it a national craze [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The blues begins, and nobody wrote it down" -->
Work songs, field hollers, and the songs of Black farm labor in the Mississippi Delta and across the South, in the decades when sharecropping and convict leasing replaced slavery [VERIFY; `slavery-freedom` and `work-workers` lead on those systems]. The blues has no first record and no single inventor; the earliest written descriptions date from around 1900 [VERIFY the earliest documented sighting and who wrote it].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Recording begins" -->
Edison's tin-foil phonograph, 1877; wax cylinders sold commercially from the late 1880s; coin-operated machines in arcades in the 1890s [VERIFY dates; `technology` leads on the machines]. George W. Johnson, a formerly enslaved man, was among the first Black recording artists and recorded the same songs over and over because early cylinders could not be copied [VERIFY the practice and his dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="scott-joplin" name="Scott Joplin" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Scott Joplin
> **Who:** Composer; ragtime's best-known writer. · **When and where:** Texas, Sedalia, St. Louis, New York, about 1868 to 1917 [VERIFY his birth year, which is uncertain — state the uncertainty].

Research targets: the Maple Leaf Rag contract and what he actually earned; the opera *Treemonisha* and why it was not staged in his lifetime; how he died.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="scott-joplin" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ella-sheppard" name="Ella Sheppard" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Ella Sheppard
> **Who:** Born enslaved; pianist, singer, and the musical arranger of the Fisk Jubilee Singers. · **When and where:** Tennessee and on tour, 1851 to 1914 [VERIFY].

Research targets: how she came to Fisk and what she paid to study there; which arrangements are hers; what she wrote about the tours in her own words.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ella-sheppard" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-philip-sousa" name="John Philip Sousa" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### John Philip Sousa
> **Who:** Bandmaster and composer of marches. · **When and where:** Washington, then touring, 1854 to 1932 [VERIFY].

Research target: his 1906 testimony to Congress against recorded music, which he called canned music and said would stop Americans from playing instruments themselves [VERIFY the words and the date — it belongs in the next era].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-philip-sousa" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="music" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
This is the half-century when American music became the music the rest of the world listened to. Jazz, blues, country, and gospel were all recorded for the first time, radio carried them into houses for free, and the people who made the music and the people who owned the records were mostly not the same people.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Jazz comes up the river" -->
New Orleans, then Chicago, New York, and Kansas City, carried north by the Great Migration [VERIFY; `migration` leads on the movement itself]. The first jazz record was made in 1917 by the Original Dixieland Jass Band, five white musicians playing a music Black New Orleans musicians had made; say that plainly [VERIFY the date and the label]. Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings, 1925 to 1928 [VERIFY]. Duke Ellington's band played the Cotton Club in Harlem from 1927; the club hired Black performers and, for most of those years, admitted only white customers [VERIFY the dates and the policy].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The blues on record, 1920" -->
Mamie Smith recorded Crazy Blues in 1920, the first blues record by a Black singer, and it sold enough to prove there was a market [VERIFY the sales figure and the source, which is often repeated loosely]. Record companies then created what they called race records, sold separately to Black buyers [VERIFY the term's use and dates]. Bessie Smith; Ma Rainey; Robert Johnson's 1936 and 1937 sessions [VERIFY]. Find what these artists were actually paid per side and whether they held any rights [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Country music on record, 1927" -->
Ralph Peer recorded the Bristol sessions in Tennessee and Virginia in 1927 and signed the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers within days of each other [VERIFY the dates and the pay]. The Grand Ole Opry began as a Nashville radio show in 1925 [VERIFY its first name]. The songs were often collected from older singers and copyrighted by whoever recorded them [VERIFY documented cases].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Radio, records, and who got paid" -->
Radio put music in the house for free from the 1920s and record sales collapsed in the Depression, then recovered [VERIFY the figures for both]. The 1942 to 1944 recording ban called by the musicians' union, over payment for records played on the air [VERIFY the dates and what was settled]. Song publishers, radio, and the fight between two licensing organizations in 1941 [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Gospel, folk, and songs about what was happening" -->
Thomas A. Dorsey turned blues phrasing toward church music in Chicago in the 1930s and is called the father of gospel [VERIFY the claim's basis]. Woody Guthrie wrote This Land Is Your Land in 1940, including verses about private property and hungry people that are usually left out of the version children are taught; print those verses [VERIFY the manuscript and its date]. Billie Holiday recorded Strange Fruit in 1939, a song about the lynching of Black Americans; her own record company refused it and a small label released it [VERIFY the label and the account]. Say what the song is about in the same sentence as its title.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Marian Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial, 1939" -->
The Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let Marian Anderson sing at Constitution Hall in Washington because she was Black. She sang on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, to a crowd reported at about 75,000, with a national radio audience [VERIFY the crowd figure and the broadcast]. `rights-movements` may also carry this; check the registry and take the music side.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="louis-armstrong" name="Louis Armstrong" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Louis Armstrong
> **Who:** Trumpeter and singer; changed how jazz was played and sung. · **When and where:** New Orleans, Chicago, New York, 1901 to 1971 [VERIFY his birth date, which he himself gave differently].

Research targets: the Waif's Home where he learned cornet; the Hot Five and Hot Seven sessions; his 1957 statement about Little Rock and what it cost him [VERIFY the words and the consequences].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="louis-armstrong" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="bessie-smith" name="Bessie Smith" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Bessie Smith
> **Who:** Blues singer; among the highest-paid Black performers of the 1920s. · **When and where:** Chattanooga and touring, 1894 to 1937 [VERIFY].

Research targets: what she earned and what her records earned for the company; the circumstances of her death in Mississippi in 1937, which have been told in several conflicting versions — state which are documented and which are not.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="bessie-smith" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billie-holiday" name="Billie Holiday" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Billie Holiday
> **Who:** Singer; recorded Strange Fruit in 1939. · **When and where:** Baltimore, New York, 1915 to 1959 [VERIFY].

Research targets: who wrote Strange Fruit and under what name; the refusal by her label and the release by another; the venues that would not let her perform it; the federal drug prosecutions against her and her death under guard in a hospital [VERIFY the record].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billie-holiday" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="maybelle-carter" name="Maybelle Carter" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Maybelle Carter
> **Who:** Guitarist and singer of the Carter Family, recorded at Bristol in 1927. · **When and where:** Virginia and Nashville, 1909 to 1978 [VERIFY].

Research targets: the guitar style named after her and how it worked; where the family's songs came from and who was credited for them; what the Bristol sessions paid.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="maybelle-carter" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="woody-guthrie" name="Woody Guthrie" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Woody Guthrie
> **Who:** Songwriter of the Dust Bowl migration and the Depression. · **When and where:** Oklahoma, Texas, California, New York, 1912 to 1967 [VERIFY].

Research targets: the 1940 manuscript of This Land Is Your Land and its unsung verses; the songs he wrote for federal projects and what he was paid; his years of illness with Huntington's disease. `migration` leads on the Dust Bowl move itself.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="woody-guthrie" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="marian-anderson" name="Marian Anderson" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Marian Anderson
> **Who:** Contralto; sang at the Lincoln Memorial in 1939 after being refused a concert hall. · **When and where:** Philadelphia, Europe, Washington, 1897 to 1993 [VERIFY].

Research targets: the exact refusal and who made it; the crowd and broadcast figures; her 1955 Metropolitan Opera debut and her age at it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="marian-anderson" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="music" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Teenagers with money became the customer the record business worked for. Rock and roll, soul, country, and hip-hop were each built by particular people in particular places, and each one was sold widest by someone other than the people who built it. By the end of the century American music was the largest single share of what the world listened to.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rock and roll, and who got paid for it" -->
Rock and roll came out of rhythm and blues played by Black musicians: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Big Mama Thornton, Sister Rosetta Tharpe [VERIFY each artist's claim and dates]. White artists recorded cover versions of Black records and outsold the originals on national charts; give at least two documented pairs with the sales figures [VERIFY]. Big Mama Thornton recorded Hound Dog in 1952 and Elvis Presley's 1956 version sold far more; find both figures and what each artist was paid [VERIFY]. Sun Records in Memphis; the payola hearings of 1959 and 1960 and what they were actually about [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Motown, soul, and gospel" -->
Motown was founded in Detroit in 1959 with a small loan and became the most successful Black-owned business in the country [VERIFY the loan figure, the founding date, and the claim]. Its house band played on the hits and went uncredited for years [VERIFY]. Ray Charles, Sam Cooke, James Brown, Aretha Franklin — and the church singing all four came out of [VERIFY each]. Sam Cooke owned his own publishing and label, which was rare; find out how rare [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Folk revival and protest songs" -->
The folk revival of the late 1950s and 1960s; Bob Dylan; Joan Baez; the songs sung on marches and in jails during the civil rights movement, and where those songs came from [VERIFY; `rights-movements` leads on the marches]. The 1963 March on Washington performances [VERIFY who sang].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Country from Nashville, and the Bakersfield answer" -->
Hank Williams; Patsy Cline; Johnny Cash and the 1968 Folsom Prison recording [VERIFY]; Loretta Lynn's songs about the lives of working women, several of which radio stations refused to play [VERIFY which and why]; Dolly Parton; the Bakersfield sound as a deliberate reaction against the Nashville studio style [VERIFY]. Country radio's treatment of women artists is measurable and should be given as numbers [VERIFY the studies and their dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hip-hop from the Bronx, 1973 onward" -->
A back-to-school party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx on August 11, 1973, where DJ Kool Herc extended the drum breaks on two copies of the same record, is the event usually named as the start [VERIFY the date and the account, and note that origin stories like this are always partly convention]. Grandmaster Flash and Afrika Bambaataa; Rapper's Delight in 1979 as the first rap record to sell widely [VERIFY]; The Message in 1982 [VERIFY]. In the same years the South Bronx had lost thousands of housing units to fires and disinvestment; the music and the place belong in the same paragraph [VERIFY the figures; `city-building` leads].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Television, cassettes, and compact discs" -->
MTV began on August 1, 1981, and in its first two years played almost no Black artists; the change and who forced it is documented [VERIFY]. Cassettes and home taping; the compact disc from 1982 and 1983 and the reselling of catalogs people already owned [VERIFY dates]. Woodstock in August 1969 and the crowd figure, which is usually given as about 400,000 [VERIFY who counted]. The 1985 Senate hearing on record labeling and what came of it [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dolly-parton" name="Dolly Parton" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Dolly Parton
> **Who:** Singer and songwriter from Tennessee. · **When and where:** Tennessee; died August 25, 2026. · **Sourcing:** one source in hand — nothing below the first paragraph has been checked.

**What the one source actually says.** Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee's 2nd district issued a statement dated Tuesday, August 25, 2026, which opens: "Today, Tennessee lost one of our greatest ambassadors in Dolly Parton." The statement credits her music and her philanthropic work on education access for young Tennesseans. It gives no age, no birth date, no cause of death, and it names no songs, films, or awards. Source: [Statement on the Passing of Dolly Parton, Rep. Tim Burchett](https://burchett.house.gov/media/press-releases/statement-passing-dolly-parton).

**Everything below this line is a research target, not a fact this book has checked.** A research agent sources each item with a date and a citation, or the item comes out. Jon asked for as many of the things she did as can be verified, so the list is long on purpose [VERIFY every line].

- Birth date, birthplace, parents, and the number of children in the family; the Sevier County childhood she described in interviews and in her own songs.
- When she moved to Nashville, her first recording contract, and her first charting record.
- The years on the Porter Wagoner television show, how that partnership began, and how it ended.
- Her songwriting: how many songs she wrote in total, and which of the famous ones she wrote alone — Coat of Many Colors, Jolene, I Will Always Love You, 9 to 5, and others. Give the writing date and the first release date for each.
- Whitney Houston's 1992 recording of I Will Always Love You: the sales, and what Parton received as the writer.
- Her recording career in numbers: albums released, singles charted, number-one country singles, and the years of the first and last.
- Awards and honors: Grammy wins and nominations with years; Country Music Association awards; the Kennedy Center Honors; the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction and her public response to being nominated; the Presidential Medal of Freedom — check carefully whether it was received, offered, or declined, because the record on this is specific.
- Film and television: 9 to 5 (1980) and the theme song she wrote for it; The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas; Steel Magnolias; her television specials and made-for-television films. Verify every title and year before naming it, and route the film-and-television telling to `storytelling-evolution` rather than repeating it here.
- Dollywood: the year it opened, where it is, who owns it, how many people it employs, and what it pays in wages — sourced figures only, no estimates.
- The Dollywood Foundation and the Imagination Library: the year it began, how the book-mailing works, how many books have been sent, how many children are enrolled, and which countries it operates in.
- Her 2020 gift to Vanderbilt University Medical Center and its role in the research behind a COVID-19 vaccine: verify the amount, the date, exactly what the money funded, and how the connection was reported, because this one is widely repeated in a loose form.
- Her giving after the 2016 Gatlinburg wildfires: the fund's name, the monthly payment, the number of families, and the total.
- Her business ownership: her publishing company, her stake in her own catalog, and what she did about the rights to her songs.
- Her literacy and education work in Tennessee beyond the Imagination Library, which is what the Burchett statement actually points at.
- The death itself: date, place, cause, and her age. The Burchett statement gives only the date, and only by implication. Find a primary announcement from the family or estate and at least two major obituaries before writing a single sentence about it.
- Whether a documentary about her exists that could carry a `> **Movie:**` line. Do not name one until it is verified; the `movie` attribute on this block stays empty until then.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dolly-parton" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elvis-presley" name="Elvis Presley" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Elvis Presley
> **Who:** Singer; the biggest-selling performer of rock and roll's first decade. · **When and where:** Tupelo, Memphis, 1935 to 1977 [VERIFY].

Research targets: the Sun sessions and what he recorded first; the Black artists and gospel singers whose records and styles he took from, named individually [VERIFY]; his manager's contract terms; the sales figures, sourced.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elvis-presley" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="aretha-franklin" name="Aretha Franklin" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Aretha Franklin
> **Who:** Singer and pianist; recorded Respect in 1967. · **When and where:** Memphis, Detroit, Muscle Shoals, New York, 1942 to 2018 [VERIFY].

Research targets: her father's Detroit church and what she recorded there as a teenager; the 1967 Muscle Shoals session; what Respect changed from the Otis Redding original and why that mattered; the 1972 gospel album and the film of it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aretha-franklin" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="bob-dylan" name="Bob Dylan" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Bob Dylan
> **Who:** Songwriter of the folk revival and after; Nobel Prize in Literature, 2016 [VERIFY]. · **When and where:** Minnesota, New York, 1941 onward [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="bob-dylan" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dj-kool-herc" name="DJ Kool Herc" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### DJ Kool Herc
> **Who:** Born Clive Campbell in Jamaica; the DJ at the 1973 Bronx party usually named as hip-hop's start. · **When and where:** Kingston to the Bronx, 1967 onward [VERIFY his dates].

Research targets: what he actually did with the two turntables and why it mattered; his sister Cindy Campbell's part in organizing the party, which is documented and often left out; what he earned from hip-hop afterward.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dj-kool-herc" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="selena-quintanilla" name="Selena Quintanilla" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Selena Quintanilla
> **Who:** Tejano singer; the best-selling Latin artist of the 1990s [VERIFY the claim]. · **When and where:** Texas, 1971 to 1995 [VERIFY].

Research targets: the Texas Tejano circuit she grew up playing; her sales figures; her murder in 1995 by the manager of her fan club, stated plainly with the court record; the album released after her death and what it sold.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="selena-quintanilla" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="music" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In about twenty-five years, music went from something people bought one album at a time to something almost nobody buys at all. Recorded music now arrives through subscriptions, and most musicians earn their living from playing live instead. Hip-hop became the most-listened-to kind of music in the country. This chapter is current through 2026; say the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="File sharing, downloads, and streaming" -->
Napster opened in 1999 and was shut down by court order in 2001 [VERIFY dates]. The iPod arrived in 2001 and the iTunes Store in 2003, selling songs one at a time [VERIFY]. Spotify launched in the United States in 2011 [VERIFY]. Recorded-music revenue fell for about fifteen years and then rose again; give the figures and the years, from the industry's own annual reports [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What a stream pays" -->
Per-stream payments are fractions of a cent and are paid to rights holders, not directly to performers; explain the difference plainly with real numbers and say who publishes them [VERIFY]. Touring and merchandise became the main income for most working musicians [VERIFY with a survey, not an assertion]. Taylor Swift re-recorded her early albums between 2021 and 2023 after her master recordings were sold without her; say what a master recording is [VERIFY the dates and the sale].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hip-hop, country, and Latin music at the top" -->
Hip-hop and R&B passed rock as the most-consumed music in the United States in 2017, by the tracking company's count [VERIFY the company and the measure]. Kendrick Lamar won the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 2018, the first winner from outside classical and jazz [VERIFY]. Latin music's share of American listening rose through the 2010s and 2020s [VERIFY figures]. Country crossed over repeatedly, and the fights over who counts as country are documented and specific [VERIFY at least one case with dates].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dolly Parton's death, 2026" -->
Dolly Parton died on August 25, 2026. On that day Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee issued a statement crediting her music and her work on education access for young Tennesseans: [Statement on the Passing of Dolly Parton](https://burchett.house.gov/media/press-releases/statement-passing-dolly-parton). That statement is the only source this book holds so far. Her career is seeded in the 1950 to 2000 section, and everything in it still needs sourcing before a word of it is written [VERIFY].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Machines that make music" -->
Auto-tune moved from a correction tool to an instrument; find when and who first used it that way [VERIFY]. Music generated by software trained on existing recordings became usable from about 2023, and musicians and labels went to court over the training; say where those cases stood at the cutoff rather than predicting [VERIFY]. The 2008 fire at a Universal Music storage vault destroyed master recordings; the scale was only reported publicly in 2019 and the number destroyed is disputed [VERIFY and state the dispute].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="taylor-swift" name="Taylor Swift" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Taylor Swift
> **Who:** Songwriter and performer; re-recorded her own catalog to own it. · **When and where:** Pennsylvania, Nashville, 1989 onward [VERIFY].

Research targets: the sale of her master recordings and the terms; the re-recording project's dates and sales; the 2023 and 2024 tour's reported gross, from a sourced figure.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="taylor-swift" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="kendrick-lamar" name="Kendrick Lamar" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Kendrick Lamar
> **Who:** Rapper; won the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 2018 [VERIFY]. · **When and where:** Compton, California, 1987 onward [VERIFY].
<!-- hb-story:end slug="kendrick-lamar" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="target-working-musician" name="(target) a working musician in the streaming era" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a working musician in the streaming era
A musician who is not famous and who has published their own figures — streaming payouts, tour costs, what a night's work pays. Interviews, union surveys, and testimony to Congress are all real sources. Use their numbers, name them, and do not average several people into one.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="target-working-musician" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->
