If the account turns out to be documented but unnamed, it belongs in the era prose, not in a story block.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="child-play-oral-history-1900s" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="sports-play" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Television turns sport into an industry, and athletes start using their platform. Television also becomes what a family does in the evening, and by the end of the century children are playing games on screens at home as well as outdoors.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="TV money, Title IX, and protest" -->
Television money and the growth of leagues; Muhammad Ali; the Super Bowl from January 1967 [VERIFY — the name came later]; Title IX, 1972, and the growth of girls' and women's sports; the 1968 Olympic protest [VERIFY]; the Miracle on Ice, 1980; free agency and player unions; youth sports becoming organized and expensive.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what a child's afternoon looked like" -->
Research targets, each to be given with its survey, its year, and its number:
- The share of children who walked or biked to school, measured from 1969 onward [VERIFY the National Personal Transportation Survey figures and the later National Household Travel Survey figures]
- Hours of unsupervised outdoor play in time-diary studies, and how the figure changed across these decades [VERIFY the study names and years]
- Suburban yards, streets, sandlots, and vacant ground as the places children played [VERIFY with named accounts]
- Children at home alone after school as more mothers worked for pay [VERIFY the labor-force numbers and the years]
- Where Black children could and could not play as parks and pools desegregated, and how long each took [VERIFY named cities and dates]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="arcades and home consoles" -->
Research targets, dates to verify for every item:
- Pong in arcades, 1972, and the arcade games that followed, including Space Invaders, 1978, and Pac-Man, 1980 [VERIFY]
- Home consoles: the Atari 2600, 1977; the Nintendo Entertainment System in the United States, 1985; the Game Boy, 1989 [VERIFY each date]
- The 1983 collapse of the American video-game business, and what came after it [VERIFY]
- The Oregon Trail, 1971, played in classrooms [VERIFY; also seeded in `migration` — the director decides which chapter leads]
- What a game cost in quarters and in dollars, and how long a child could play for that [VERIFY]
- The 1993 congressional hearings on violent games and the ratings board set up the following year [VERIFY the dates and the body's name]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="youth sport turns into a schedule" -->
Research targets: when travel teams, year-round seasons, and single-sport specialization spread, and on what evidence [VERIFY]; participation numbers by sport and year [VERIFY]; what a season cost a family, and how that differed by income [VERIFY]. `education` leads on school sport as part of schooling; this chapter keeps the family's calendar and the bill.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="muhammad-ali" name="Muhammad Ali" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Muhammad Ali
Heavyweight champion who refused the draft and lost years of his career.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="muhammad-ali" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billie-jean-king" name="Billie Jean King" movie="" kind="famous" status="candidate" -->
### Billie Jean King
Won the "Battle of the Sexes" and fought for equal prize money.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billie-jean-king" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="title-ix-athlete" name="(target) a Title IX athlete" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->

<!-- hb-story:end slug="title-ix-athlete" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="postwar-child-outdoor-play" name="(target) a child of these decades whose play is documented by name" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a child of these decades whose play is documented by name
Oral-history collections and named interviews carry people describing their own childhood afternoons: where they went, with whom, and until when. Use a named account; unnamed material goes in the era prose.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="postwar-child-outdoor-play" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="sports-play" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Sports are worth billions, and the biggest arguments are about safety, fairness, and money. Most American teenagers now carry a phone, much of what children play is online and with people they never meet, and organized youth sport costs money to join. How much that change matters, and to what, is something researchers are still measuring and still arguing about.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="concussions, pay, and betting" -->
Concussion science and what it changed about football; women's sports growth and the pay fight; athlete protest; esports; legal sports betting after 2018 [VERIFY]; college athletes paid for their names. Current through 2026; state the cutoff.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="phones, consoles, and games played with strangers" -->
Research targets, dates and figures to verify for every item:
- Smartphone ownership among American teenagers, by year [VERIFY Pew Research Center teen surveys]
- The games most children play, and when each arrived: Minecraft, 2011; Fortnite, 2017; Roblox [VERIFY release dates and player counts]
- Playing with people you have never met: voice chat, matchmaking, and who a child is actually playing with [VERIFY]
- Esports as paid competition: prize money, teams, and the ages of the players [VERIFY]
- What money buys inside a game that is free to start, and how much children spend [VERIFY]
- Boundaries: `technology` leads on the devices, `storytelling-evolution` on games as acted story, `marketplace` on what is sold inside them. This chapter keeps the hours and what children do with them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what is measured" -->
The move from outdoors to screens is measured, and the book gives the measurements with their sources rather than an impression. Research targets:
- Daily screen use for 8- to 12-year-olds and for 13- to 18-year-olds, with the survey and the year [VERIFY Common Sense Media census reports]
- Time spent outdoors and in unstructured play, with the study named [VERIFY]
- The share of children walking or biking to school in 1969 against the most recent figure, taken from the same survey family [VERIFY National Household Travel Survey and Safe Routes to School reporting]
- Youth sport participation by age, sex, and family income, and the share of children who play no sport at all [VERIFY Aspen Institute Project Play State of Play reports; Sports and Fitness Industry Association data]
- What a year of one child's organized sport costs, and the participation gap between higher- and lower-income families [VERIFY the figures and the years]
- Minutes of recess in schools, and how many states require any [VERIFY]
- Physical-activity and childhood-obesity measurements over the same span [VERIFY CDC and National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data; `health` leads on obesity as health, this chapter cites it only as one measure of how children spend their time]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what researchers disagree about" -->
This is a contested research area and the chapter treats it as one. Research targets:
- ADHD diagnoses among American children over time [VERIFY CDC and National Survey of Children's Health figures and years], reported alongside how diagnosis criteria and screening changed over the same period [VERIFY]
- Studies of screen use and attention, sleep, and mood: name each study, say what it measured, how many children it followed, and how large the reported effect was [VERIFY]
- Name the researchers on each side from their own published work rather than from summaries of it, and give the disagreement in their own terms [VERIFY every position before attributing it]
- Handling rule for the writer: the book states what the studies measured and where researchers disagree. It does not state, and does not imply by arrangement, that screens cause ADHD.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="holidays" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Nations here kept calendars of their own, marked by the sun, the seasons, and the harvest.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ceremonies of the seasons" -->
Green Corn ceremonies; solstice observances and the buildings aligned to them; first-salmon and first-fruits ceremonies; midwinter ceremonies; ceremonies as obligations rather than days off.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="continuing-ceremony-keeper" name="(target) a keeper of a continuing ceremony" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) a keeper of a continuing ceremony
Research target — many of these ceremonies continue and are documented today.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="continuing-ceremony-keeper" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="holidays" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first European holy days observed here came with missions and soldiers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Saints' days in the missions" -->
Saints' days and feast days in Spanish Florida and New Mexico; Native ceremonies suppressed or absorbed into the church calendar.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="holidays" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
New England's colonists cancel Christmas; the harvest feast that later became Thanksgiving happens once and is not a holiday for two centuries.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The 1621 harvest and the Christmas ban" -->
The 1621 harvest gathering at Plymouth with about 90 Wampanoag men present [VERIFY the numbers]; the Massachusetts ban on celebrating Christmas [VERIFY 1659]; days of thanksgiving and days of fasting proclaimed for specific events; Dutch and Anglican colonies celebrating differently. (Note: the schoolbook "first Thanksgiving" story is a later construction — the Afterword `how-we-know` handles the myth; this chapter states the documented facts.)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="holidays" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="seed" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial celebration is mostly local, political, or military — and sometimes anti-Catholic.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pope's Day and muster days" -->
Pope's Day, November 5, with effigies and street processions; militia muster days; the king's birthday; election days as festivals.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="holidays" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A new country invents its own holiday within a year of declaring independence.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first Fourth of July" -->
The first Fourth of July celebration, 1777 [VERIFY]; Washington's Birthday observed; days of national thanksgiving proclaimed by presidents; no fixed national holiday calendar yet.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="early-fourth-of-july-organizer" name="(target) an early Fourth of July organizer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="target" -->
### (target) an early Fourth of July organizer
Research target — newspaper accounts of early Fourth of July celebrations name organizers.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="early-fourth-of-july-organizer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="holidays" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Christmas softens from a rowdy street holiday into a family day, and Thanksgiving spreads state by state.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Christmas domesticated, Thanksgiving spreading" -->
Christmas becoming domestic — trees, cards, and Clement Moore's poem [VERIFY 1823]; state-by-state Thanksgiving proclamations; the Fourth of July as a political stage, including Frederick Douglass's 1852 speech asking what it meant to the enslaved [VERIFY — that date falls in the next era].
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sarah-josepha-hale" name="Sarah Josepha Hale" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sarah Josepha Hale
Magazine editor who campaigned for decades until Thanksgiving became national.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sarah-josepha-hale" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="holidays" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="seed" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The country builds a national holiday calendar out of a war, a strike, and a magazine campaign.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Thanksgiving, Memorial Day, and Labor Day" -->
